Ista præsenti capitulo recitatur, viditque eam Nabuchodonosor secundo regni sui anno, non computando a sui regni inchoatione : præsertim quum Daniel et ceteri pueri a rege hoc capti, ad eum ingressi sunt tribus annis expletis a tempore quo in palatium regis fuerunt inducti ; et ex præcedentis capituli elucidatione jam patuit, quod quartus annus regni Joakim regis, fuit primus annus regni Nabuchodonosor, qui cepit Joakim regem undecimo regni sui anno, qui fuit septimus annus Nabuchodonosor regis : quibus si addantur tres anni, quibus pueri præfati instruebantur, decem anni habentur ; nec certum videtur, quam cito post hos vidit hoc somnium. Itaque annus iste secundus computatur ex eo tempore, quo regnum suum fuit dilatatum, ita quod omnibus pene gentibus non nimis distantibus imperavit, scilicet Assyriis, Moabitis, Ammonitis, Judæis, Idumæis, Ægyptiis : et ita exponunt Hieronymus, Albertus, Scholastica historia, ceterique communiter. Nam et Josephus decimo Antiquitatum libro, Post secundum, inquit, […] magnitudinem ejus, juxta illud Job : In horrore visionis nocturnæ, quando solet sopor occupare homines, pavor tenuit me et tremor, et omnia ossa mea perterrita sunt ; et rursus, Terrebis me per somnia, et per visiones horrore concuties. Albertus hoc loco per spiritum, intelligit spiritum corporalem qui est rector formarum, estque vel corpus subtile, vel humor subtilis : qui quando in terrore confunditur, delentur formæ quæ in eo sunt, quibus deletis, somnium cadit in oblivionem. Verumtamen huic spiritui non proprie competit terror.
paras.en: [[2:1|In the second year of the reign of Nabuchodonosor, Nabuchodonosor had a dream|In anno secundo regni Nabuchodonosor, vidit Nabuchodonosor somnium]]. As is known from what was said before, this book of Daniel contains ten visions, in which he either saw something himself or explained what others had seen. The first is of the great statue which the stone cut out of the mountain without hands broke in pieces and crushed. This is related in the present chapter, and Nabuchodonosor saw it in the second year of his reign, not counting from the beginning of his reign: above all since Daniel and the other youths taken by this king went in to him when three years were completed from the time they were brought into the king's palace; and from the explanation of the preceding chapter it is already clear that the fourth year of the reign of King Joakim was the first year of the reign of Nabuchodonosor, who took King Joakim in the eleventh year of his reign, which was the seventh year of King Nabuchodonosor: if to these are added the three years in which the aforesaid youths were being instructed, we have ten years; nor does it seem certain how soon after these he saw this dream. So this second year is counted from the time when his kingdom was enlarged, so that he ruled over nearly all the nations not too far distant, namely the Assyrians, Moabites, Ammonites, Jews, Idumeans and Egyptians: and so Jerome, Albert, the Scholastic History and the others commonly explain it. For Josephus too, in the tenth book of the Antiquities, says: After the second […] [the text is lost here, at the foot of p. 16 of the printed volume; it resumes in mid-sentence] its greatness, according to that of Job: [[Job 4:13|In the horror of a vision by night, when deep sleep is wont to hold men|In horrore visionis nocturnæ, quando solet sopor occupare homines]], [[Job 4:14|Fear seized upon me, and trembling, and all my bones were affrighted|pavor tenuit me et tremor, et omnia ossa mea perterrita sunt]]; and again, [[Job 7:14|Thou wilt frighten me with dreams, and terrify me with visions.|Terrebis me per somnia, et per visiones horrore concuties]] Albert takes spirit in this place to mean the bodily spirit which governs the forms [that is, the images held in the imagination], and is either a subtle body or a subtle humour: when this is thrown into confusion by terror, the forms that are in it are wiped out, and once they are wiped out the dream falls into oblivion. Yet terror does not properly belong to this spirit.

paras.t: Et somnium ejus fugit ab eo, id est, per oblivionem recessit. Oblivio quippe causatur ex magna motione humorum : propter quod pueri et multum antiqui, solent esse malæ memoriæ, sicut in libro de Memoria et reminiscentia scribit Philosophus. Terror autem efficit grandem humorum commotionem, idcirco induxit somnii oblivionem. Quod tamen factum est ordinatione divina, ut hujus oblivionis occasione Daniel vocaretur, somniumque interpretaretur ad Dei gloriam, et populi Judæorum relevationem per somnii expositionem.
paras.en: [[2:1|and his dream went out of his mind|Et somnium ejus fugit ab eo]], that is, it departed through forgetfulness. For forgetfulness is caused by a great movement of the humours: which is why children and the very old usually have poor memories, as the Philosopher writes in the book On Memory and Recollection. Now terror produces a great stirring of the humours, and so it brought on the forgetting of the dream. Yet this was done by divine ordinance, so that on the occasion of this forgetting Daniel might be called and interpret the dream, to the glory of God and the relief of the Jewish people through the explanation of the dream.

paras.t: Præcepit ergo rex, ut convocarentur arioli et magi. De significatione ac distinctione ariolorum et magorum, circa finem præcedentis capituli dictum est. Præterea, secundum Hieronymum, pro ariolis alii transtulerunt, Incantatores, quia arioli animalia interfecta cum carminibus sacrificant. Et malefici. Secundum Hieronymum et Glossam, malefici sunt, qui sanguine utuntur et victimis, et sæpe contingunt corpora mortuorum : qui, secundum Albertum, proprie dicti sunt necromantici, a νεκρός, quod est mortuus, quia in mortuis divinant. Hoc tamen secundum prædicta ad ariolos quasi pertinere videtur : idcirco maleficos aliqui dicunt eos, qui avertunt sensus humanos per aliquod dictum vel factum circa eos, sicque aversis seu alienatis sensibus, aliqua eis occulta a dæmonibus revelantur.
paras.en: [[2:2|Then the king commanded to call together the diviners and the wise men|Præcepit ergo rex, ut convocarentur arioli et magi]]. Of the meaning of diviners and wise men [Latin arioli and magi], and the difference between them, we spoke near the end of the preceding chapter[[Dan 1:20||]]. Further, according to Jerome, others translated diviners as Enchanters, because diviners sacrifice slain animals with incantations. [[2:2|and the magicians|Et malefici]] [Latin malefici, literally evil-doers, that is, sorcerers]. According to Jerome and the Gloss, the malefici are those who use blood and victims and often touch the bodies of the dead: who, according to Albert, are properly called necromancers, from νεκρός, which means dead, because they divine among the dead. Yet by what was said before this seems rather to belong to the diviners: and so some say the malefici are those who turn aside men's senses by some word or deed done about them, and so, with their senses turned aside or estranged, some hidden things are revealed to them by the demons.

paras.t: Et Chaldæi, id est astronomi, secundum Glossam, seu mathematici, secundum Hieronymum : quod redit in idem, quoniam in Chaldæis viguit astronomia. Chaldæi autem per considerationem astrorum divinabant, et circa cœlestium motus erant intenti. Propter quod visa solis retrocessione sub Ezechia, rex Babylonis, quæ est in Chaldæa, litteras misit et munera Ezechiæ per nuntios, ut sciscitarentur de causa et modo retrocessionis solis tunc factæ, prout quarto Regum et secundo Paralipomenon describitur. Hieronymus quoque hic ait, quod Chaldæi, puta tres Magi, nativitatem Salvatoris primo intellexerunt, et venientes in sanctam Bethlehem, Puerum adoraverunt, stella desuper radiante. Verumtamen, sicut Albertus hæc verba exponit, non est hoc sic intelligendum, quasi per naturalem cursum stellarum deprehensus sit ortus Salvatoris. Hujus namque oppositum tenet Ecclesia ; nec Hieronymus negat novæ stellæ creationem, sed dicit quod quum mathematici semper cœlestia contemplentur, inter alios primi lucem creatæ stellæ viderunt in Christi nativitate, quam non vidissent nisi cœlestia contemplati fuissent. Quod autem in Chaldæa viguit astronomia, constat ex eo quod scriptum est in Isaia de Babylone : Stent, et salvent te augures tui, qui contemplantur sidera, et supputabant menses, ut ex eis annuntiarent ventura tibi.
paras.en: [[2:2|and the Chaldeans|Et Chaldæi]], that is, astronomers, according to the Gloss, or mathematicians [that is, astrologers], according to Jerome: which comes to the same, since astronomy flourished among the Chaldeans. The Chaldeans divined by studying the stars, and were intent upon the movements of the heavenly bodies. For this reason, when the sun was seen to go back under Ezechias[[4 Kings 20:11||]], the king of Babylon, which is in Chaldea, sent letters and presents to Ezechias by messengers[[4 Kings 20:12||]], to inquire into the cause and manner of the going back of the sun that had then taken place, as is related in the fourth book of Kings and the second of Paralipomenon[[2 Par 32:31||]]. Jerome also says here that the Chaldeans, that is, the three Magi, were the first to understand the birth of the Saviour, and coming to holy Bethlehem[[Matt 2:1||]], adored the Child[[Matt 2:11||]], while the star shone above. Yet, as Albert explains these words, this is not to be understood as though the rising of the Saviour was discovered through the natural course of the stars. For the Church holds the opposite of this; nor does Jerome deny the creation of a new star, but he says that, since the mathematicians are always contemplating the heavens, they were among the first to see the light of the star created at Christ's birth, which they would not have seen had they not been contemplating the heavens. That astronomy flourished in Chaldea is plain from what is written in Isaias of Babylon: [[Is 47:13|let now the astrologers stand and save thee, they that gazed at the stars, and counted the months, that from them they might tell the things that shall come to thee|Stent, et salvent te augures tui, qui contemplantur sidera, et supputabant menses, ut ex eis annuntiarent ventura tibi]].

paras.t: Ut indicarent regi somnia sua. Pluraliter dicit, Somnia, propter plures somnii hujus partes. Reges autem et principes terræ illius ad artem scientiæ hujus, id est secundum astronomorum divinationem, omnia agunt, secundum Hieronymum.
paras.en: [[2:2|to declare to the king his dreams|Ut indicarent regi somnia sua]]. He says dreams in the plural because of the several parts of this dream. And the kings and princes of that land do everything by the art of this science, that is, according to the divination of the astronomers, according to Jerome.

paras.t: Qui quum venissent, steterunt coram rege ; et dixit ad eos rex : Vidi somnium, id est, apparitionem quamdam in somno per visionem imaginariam habui, et mente confusus, quia terrore turbatus, admiratione oppressus, ignoro distincte quid viderim, quia nec somnii reminiscor in particulari et sigillatim, nec significationem ejus agnosco. Recordabatur se aliquid magni vidisse, sed determinate quid fuerat, erat oblitus. Unde ait S. Hieronymus : Umbra quædam, et ut ita dicam, aura et vestigium somnii mansit in corde regis, ut referentibus aliis, posset reminisci eorum quæ viderit, et nequaquam eum deciperent mentientes.
paras.en: [[2:2|so they came and stood before the king|Qui quum venissent, steterunt coram rege]]; [[2:3|And the king said to them: I saw a dream|et dixit ad eos rex : Vidi somnium]], that is, I had an appearance in sleep through an imaginary vision [that is, a vision formed of images in the imagination], [[2:3|and being troubled in mind|et mente confusus]], since I am disturbed by terror and overwhelmed with wonder, [[2:3|I know not what I saw|ignoro distincte quid viderim]] distinctly, since I neither remember the dream in its particulars and one thing by one, nor know its meaning. He remembered that he had seen something great, but had forgotten precisely what it was. Hence St Jerome says: A kind of shadow, and so to speak a breath and trace of the dream remained in the king's heart, so that when others told it he could remember what he had seen, and liars could in no way deceive him.

paras.t: Responderuntque Chaldæi regi Syriace, id est Chaldaica lingua. Syra namque et Chaldaica lingua, est una et eadem. Dicit quoque Hieronymus, quod liber iste hucusque scriptus est sermone Hebræo ; ab hoc loco usque ad visionem anni tertii Balthasar regis, quam Daniel vidit in Susis, Hebraicis quidem litteris, sed lingua scribitur Chaldaica, quam hic Syriacam vocat. Aliqui autem affirmant, quod lingua Syriaca et Chaldaica, quantum ad litteratos, sit eadem ; sed quantum ad vulgares, aliquo modo discordat. Rex, in æternum vive. His verbis regem salutant, et benevolentiam captant ipsius ; et secundum Albertum, non audebant alloqui regem, nisi postquam primo allocutus est eos. Denique, quia ponebant homines bonos ad consortium transferri deorum post vitam præsentem, quemadmodum secundo libro Machabæorum Antiochus rex adolescens ait de genitore suo defuncto, Patre nostro inter deos translato ; ideo regi dixerunt, Rex, in æternum vive. Dic somnium servis tuis, et interpretationem, id est significationem, ejus indicabimus tibi. Superius dictum est, quod non solum Chaldæos, sed et alios multos rex advocavit. Chaldæi tamen tanquam regi familiariores, concives et magis audaces, primitus et pro omnibus responderunt : principaliores etiam et rationabiliores fuerunt, quantum ad hoc quod secundum considerationem cursus stellarum, alii autem omnino superstitiose, conjiciebant seu divinabant.
paras.en: [[2:4|And the Chaldeans answered the king in Syriac|Responderuntque Chaldæi regi Syriace]], that is, in the Chaldean tongue. For the Syrian and Chaldean tongue is one and the same. Jerome also says that this book up to here is written in the Hebrew language; from this place up to the vision of the third year of King Baltasar, which Daniel saw in Susa, it is written in Hebrew letters indeed, but in the Chaldean tongue, which he here calls Syriac. Some, however, affirm that the Syriac and Chaldean tongue is the same as far as the learned are concerned, but differs somewhat as far as the common people are concerned. [[2:4|O king, live for ever|Rex, in æternum vive]]. With these words they greet the king and seek to win his goodwill; and according to Albert they did not dare to address the king until he had first addressed them. Moreover, because they held that good men are taken up into the company of the gods after the present life, as the young king Antiochus says in the second book of Machabees of his dead father, [[2 Mach 11:23|Our father being translated amongst the gods|Patre nostro inter deos translato]], they therefore said to the king, [[2:4|O king, live for ever|Rex, in æternum vive]] [[2:4|tell to thy servants thy dream|Dic somnium servis tuis]], [[2:4|and we will declare the interpretation|et interpretationem]], that is, the meaning, [[2:4|thereof|ejus indicabimus]] to thee. It was said above that the king called not only the Chaldeans but many others as well. Yet the Chaldeans, as more familiar with the king, his fellow citizens and bolder, answered first and for all: they were also the chief and the more reasonable, inasmuch as they conjectured or divined by considering the course of the stars, while the others did so wholly superstitiously.

paras.t: Respondens rex ait Chaldæis : Sermo recessit a me, id est, præ terrore et confusione loqui vix possum. Excessivæ equidem passiones loquelam impediunt, juxta illud Job : Nec enim possum metuens respondere. Vel, Sermo de somnio isto, recessit a me, quia oblitus sum somnii. Nisi indicaveritis mihi somnium et conjecturam, id est significationem ejus probabilem, peribitis vos, id est, me jubente occidemini ; et domus, id est possessiones, habitacula, familiæ, vestræ publicabuntur, id est, publicæ direptioni adjudicabuntur. Vel, secundum Glossam, Publicabuntur, id est confiscabuntur. Sed quomodo publicabuntur, si in bursa regis reponentur ? Respondetur, quoniam quæ ponebantur in fisco, pro publicis expendebantur negotiis.
paras.en: [[2:5|And the king, answering, said to the Chaldeans: The thing is gone out of my mind|Respondens rex ait Chaldæis : Sermo recessit a me]] [Latin sermo recessit a me, literally the word has gone from me], that is, for terror and confusion I can hardly speak. For excessive passions hinder speech, according to that of Job: [[Job 9:35|for I cannot answer while I am in fear|Nec enim possum metuens respondere]]. Or, the word about this dream has gone from me, because I have forgotten the dream. [[2:5|unless you tell me the dream, and the meaning|Nisi indicaveritis mihi somnium et conjecturam]], that is, the probable meaning, [[2:5|thereof|ejus]], [[2:5|you shall be put to death|peribitis vos]], that is, you will be slain at my command; [[2:5|and your houses|et domus]], that is, possessions, dwellings, households, [[2:5|shall be confiscated|vestræ publicabuntur]] [Latin publicabuntur, literally shall be made public], that is, shall be given over to public plunder. Or, according to the Gloss, publicabuntur, that is, shall be confiscated. But how will they be made public if they are put into the king's purse? The answer is that what was put into the treasury was spent on public business.

paras.t: Si autem somnium et conjecturam ejus narraveritis, præmia pro labore vestro, et dona ultra condignum ex liberalitate regali, et honorem multum accipietis a me, qui vos tanquam sapientissimos honorabo per me ipsum et alios. His verbis efficit eos diligentes atque sollicitos, dum ex una parte maximam minatur adversitatem, et ex alia parte maximam pollicetur prosperitatem : ut opposita juxta se posita, clarius innotescant, et ipsi duplici incitamento provocentur ad inquisitionem. Ita et Deus omnipotens nobis, si sua servaverimus jussa, inæstimabilem promittit felicitatem ; si vero transgressi ea fuerimus, summam minatur calamitatem. Somnium igitur et interpretationem ejus indicate mihi.
paras.en: [[2:6|but if you tell the dream, and the meaning of it|Si autem somnium et conjecturam ejus narraveritis]], [[2:6|you shall receive of me|accipietis a me]] [[2:6|rewards|præmia]] for your labour, [[2:6|and gifts|et dona]] beyond what is deserved, out of royal liberality, [[2:6|and great honour|et honorem multum]], for I will honour you as the wisest of men, by myself and by others. With these words he makes them diligent and careful, threatening the greatest adversity on the one side and promising the greatest prosperity on the other: so that the opposites, set side by side, may be known more clearly, and they may be spurred to the search by a double incentive. So too almighty God promises us a happiness beyond reckoning if we keep his commands, but threatens the utmost calamity if we transgress them. [[2:6|therefore, tell me the dream, and the interpretation thereof|Somnium igitur et interpretationem ejus indicate mihi]].

paras.t: Responderunt secundo, atque dixerunt : Rex somnium dicat servis suis, et interpretationem ejus indicabimus. In hoc quod petierunt somnium sibi notificari, rationabiliter sunt locuti ; præsumptuose vero, in eo quod addunt, Interpretationem ejus indicabimus. Non enim omnia poterant somnia interpretari ; et si rex somnium istud eis insinuasset, non valuissent ipsum exponere, quia naturalem inquisitionem transcendit. Denique somnium alterius interpretari homo non potest, nisi prius dicatur. Dicit namque Philosophus in libro de Somno et vigilia, illum esse artificiosum somniorum judicem, qui visas similitudines novit perpendere, partesque ad invicem comparare, comparationem quoque ad dispositionem cœli, et passiones ac similitudines somniantis, et ad mores ipsius et complexionem : quæ omnia attendenda sunt ibi.
paras.en: [[2:7|They answered again and said|Responderunt secundo, atque dixerunt]]: [[2:7|Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will declare the interpretation of it|Rex somnium dicat servis suis, et interpretationem ejus indicabimus]]. In asking that the dream be made known to them they spoke reasonably; but presumptuously in what they add, We will declare the interpretation of it. For they could not interpret all dreams; and had the king told them this dream, they would not have been able to explain it, since it surpasses natural inquiry. Again, a man cannot interpret another's dream unless it is first told. For the Philosopher says in the book On Sleep and Waking that he is a skilful judge of dreams who knows how to weigh the likenesses seen and compare the parts with one another, and to compare them also with the disposition of the heavens, and with the passions and likenesses of the dreamer, and with his habits and complexion [that is, his bodily temperament]: all of which must be attended to there.

paras.t: Respondit rex, et ait : Certe scio, quod tempus redimitis, id est, infructuose expenditis, et verborum circuitu illud deducitis, volentes vos ipsos de manu mea redimere ambage verborum, scientes quod recesserit a me sermo (secundum sensum duplicem jam inductum), ideo non deberetis a me somnium investigare. Si ergo somnium non indicaveritis mihi, una, id est communis et par, sententia est de vobis apud me, quod interpretationem quoque fallacem, et deceptionem composueritis, ut loquamini mihi incerta, falsa ac deceptoria pro veris et certis, tenentes me occupatum donec tempus pertranseat, id est, aliis intendere cogar, et ista dimittam. Somnium itaque dicite mihi, ut sciam quod interpretationem quoque ejus veram loquamini. Quum enim difficilius fuerit somnium alterius scire, illo non revelante, videlicet cogitationes ejus, quam somnium interpretari : certum regi fuisset interpretationem eorum veram consistere, si somnium sibi potuissent edicere ; nec tamen consequens fuit, eos non posse somnium aliquod interpretari, nisi quivissent illud præfato modo dignoscere. Verum reges ex sua superbia plerumque sequuntur voluntates et passiones magis quam rationem. Unde exactio regis fuit irrationabilis. Potest tamen inquiri, cur exegit ab istis somnia sua indicari, quum hoc impossibile fuerit. Respondet Albertus, quod Chaldæi isti mathematici exsistentes, dicebant ex astris inferiora causari, influentiisque cœlestibus hominum animas subjacere : et ideo quum se profiterentur scire cursus stellarum, et quas in inferioribus facerent impressiones, quærebat ab eis rex, quas in spiritu suo impressiones fecissent.
paras.en: [[2:8|The king answered and said: I know for certain, that you seek to gain time|Respondit rex, et ait : Certe scio, quod tempus redimitis]] [the margin gives the reading novi for scio, both meaning I know; Latin tempus redimitis, literally you are buying time], that is, you spend it fruitlessly and draw it out with roundabout words, wishing to buy yourselves out of my hand by the windings of words, [[2:8|since you know that the thing is gone from me|scientes quod recesserit a me sermo]] (in the double sense already given), and that therefore you should not have to find out the dream from me. [[2:9|If, therefore, you tell me not the dream|Si ergo somnium non indicaveritis mihi]], [[2:9|there is one|una]], that is, a common and equal, [[2:9|sentence concerning you|sententia est de vobis apud me]] with me, [[2:9|that you have also framed a lying interpretation, and full of deceit|quod interpretationem quoque fallacem, et deceptionem composueritis]] [the margin gives the reading deceptione plenam, full of deceit, for deceptionem, deceit], [[2:9|to speak before me|ut loquamini mihi]] uncertain, false and deceitful things in place of true and certain ones, keeping me occupied [[2:9|till the time pass away|donec tempus pertranseat]], that is, till I am forced to attend to other things and let these go. [[2:9|Tell me, therefore, the dream, that I may know that you also give a true interpretation thereof|Somnium itaque dicite mihi, ut sciam quod interpretationem quoque ejus veram loquamini]]. For since it would be harder to know another's dream when he does not reveal it, that is, his thoughts, than to interpret the dream, the king would have been certain that their interpretation was true if they could have told him the dream; and yet it did not follow that they could not interpret any dream unless they could discern it in that way. But kings, out of their pride, mostly follow their wills and passions rather than reason. Hence the king's demand was unreasonable. Yet it may be asked why he demanded that they tell him his dreams, since this was impossible. Albert answers that these Chaldeans, being mathematicians [that is, astrologers], said that things below are caused by the stars and that the souls of men are subject to heavenly influences: and so, since they professed to know the courses of the stars and the impressions they make on things below, the king asked them what impressions they had made in his spirit.

paras.t: Respondentes ergo Chaldæi coram rege, dixerunt : Non est homo super terram, qui sermonem tuum, rex, possit implere. Et hoc verum fuit, loquendo de naturali hominum potestate : cordium enim secreta cognoscere, non est facultatis humanæ. Sed neque regum quisquam magnus et potens, ut tu, verbum hujusmodi sciscitatur ab omni ariolo, et mago, et Chaldæo. Verba ultima supra exposita sunt. Quasi dicant : Contra laudabilem consuetudinem, quæ habet vim legis, tu facis; nec tibi potentissimo regi competit, ceteris regibus crudelius agere, quum ad regem spectet clementia : sicut in Proverbiis Salomon loquitur, Clementia roboratur thronus regis.
paras.en: [[2:10|Then the Chaldeans answered before the king, and said: There is no man upon earth, that can accomplish thy word, O king|Respondentes ergo Chaldæi coram rege, dixerunt : Non est homo super terram, qui sermonem tuum, rex, possit implere]]. And this was true, speaking of the natural power of men: for to know the secrets of hearts is not within human power[[1 Kings 16:7||]]. [[2:10|neither doth any king, though great and mighty, ask such a thing of any diviner, or wise man, or Chaldean|Sed neque regum quisquam magnus et potens, ut tu, verbum hujusmodi sciscitatur ab omni ariolo, et mago, et Chaldæo]]. The last words were explained above. As if they said: You act against a praiseworthy custom, which has the force of law; nor is it fitting for you, a most powerful king, to act more cruelly than other kings, since clemency belongs to a king: as Solomon says in the Proverbs, [[Prov 20:28|his throne is strengthened by clemency|Clementia roboratur thronus regis]].

paras.t: Sermo enim quem tu quæris, rex, gravis est, id est difficilis ad complendum; nec reperietur quisquam qui indicet illum in conspectu regis. In hoc verum dicere se putabant, ignorantes veri summique Dei cultoribus, scilicet Israelitis, occultissima desuper revelari.
paras.en: [[2:11|For the thing that thou asketh, O king, is difficult|Sermo enim quem tu quæris, rex, gravis est]], that is, hard to accomplish; [[2:11|nor can any one be found that can shew it before the king|nec reperietur quisquam qui indicet illum in conspectu regis]]. In this they thought they spoke the truth, not knowing that to the worshippers of the true and supreme God, namely the Israelites, the most hidden things are revealed from above.

paras.t: Exceptis diis, quorum non est cum hominibus conversatio. Gentiles ponebant varios ordines deorum : nam et corpora cœlestia, ac motores eorum deos ponebant ; animas quoque hominum quorumdam ad consortium transferri deorum, ac deificari, quibus occultorum scientiam attribuebant, quæ homines scire non possent, nisi revelantibus illis. Et dicunt hic aliqui, quod Chaldæi dicebant sicut Platonici, puta quod dæmones essent animalia corpore aeria, mente rationalia, animo passiva, et tempore æterna : quæ, secundum eos, habitant in aere, et cum hominibus sæpe junguntur, et quodammodo conversantur ; a quibus per artes magicas aliqua possunt inquiri ac sciri, sed non omnia. Deos autem quorum non est cum hominibus conversatio, ponebant substantias separatas, quæ sunt altioris scientiæ, ad quas ars divinativa ac magica se non extendit ad aliquid inquirendum ab eis. Albertus per deos intelligit homines divinos : quorum conversatio dicitur non esse cum hominibus, quia conversatio talium est in cœlis. Hoc tamen non videtur fuisse intentio Chaldæorum, qui neminem se in terris diviniorem censebant. Hieronymus demum hic ait : Confitentur magi, confitentur arioli, et omnis scientia sæcularis litteraturæ, præscientiam futurorum, non hominum esse, sed Dei. Ex quo probatur, Prophetas spiritu Dei locutos. Hinc nempe et Isaias effatur : Quæ futura sunt annuntiate, et sciemus quia dii estis vos.
paras.en: [[2:11|except the gods, whose conversation is not with men|Exceptis diis, quorum non est cum hominibus conversatio]]. The Gentiles held various orders of gods: for they held the heavenly bodies and their movers to be gods; and also that the souls of certain men are taken up into the company of the gods and made divine, and to these they attributed a knowledge of hidden things which men could not know unless they revealed them. And some say here that the Chaldeans spoke as the Platonists did, namely that demons are living beings airy in body, rational in mind, passible in soul [that is, subject to passions] and eternal in time: who, according to them, dwell in the air, and are often joined with men and in a way hold converse with them; from whom some things, but not all, can be inquired into and known by magic arts. But the gods whose conversation is not with men they held to be the separate substances [that is, pure spirits without bodies], which are of higher knowledge, and to which the art of divination and magic does not reach so as to inquire anything of them. Albert takes the gods to mean divine men: whose conversation is said not to be with men, because the conversation of such men is in heaven[[Phil 3:20||]]. Yet this does not seem to have been the meaning of the Chaldeans, who thought no one on earth more divine than themselves. Lastly Jerome says here: The magi confess, the diviners confess, and all the knowledge of worldly learning confesses, that foreknowledge of things to come belongs not to men but to God. By this it is proved that the Prophets spoke by the Spirit of God. Hence indeed Isaias too says: [[Is 41:23|Shew the things that are to come hereafter, and we shall know that ye are gods|Quæ futura sunt annuntiate, et sciemus quia dii estis vos]].

paras.t: Quo audito, rex in furorem versus est : et hoc, irrationabiliter valde. Superbi enim non patiuntur se informari, nec instructionem, quamvis caritativam rationabilemque, admittunt. Et in ira magna præcepit ut perirent, id est interficerentur, omnes sapientes Babylonis. Quemadmodum apud Jacobum habetur : Ira viri justitiam Dei non operatur. Propter quod in Proverbiis scriptum est : Ira non habet misericordiam, nec erumpens furor ; impetum autem concitati spiritus ferre quis poterit?
paras.en: [[2:12|Upon hearing this, the king in fury|Quo audito, rex in furorem versus est]]: and that most unreasonably. For the proud do not suffer themselves to be taught, nor do they accept instruction, however charitable and reasonable. [[2:12|and in great wrath, commanded that|Et in ira magna præcepit]] [[2:12|all the wise men of Babylon|omnes sapientes Babylonis]] [[2:12|should be put to death|ut perirent]], that is, should be slain. As we have in James: [[Jas 1:20|For the anger of man worketh not the justice of God|Ira viri justitiam Dei non operatur]]. For which reason it is written in the Proverbs: [[Prov 27:4|Anger hath no mercy: nor fury, when it breaketh forth: and who can bear the violence of one provoked?|Ira non habet misericordiam, nec erumpens furor ; impetum autem concitati spiritus ferre quis poterit?]]

paras.t: Et egressa, id est prolata ac publicata, sententia occisionis, sapientes Babylonis interficiebantur, id est, ad occidendum quærebantur, et disponebatur de morte eorum. Res autem dicitur facta seu fieri, quando in proximo est ut fiat, vel quasi facta est : sicut de agonizante dicimus, quod sit mortuus homo. Infra autem patebit, quod sapientes isti non fuerunt occisi, nisi forsitan aliqui. Sed cur tanto furore exarsit in eos? Ad hoc Lyra respondet, quod vacantes philosophiæ conjecturisque futurorum ac similibus, vestitum et victum, imo sumptus magnos habebant a rege : sicut capitulo præcedenti dictum est de Daniele et sociis ejus. Unde in Genesi legitur, quod sacerdotes Ægypti non sunt tempore famis compulsi vendere terram suam ut alii : quoniam victum recipiebant ex horreis regis. Quoniam ergo rex Babylonis multa expendit pro sustentatione sapientium suorum, iratus fuit intense, quando ad suam voluntatem, et sicut speravit, non responderunt.
paras.en: [[2:13|And the decree being gone forth|Et egressa]], that is, the sentence of death being uttered and published, [[2:13|the wise men were slain|sapientes Babylonis interficiebantur]], that is, they were being sought out to be killed, and their death was being arranged. For a thing is said to be done, or to be being done, when it is about to be done, or is as good as done: as we say of a man in his agony that he is dead. It will appear below that these wise men were not slain, except perhaps some. But why did he blaze out against them with such fury? To this Lyra answers that, as they gave their time to philosophy and to conjectures about the future and the like, they had clothing and food, indeed great allowances, from the king[[Dan 1:5||]]: as was said in the preceding chapter of Daniel and his companions. Hence we read in Genesis that the priests of Egypt were not forced in the time of famine to sell their land as the others were, since they received their food from the king's granaries[[Gen 47:22||]]. Since, then, the king of Babylon spent a great deal on the upkeep of his wise men, he was intensely angry when they did not answer to his will and as he had hoped.

paras.t: Quærebanturque Daniel et socii ejus, Ananias, Misael et Azarias, ut perirent, id est interficerentur, quia et ipsi de numero sapientium fuerunt. Circa hoc scribit Hieronymus : Quærunt Hebræi, cur Daniel et tres pueri non sunt cum aliis sapientibus ad regem ingressi, et tamen prolata sententia, jubebantur occidi cum eis. Respondet, quod eo tempore quo rex dona, præmia et honorem promittebat, ire noluerunt, ne impudenter divitias et dignitatem Chaldaicam viderentur appetere. Aut certe ipsi Chaldæi invidentes gloriæ et scientiæ eorum, soli ingressi sunt, quasi soli præmia recepturi; et postea in periculo voluerunt Chaldæi istos habere consortes, quos in spe gloriæ refutarunt. Sed mirum quod rex non vocavit eos ex nomine, quia ut dictum est capitulo præcedenti, jamdudum rex invenit decuplum in eis sapientiæ et intellectus, quam in ariolis, magis atque Chaldæis. Ad quod dicere quis potest, quod rex mente confusus, oblitus sit eos vocare.
paras.en: [[2:13|and Daniel and his companions were sought for|Quærebanturque Daniel et socii ejus]], Ananias, Misael and Azarias, [[2:13|to be put to death|ut perirent]], that is, to be slain, since they too were of the number of the wise men. On this Jerome writes: The Hebrews ask why Daniel and the three youths did not go in to the king with the other wise men, and yet, when the sentence was given, were ordered to be killed with them. He answers that at the time when the king was promising gifts, rewards and honour they would not go, lest they should seem shamelessly to covet the riches and dignities of Chaldea. Or else the Chaldeans themselves, envying their glory and knowledge, went in alone, as if to receive the rewards alone; and afterwards, in danger, the Chaldeans wanted to have as companions those whom they had shut out in the hope of glory. But it is strange that the king did not call them by name, since, as was said in the preceding chapter, the king had long since found in them ten times more wisdom and understanding than in the diviners, wise men and Chaldeans[[Dan 1:20||]]. To this one may say that the king, troubled in mind, forgot to call them.

paras.t: Tunc Daniel requisivit de lege, id est præcepto occidendi sapientes, atque sententia damnationis latæ in eos, ab Arioch principe militiæ regis, qui egressus fuerat ad interficiendum sapientes Babylonis : et tamen non festinavit in hoc, quia invite exsequebatur imperium regis, cujus indiscretionem bene advertit. Et interrogavit eum qui a rege potestatem acceperat occidendi, scilicet Arioch, quam ob causam tam crudelis sententia a facie, id est ore et præsentia, regis esset egressa.
paras.en: [[2:14|Then Daniel inquired concerning the law|Tunc Daniel requisivit de lege]], that is, the command to kill the wise men, [[2:14|and the sentence|atque sententia]] of condemnation passed upon them, [[2:14|of Arioch, the general of the king's army, who was gone forth to kill the wise men of Babylon|ab Arioch principe militiæ regis, qui egressus fuerat ad interficiendum sapientes Babylonis]]: and yet he did not make haste in this, because he carried out the king's command unwillingly, being well aware of its want of discretion. [[2:15|And he asked|Et interrogavit]] him who had received from the king the power to kill, namely Arioch, [[2:15|why so cruel a sentence was gone forth from the face|quam ob causam tam crudelis sententia a facie]], that is, from the mouth and presence, of the king.

paras.t: Quum ergo rem, id est causam hanc, indicasset Arioch Danieli, Daniel ingressus, rogavit regem ut tempus daret sibi ad solutionem indicandam regi. Non solum secundum Sanctos, sed et secundum Aristotelem, qui bene se habent in divinis, melioris sunt spei. Ideo Daniel tanquam vir sanctus, confidit de misericordia Dei quod sibi hæc revelaturus esset. Regem quoque confidenter accessit, tanquam de ejus exsistens palatio, et quia jam ante perpendit circa se regis favorem. In hoc autem Daniel non egit contra documentum Christi, dicentis : Nolite præmeditari quemadmodum respondeatis; dabitur enim vobis in illa hora quid loquamini : quia, ut ait Albertus, Dominus non prohibet deliberationem simpliciter, sed deliberationem et præmeditationem rationis humanæ : quia si huic sancti inniterentur, viderentur dubitare de fide. Inducias autem faciendæ orationis, et impetrandæ revelationis, ac ordinandæ responsionis secundum fidem, Christus non prohibet. Hinc ait Hieronymus : Tempus postulat, non quod tractatione et sagacitate mentis occulta perquireret, sed quod occultorum Dominum precaretur. Et iterum ait Hieronymus : Scientes Chaldæi, quod decuplum super cunctos ariolos et magos qui erant in universa Chaldæa, Daniel et tres pueri saperent, celaverunt eos interrogationem regis, ne sibi in interpretatione somnii præferrentur. Ideo Daniel ab Arioch de crudelitate sententiæ interrogavit, quoniam causam sui ignoravit periculi.
paras.en: [[2:15|And when Arioch had told the matter|Quum ergo rem]], that is, this cause, [[2:15|to Daniel|indicasset Arioch Danieli]], [[2:16|Daniel went in, and desired of the king, that he would give him time to resolve the question, and declare it to the king|Daniel ingressus, rogavit regem ut tempus daret sibi ad solutionem indicandam regi]]. Not only according to the Saints but also according to Aristotle, those who stand well in divine things are of better hope. So Daniel, as a holy man, trusted in the mercy of God that he would reveal these things to him. He also approached the king with confidence, as one belonging to his palace, and because he had already perceived the king's favour towards him. In this Daniel did not act against the teaching of Christ, who says: [[Luke 21:14|not to meditate before how you shall answer|Nolite præmeditari quemadmodum respondeatis]]; [[Matt 10:19|for it shall be given you in that hour what to speak|dabitur enim vobis in illa hora quid loquamini]][[Luke 21:15||]]: since, as Albert says, the Lord does not forbid deliberation simply, but the deliberation and forethought of human reason: for if the saints relied on this, they would seem to doubt of the faith. But a delay in which to pray, to obtain a revelation, and to order one's answer according to faith, Christ does not forbid. Hence Jerome says: He asks for time, not to search out the hidden thing by reasoning and sharpness of mind, but to pray to the Lord of hidden things. And again Jerome says: The Chaldeans, knowing that Daniel and the three youths were ten times wiser than all the diviners and wise men in the whole of Chaldea, hid the king's question from them, lest they should be preferred to themselves in the interpretation of the dream. That is why Daniel asked Arioch about the cruelty of the sentence: because he did not know the cause of his danger.

paras.t: Et ingressus est domum suam sibi a rege concessam. Principales enim de curia, habitacula certa habent. Itaque ab aliis se subtraxit, ingrediens domum, ut Deum quietius liberiusque oraret, et in silentio contemplationi vacaret, auditurus quid loqueretur in ipso Dominus Deus, juxta illud : Tu autem quum oraveris, intra in cubiculum; et clauso ostio, ora Patrem tuum in abscondito. Et Sapiens ait : Intrans in domum meam, conquiescam cum ea, scilicet cum sapientia.
paras.en: [[2:17|And he went into his house|Et ingressus est domum suam]], given him by the king. For the chief men of the court have fixed dwellings. So he withdrew from the others, going into his house, that he might pray to God more quietly and freely, and give himself to contemplation in silence, to hear what the Lord God would speak in him[[Ps 84:9||]], according to that saying: [[Matt 6:6|But thou when thou shalt pray, enter into thy chamber, and having shut the door, pray to thy Father in secret|Tu autem quum oraveris, intra in cubiculum; et clauso ostio, ora Patrem tuum in abscondito]]. And the Wise Man says: [[Wis 8:16|When I go into my house, I shall repose myself with her|Intrans in domum meam, conquiescam cum ea]], namely with wisdom.

paras.t: Ananiæque et Misaeli et Azariæ sociis suis indicavit negotium, ut quærerent misericordiam, scilicet revelationem piam, a facie, id est clementi adspectu, Dei cæli super sacramento isto, id est sacro atque divino isto secreto, quod in somnio regis continebatur : in quo aliquid de regno atque mysteriis Christi fuerat designatum. Secundum Hieronymum, Daniel socios suos sibi in oratione conjungit, ne solus de suo merito præsumere videretur : ut quorum commune erat discrimen, communis esset oratio. Denique, oratio multorum, præsertim justorum, multum est exaudibilis. Et non perirent, id est, ne occiderentur, Daniel et socii ejus : ex quorum vita dependebat consolatio omnium Judæorum captivorum; cum ceteris sapientibus Babylonis, id est, ut nec illi perirent : sicque pro inimicis oravit. Vel sensus est, Ut non perirent, quemadmodum dum illi perire jussi fuerunt. Juxta primum sensum, in hoc magna Danielis insinuatur caritas atque perfectio, quod pro insidiantibus invidentibusque oravit, evangelicum illud adimplens : Diligite inimicos vestros, benefacite his qui oderunt vos, et orate pro persequentibus et calumniantibus vos.
paras.en: [[2:17|and told the matter to Ananias, and Misael, and Azarias, his companions|Ananiæque et Misaeli et Azariæ sociis suis indicavit negotium]], [[2:18|To the end that they should ask mercy|ut quærerent misericordiam]], namely a merciful revelation, [[2:18|at the face|a facie]], that is, the gracious regard, [[2:18|of the God of heaven, concerning this secret|Dei cæli super sacramento isto]] [Latin sacramentum, a sacred thing or mystery], that is, this sacred and divine secret, which was contained in the king's dream: in which something of the kingdom and the mysteries of Christ had been signified. According to Jerome, Daniel joins his companions with himself in prayer, lest he should seem to presume on his own merit alone: so that those who shared the danger might share the prayer. Moreover, the prayer of many, above all of the just, is readily heard. [[2:18|might not perish|Et non perirent]], that is, that they might not be slain, [[2:18|Daniel and his companions|Daniel et socii ejus]], on whose life the comfort of all the captive Jews depended; [[2:18|with the rest of the wise men of Babylon|cum ceteris sapientibus Babylonis]], that is, that neither might they perish: and so he prayed for his enemies. Or the sense is, that they might not perish as the others had been ordered to perish. According to the first sense, this shows Daniel's great charity and perfection, in that he prayed for those who plotted against and envied him, fulfilling that saying of the Gospel: [[Matt 5:44|Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you: and pray for them that persecute and calumniate you|Diligite inimicos vestros, benefacite his qui oderunt vos, et orate pro persequentibus et calumniantibus vos]].

paras.t: Tunc Danieli mysterium, id est secretum somnii hujus, per visionem nocte revelatum est ministerio angeli sancti : quia per angelos, secundum divinum Dionysium, prophetice revelationes fiebant. Porro qualis fuerit revelatio ista, an scilicet imaginaria, vel intellectualis tantum, an etiam facta sit in somno, vel in vigilia, in textu non dicitur, nec certum videtur. Hieronymus tamen innuit eam fuisse in somnis, dicendo : Somnium regis suo discit somnio ; imo et somnium et interpretationem ejus Dei revelatione cognoscit, quod dæmones ignorabant. Glossa quoque hic dicit, et aliqui asserunt, quod idem somniavit quod rex, moxque post hoc revelata sit ei expositio somnii. Lyra etiam scribit hic : Probabile videtur, quod vidit in somno consimilem visionem visioni regis, et ultra hoc, intellectum ipsius : nam dicitur, Nocte. Tales enim visiones magis notæ sunt fieri nocte sensibus quietatis, juxta illud in Job : Per somnium in visione nocturna, quando irruit sopor super homines, et dormiunt in lectulo, tunc aperit Deus aures virorum, et erudiens eos instruit disciplina. Albertus aliter dicit. Sic enim exponit : Per visionem, non per somnium, sed per apertam rerum demonstrationem.
paras.en: [[2:19|Then was the mystery|Tunc Danieli mysterium]], that is, the secret of this dream, [[2:19|revealed to Daniel by a vision in the night|per visionem nocte revelatum est]] through the ministry of a holy angel: for, according to the divine Dionysius, prophetic revelations were made through the angels. But what kind of revelation this was, whether imaginary [that is, made through images in the imagination] or intellectual only, and whether it was made in sleep or awake, the text does not say, nor does it seem certain. Jerome, however, implies that it was in a dream, saying: He learns the king's dream by his own dream; indeed he knows both the dream and its interpretation by God's revelation, which the demons did not know. The Gloss also says here, and some assert, that he dreamed the same as the king, and soon after this the explanation of the dream was revealed to him. Lyra too writes here: It seems probable that he saw in sleep a vision like the king's vision, and beyond this its meaning: for it says, In the night. For such visions are better known to take place at night, when the senses are at rest, according to that in Job: [[Job 33:15|By a dream in a vision by night, when deep sleep falleth upon men, and they are sleeping in their beds|Per somnium in visione nocturna, quando irruit sopor super homines, et dormiunt in lectulo]], [[Job 33:16|Then he openeth the ears of men, and teaching instructeth them in what they are to learn.|tunc aperit Deus aures virorum, et erudiens eos instruit disciplina]] Albert says otherwise. For he explains it thus: By a vision, not by a dream, but by an open showing of the things.

paras.t: Et Daniel benedixit, id est, laudavit, et bonum sibi impensum Deo dixit atque adscripsit, Deum cæli. Deum enim a suis effectibus nominamus : cœlum autem est opus Dei præclarum; et nomine cœli intelligendus est gloriosus Beatorum exercitus inhabitans cœlum. Et hic solus verus est Deus : propter quod ait Jeremias, Dii qui non fecerunt cœlum et terram, perierant. Secundum Hieronymum, Benedixit Deo cœli, ad distinctionem eorum qui versantur in terra, et dæmoniacis artibus atque præstigiis deludunt terrena.
paras.en: [[2:19|and Daniel blessed|Et Daniel benedixit]], that is, praised, and spoke of [Latin bene dixit, a play on benedixit, blessed: he spoke well of] the good done him as God's, and ascribed it to him, [[2:19|the God of heaven|Deum cæli]]. For we name God from his effects: and heaven is a glorious work of God; and by the name of heaven is to be understood the glorious host of the Blessed who dwell in heaven. And he alone is the true God: for which reason Jeremias says, [[Jer 10:11|The gods that have not made heaven and earth, let them perish|Dii qui non fecerunt cœlum et terram, perierant]]. According to Jerome, he blessed the God of heaven to distinguish him from those who dwell on earth and delude earthly things with demonic arts and conjuring tricks.

paras.t: Et locutus ait, gratias referendo pro tam supernaturali et grandi revelatione : qui enim de acceptis beneficiis gratias refert, ad majora sortienda se aptat : Sit nomen Domini, scilicet nomen nominatum, quod est ipsemet Dominus, nomine nominante signatus, benedictum, id est laudatum et sanctum, ita ut omnes Domino benedicant. Denique verus Dei amator et gratus donorum ejus susceptor, contentus non est per se solum benedicere Deum, sed ab universis et singulis eum appetit benedici. A sæculo et usque in sæculum, id est per sæcula cuncta, seu æternaliter; vel, A sæculo omnium patrum, in sæcula omnium filiorum, in quibus nunquam defecerunt illuminationes et miserationes divinæ.
paras.en: [[2:20|And speaking, he said|Et locutus ait]], giving thanks for so supernatural and great a revelation: for he who gives thanks for benefits received fits himself to obtain greater ones: [[2:20|Blessed|benedictum]] [[2:20|be the name of the Lord|Sit nomen Domini]]: the name, that is, the name named, which is the Lord himself, signified by the naming name [the scholastic distinction between the thing named and the word that names it]; blessed, that is, praised and holy, so that all may bless the Lord. Moreover, a true lover of God and a grateful receiver of his gifts is not content to bless God by himself alone, but desires that he be blessed by each and all. [[2:20|from eternity and for evermore|A sæculo et usque in sæculum]] [Latin a sæculo et usque in sæculum, literally from age even to age], that is, through all ages, or eternally; or, from the age of all the fathers to the ages of all the sons, in which the divine enlightenments and mercies have never failed.

paras.t: Quia sapientia et fortitudo ejus sunt. Hoc dupliciter intelligi potest. Primo, quod sapientia et fortitudo, seu virtus ac potestas in Deo sunt, et ei vere ac plene conveniunt, imo sunt ipsemet supersapiens omnipotens Deus : cujus comparatione sicut nullus bonus, ita nullus est sapiens, juxta illud ad Romanos, Soli sapienti Deo honor et gloria. De quo scriptum est in Job : Sapiens corde est, et fortis robore; itemque, Potestas et terror apud ipsum est. Secundo accipitur, quod omnis sapientia et fortitudo cujuscumque creaturæ a Deo profluxit, ejusque donum est, juxta illud Ecclesiastici, Omnis sapientia a Domino Deo est; et ad Romanos, Non est potestas nisi a Deo. Sapientia autem hic dicitur, vel cognitio secretorum cœlestium, vel scientia dispositionis universorum : sapientis namque est ordinare. Fortitudo vero accipitur pro virtute et efficacia exsequendi disposita. Et hæc duo præcipue ad dominos ac judices pertinent. Propter quod Ecclesiasticus ait : Noli quærere fieri judex, nisi valeas virtute irrumpere iniquitates; et alibi, Væ terræ cujus rex puer est.
paras.en: [[2:20|for wisdom and fortitude are his|Quia sapientia et fortitudo ejus sunt]]. This can be understood in two ways. First, that wisdom and fortitude, or strength and power, are in God, and belong to him truly and fully, indeed are the all-wise almighty God himself: compared with whom, as no one is good, so no one is wise, according to that to the Romans, [[Rom 16:27|To God, the only wise|Soli sapienti Deo]], [[Rom 16:27|honour and glory|honor et gloria]]. Of whom it is written in Job: [[Job 9:4|He is wise in heart, and mighty in strength|Sapiens corde est, et fortis robore]]; and again, [[Job 25:2|Power and terror are with him|Potestas et terror apud ipsum est]]. Secondly it is taken to mean that all the wisdom and fortitude of any creature whatever has flowed from God and is his gift, according to that of Ecclesiasticus, [[Ecclus 1:1|All wisdom is from the Lord God|Omnis sapientia a Domino Deo est]] [the margin gives Ecclus. v, 1; the words are Ecclus 1:1]; and to the Romans, [[Rom 13:1|there is no power but from God|Non est potestas nisi a Deo]]. Wisdom here means either the knowledge of heavenly secrets or the knowledge of the ordering of all things: for it belongs to the wise man to set in order. Fortitude is taken for the strength and power to carry out what has been ordered. And these two belong above all to lords and judges. For which reason Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 7:6|Seek not to be made a judge, unless thou have strength enough to extirpate iniquities|Noli quærere fieri judex, nisi valeas virtute irrumpere iniquitates]]; and elsewhere, [[Eccles 10:16|Woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child|Væ terræ cujus rex puer est]] [Denis says Ecclesiasticus, but this is in Ecclesiastes, as the margin gives it].

paras.t: Et ipse mutat, id est distinguit, tempora et ætates, id est rerum periodos : sicut in Hymno cantamus : Rector potens, verax Deus, qui temperas rerum vices. Deus autem excelsus est universorum creator, qui per motum cœlestium corporum efficit dies et noctes, æstatem et hiemem, menses et annos, juxta illud Genesis : Dixit Deus, Fiant luminaria in firmamento cœli, et dividant diem et noctem, et sint in signa, et tempora, et dies, et annos. De quibus legitur apud Amos : Convertens tenebras in mane, et diem nocte mutans. Præterea, Deus per omnipotentiam suam tempora potest mutare, diem supernaturaliter prolongando, ut tempore Josue et Ezechiæ. Dicit autem Albertus, quod tempora dicuntur secundum quod spatia sunt in motibus cœlestibus; ætates vero, secundum quod spatia illa relinquuntur in inferioribus. Ætates autem seu periodos rerum corruptibilium Deus immutat, vitam et durationem entium ad libitum prolongando et abbreviando. Nam et ante diluvium longior fuit ætas humana, quam postea.
paras.en: [[2:21|And he changeth|Et ipse mutat]], that is, distinguishes, [[2:21|times and ages|tempora et ætates]], that is, the periods of things: as we sing in the Hymn: O mighty Ruler, truthful God, who orderest the changes of things [the hymn Rector potens, verax Deus, sung at Sext]. For God most high is the creator of all things, who by the motion of the heavenly bodies makes days and nights, summer and winter, months and years, according to that of Genesis: [[Gen 1:14|And God said: Let there be lights made in the firmament of heaven, to divide the day and the night, and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years|Dixit Deus, Fiant luminaria in firmamento cœli, et dividant diem et noctem, et sint in signa, et tempora, et dies, et annos]]. Of which we read in Amos: [[Amos 5:8|that turneth darkness into morning, and that changeth day into night|Convertens tenebras in mane, et diem nocte mutans]]. Moreover, God by his almighty power can change the times, lengthening the day supernaturally, as in the time of Josue[[Jos 10:13||]] and of Ezechias[[4 Kings 20:11||]] [the margin gives IV Reg. ix, 11; the sign given to Ezechias is at 4 Kings 20:11]. Albert says that times are so called inasmuch as they are spaces in the heavenly motions, and ages inasmuch as those spaces are left behind in things below. God changes the ages or periods of corruptible things, lengthening and shortening at his pleasure the life and duration of beings. For before the flood the age of man was longer than afterwards.

paras.t: Et transfert regna atque constituit, id est, destruit secundum ordinem sapientiæ atque justitiæ suæ infallibilis atque immensæ : et hoc communiter propter hominum merita et demerita, prout Ecclesiasticus ait : Sedes ducum superborum destruxit Deus, et sedere fecit mites pro eis; et rursus, Regnum a gente in gentem transfertur propter injustitias, et injurias, et contumelias. Interdum autem aliqui a Deo constituuntur in reges aut regna, non propter suas justitias, sed ad punitionem pravorum, quemadmodum per Isaiam protestatur : Dabo pueros principes eorum, et effeminati dominabuntur eis. In Job quoque : Deus regnare facit hominem hypocritam propter peccata populi. Denique in Deuteronomio Moyses populo Israeli ait : Ne dicas in corde tuo, Propter justitiam meam introduxit me Dominus in terram hanc, scilicet Chananæorum, quum durissimæ cervicis sis populus. Frequenter etiam Deus dat alicui regnum, propter aliquod opus ex genere bonum, quamvis non meritorium vitæ æternæ, quemadmodum Cyro, eo quod liberaturus erat filios Israel de Babylonica captivitate, sicut in Isaia habetur. Aliquando demum impiis regnum conceditur ad correctionem et exercitium electorum, sicut et Attila rex Hunnorum dixit se esse flagellum Dei. Et in Isaia Dominus loquitur, Væ Assur, virga furoris mei et baculus ipse est : quod ad litteram dicitur de Sennacherib rege Assyriorum.
paras.en: [[2:21|taketh away kingdoms, and establisheth them|Et transfert regna atque constituit]] [Latin transfert, transfers], that is, he destroys, according to the order of his infallible and immeasurable wisdom and justice: and this commonly because of the merits and demerits of men, as Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 10:17|God hath overturned the thrones of proud princes, and hath set up the meek in their stead|Sedes ducum superborum destruxit Deus, et sedere fecit mites pro eis]]; and again, [[Ecclus 10:8|A kingdom is translated from one people to another, because of injustices, and wrongs, and injuries|Regnum a gente in gentem transfertur propter injustitias, et injurias, et contumelias]]. Sometimes, however, some are set up by God as kings or kingdoms not for their own justice but for the punishment of the wicked, as he declares through Isaias: [[Is 3:4|And I will give children to be their princes, and the effeminate shall rule over them.|Dabo pueros principes eorum, et effeminati dominabuntur eis]] In Job also: God [[Job 34:30|maketh a man that is a hypocrite to reign for the sins of the people|regnare facit hominem hypocritam propter peccata populi]]. Again, in Deuteronomy Moses says to the people of Israel: [[Deut 9:4|Say not in thy heart|Ne dicas in corde tuo]], [[Deut 9:4|For my justice hath the Lord brought me in|Propter justitiam meam introduxit me Dominus]] into this land, namely that of the Chanaanites, [[Deut 9:6|for thou art a very stiffnecked people|quum durissimæ cervicis sis populus]]. Often, too, God gives someone a kingdom for some work good in its kind, though not meritorious of eternal life, as to Cyrus, because he was to free the children of Israel from the Babylonian captivity, as we have in Isaias[[Is 45:1||]]. Sometimes, lastly, a kingdom is granted to the wicked for the correction and exercise of the elect, as Attila king of the Huns also said that he was the scourge of God. And in Isaias the Lord says, [[Is 10:5|Woe to the Assyrian, he is the rod and the staff of my anger|Væ Assur, virga furoris mei et baculus ipse est]]: which is said in the literal sense of Sennacherib king of the Assyrians.

paras.t: Dat sapientiam sapientibus : ab eo enim est omnis notitia veritatis. Sed variis modis dat et infundit sapientiam mentibus. Siquidem donum sapientiæ est immediate per creationem a Deo; sapientiam vero prophetalium visionum infundit per angelos. Aliquando autem sapientiam quæ est donum gratiæ gratis datæ, et gratiam prophetiæ ac Scripturarum notitiam, immediate per se ipsum largitur, sicut Apostolis in die Pentecostes, et Paulo in raptu. Sed et sapientia tam philosophica quam theologica per studium acquisita, dona sunt Dei, qui naturale lumen intellectus contulit et conservat : a quo omnium rerum esse et posse ac agere incessanter dependent. Unde de philosophis ait Apostolus ad Romanos : Deus illis revelavit. Et scientiam intelligentibus disciplinam, id est vere moralibus, morigeratis, passionum victoribus, qui apti sunt illuminari a Deo. Disciplina autem est morum correctio, justa punitio, seu moralis doctrina : cujus passionum secutor est inanis auditor, secundum Philosophum primo Ethicorum. Hinc in Proverbiis scriptum est : Dominus dat sapientiam, et ex ore illius scientia et prudentia. Et Jacobus ait : Si quis indiget sapientia, postulet a Deo, et dabitur ei.
paras.en: [[2:21|giveth wisdom to the wise|Dat sapientiam sapientibus]]: for from him is all knowledge of truth. But he gives and pours wisdom into minds in various ways. The gift of wisdom is from God immediately by creation; but the wisdom of prophetic visions he pours in through the angels. Sometimes, however, he bestows by himself, immediately, the wisdom that is a gift of grace freely given [that is, a grace given for the good of others rather than for the holiness of the receiver], and the grace of prophecy and the knowledge of the Scriptures, as on the Apostles on the day of Pentecost, and on Paul in his rapture. And wisdom too, both philosophical and theological, acquired by study, is the gift of God, who gave and preserves the natural light of the understanding: on whom the being, the power and the acting of all things depend unceasingly. Hence the Apostle says of the philosophers to the Romans: [[Rom 1:19|God hath manifested it unto them|Deus illis revelavit]]. [[2:21|and knowledge to them that have understanding|Et scientiam intelligentibus disciplinam]] [Latin intelligentibus disciplinam, to them that understand discipline], that is, to those who are truly moral, well-mannered, conquerors of their passions, who are fit to be enlightened by God. For discipline is the correction of morals, just punishment, or moral teaching: of which the follower of the passions is a useless hearer, according to the Philosopher in the first book of the Ethics. Hence it is written in the Proverbs: [[Prov 2:6|the Lord giveth wisdom: and out of his mouth cometh prudence and knowledge|Dominus dat sapientiam, et ex ore illius scientia et prudentia]]. And James says: [[Jas 1:5|if any of you want wisdom, let him ask of God|Si quis indiget sapientia, postulet a Deo]], [[Jas 1:5|And it shall be given him|et dabitur ei]].

paras.t: Ipse revelat, id est, hominibus manifestat, imo et angelis, profunda, id est alta seu difficilia, et abscondita, id est hominibus naturaliter ignota, quæ naturalem capacitatem seu facultatem transcendunt : de quibus ait Apostolus, Nobis autem revelavit Deus per Spiritum suum ; et Job, Revelat profunda de tenebris, et producit in lucem umbram mortis.
paras.en: [[2:22|He revealeth|Ipse revelat]], that is, makes manifest to men, and indeed to angels, [[2:22|deep|profunda]], that is, high or difficult things, [[2:22|and hidden things|et abscondita]], that is, things naturally unknown to men, which surpass natural capacity or power: of which the Apostle says, [[1 Cor 2:10|But to us God hath revealed them by his Spirit|Nobis autem revelavit Deus per Spiritum suum]]; and Job, [[Job 12:22|He discovereth deep things out of darkness, and bringeth up to light the shadow of death.|Revelat profunda de tenebris, et producit in lucem umbram mortis]]

paras.t: Et novit in tenebris constituta, id est in occulto : vel in tenebris ignorantiæ, quoad eos qui ea ignorant; vel in tenebris impietatis, id est peccata quantumlibet occulta et parva, secundum illud in Job : Ipse novit hominum vanitatem, et videns iniquitatem, nonne considerat? Aut certe in tenebris exterioribus seu locis caliginosis, contra quosdam indoctos, qui ea quæ in tenebris talibus fiunt aut sunt, Deum latere putabant. In quorum persona fertur in Psalmo : Et dixi, Forsitan tenebræ conculcabunt me. Hinc per Jeremiam Dominus ait : Si occultabitur vir in absconditis suis, et ego non videbo eum?
paras.en: [[2:22|and knoweth what is in darkness|Et novit in tenebris constituta]], that is, in secret: either in the darkness of ignorance, as regards those who do not know them; or in the darkness of ungodliness, that is, sins however hidden and small, according to that in Job: [[Job 11:11|For he knoweth the vanity of men, and when he seeth iniquity, doth he not consider it?|Ipse novit hominum vanitatem, et videns iniquitatem, nonne considerat?]] Or else in outward darkness or dark places, against certain unlearned people who thought that what is done or is in such darkness is hidden from God. In whose person it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 138:11|And I said: Perhaps darkness shall cover me|Et dixi, Forsitan tenebræ conculcabunt me]] [Latin conculcabunt, shall trample on]. Hence the Lord says through Jeremias: [[Jer 23:24|Shall a man be hid in secret places, and I not see him|Si occultabitur vir in absconditis suis, et ego non videbo eum?]]?

paras.t: Et lux cum eo est. In Deo enim est sapientia et veritas, qua nihil splendidius : imo Deus est lux, pulchritudo, et claritas superpurissima et immensa. De quo in prima Joannis epistola habetur : Deus lux est, et tenebræ non sunt in eo ullæ. Et tanta est claritas hujus lucis, ut ejus respectu cuncta sint tenebrosa, juxta illud in Job : Ecce etiam luna non splendet, et stellæ non sunt mundæ in conspectu ejus. Qui, secundum Apostolum, lucem habitat inaccessibilem. Circa prædicta scribit Hieronymus : Cui Deus revelat profunda, dicere potest, O altitudo divitiarum sapientiæ et scientiæ Dei! et habitante in se Spiritu Sancto, scrutatur etiam profunda Dei; et in profundo animæ suæ puteos fodit altissimos, omnemque terram, videlicet terrenas affectiones, egerit, quæ profundas aquas sapientiæ operire consuevit; servatque mandatum Salomonis, dicentis, Bibe aquas de cisternis tuis.
paras.en: [[2:22|and light is with him|Et lux cum eo est]]. For in God is wisdom and truth, than which nothing is more resplendent: indeed God is light, beauty and brightness, most pure beyond all purity and immeasurable. Of whom we have in the first epistle of John: [[1 John 1:5|God is light and in him there is no darkness|Deus lux est, et tenebræ non sunt in eo ullæ]]. And so great is the brightness of this light that in comparison with it all things are dark, according to that in Job: [[Job 25:5|Behold even the moon doth not shine, and the stars are not pure in his sight.|Ecce etiam luna non splendet, et stellæ non sunt mundæ in conspectu ejus]] Who, according to the Apostle, [[1 Tim 6:16|inhabiteth light inaccessible|lucem habitat inaccessibilem]]. On the foregoing Jerome writes: He to whom God reveals deep things can say, [[Rom 11:33|O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God!|O altitudo divitiarum sapientiæ et scientiæ Dei!]] and, the Holy Ghost dwelling in him, he searches even [[1 Cor 2:10|the deep things of God|profunda Dei]]; and in the depth of his soul he digs very deep wells, and clears out all the earth, that is, earthly affections, which is wont to cover over the deep waters of wisdom; and he keeps the command of Solomon, who says, [[Prov 5:15|Drink water out of thy own cistern|Bibe aquas de cisternis tuis]].

paras.t: Tibi Deus patrum nostrorum, scilicet Abrahæ, Isaac et Jacob, confiteor nostra mala, et tua bona; teque laudo gratias referendo, et tuam pietatem ac veritatem profitendo. Meminit autem patrum suorum, quia illorum meritis multa beneficia filiis Israel præstitit Deus. Et item, secundum Hieronymum, ne videatur suis tribuere meritis, refert hoc ad patrum justitiam, veritatemque Dei, qui seminis illorum etiam in captivitate miseretur.
paras.en: [[2:23|To thee, O God of our fathers|Tibi Deus patrum nostrorum]], namely of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, [[2:23|I give thanks|confiteor]] [Latin confiteor, I confess, which also means I give praise], confessing our evils and thy goods; [[2:23|and I praise thee|teque laudo]], giving thanks, and professing thy mercy and truth. He remembers his fathers because for their merits God bestowed many benefits on the children of Israel. And again, according to Jerome, lest he should seem to ascribe it to his own merits, he refers this to the justice of the fathers and to the truth of God, who has mercy on their seed even in captivity.

paras.t: Quia sapientiam ad cognoscendum divina mysteria, et fortitudinem et constantiam inconcussam inter prospera et adversa, dedisti mihi. Et nunc ostendisti mihi significata per somnium regis, ipsumque somnium, quæ rogavimus te ego et tres socii mei alicui nostrum ostendi, quia sermonem regis de somnio suo aperuisti nobis seu indicasti mihi, videlicet interpretationem quam cupit audire. In quo illud Amos est impletum : Non faciet Dominus verbum, nisi secretum suum revelaverit ad servos suos Prophetas.
paras.en: [[2:23|because thou hast given me wisdom|Quia sapientiam]] for knowing the divine mysteries, [[2:23|and strength|et fortitudinem]] and unshaken constancy amid prosperity and adversity. [[2:23|And now thou hast shewn me|Et nunc ostendisti mihi]] the things signified by the king's dream, and the dream itself, [[2:23|what we desired of thee|quæ rogavimus te]], that is, what I and my three companions asked to be shown to one of us, [[2:23|for thou hast made known to us the king's discourse|quia sermonem regis de somnio suo aperuisti nobis]], or hast shown it to me, namely the interpretation he desires to hear. In this was fulfilled that saying of Amos: [[Amos 3:7|the Lord God doth nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets|Non faciet Dominus verbum, nisi secretum suum revelaverit ad servos suos Prophetas]].

paras.t: Post hæc Daniel ingressus ad Arioch, quem constituerat rex ut perderet sapientes Babylonis, sic ei locutus est : Sapientes Babylonis ne perdas. Circa quod ait Hieronymus : Imitatur Daniel clementiam Dei, qui pro persecutoribus deprecatur, et non vult eos perire propter quos fuerat periturus. Introduc me in conspectum regis, et solutionem regi narrabo, tam super quæstione de somnio, quam super interpretatione ejus. Et in hoc arrogantiam evitavit : nam ipse recto itinere poterat ire ad regem, et tamen postulat introduci.
paras.en: [[2:24|After this Daniel went in to Arioch, to whom the king had given orders to destroy the wise men of Babylon, and|Post hæc Daniel ingressus ad Arioch, quem constituerat rex ut perderet sapientes Babylonis, sic]] [[2:24|he spoke thus to him: Destroy not the wise men of Babylon|ei locutus est : Sapientes Babylonis ne perdas]]. Concerning this Jerome says: Daniel imitates the clemency of God, who prays for his persecutors[[Luke 23:34||]], and does not wish those to perish on whose account he had been about to perish. [[2:24|bring me in before the king|Introduc me in conspectum regis]], [[2:24|and I will tell the solution to the king|et solutionem regi narrabo]], both on the question of the dream and on its interpretation. And in this he avoided arrogance: for he could have gone straight to the king, and yet he asks to be brought in.

paras.t: Tunc Arioch festinus introduxit Danielem ad regem. Festinavit, sciens se læta regique placitissima nuntiare, et quia sapientibus Babylonis parcere præoptavit. Quæritur, cur Arioch tam cito credidit Danieli. Respondent aliqui, quod Arioch aliunde habuit experimentum quod Daniel haberet spiritum propheticum : ideo etiam credidit eum veracem, quoniam vidit tam justum, studiosum ac temperatum, ut in exordio patuit. Et dixit ei : Inveni hominem de filiis transmigrationis Juda, id est de numero eorum qui cum Joakim de Judæa translati sunt huc, qui solutionem regi annuntiet. Arioch loquitur quasi sua inquisitione atque industria invenisset Danielem, volens per hoc regi placere more servorum, qui quum bona annuntiant, sua videri volunt, et sibi adscribi. Quandoque tamen dicitur aliquis invenire, non solum quod quærit, sed quod sibi etiam inopinate aut a casu occurrit, sicut qui improvise thesaurum inveniunt.
paras.en: [[2:25|Then Arioch in haste brought in Daniel to the king|Tunc Arioch festinus introduxit Danielem ad regem]]. He made haste, knowing that he brought news glad and most pleasing to the king, and because he much preferred that the wise men of Babylon be spared. It is asked why Arioch believed Daniel so quickly. Some answer that Arioch had proof from elsewhere that Daniel had the prophetic spirit; and he believed him truthful also because he saw him so just, studious and temperate, as appeared at the beginning[[Dan 1:8||]]. [[2:25|and said to him|Et dixit ei]]: [[2:25|I have found a man of the children of the captivity of Juda|Inveni hominem de filiis transmigrationis Juda]], that is, of the number of those who were carried over hither from Judea with Joakim, [[2:25|that will resolve the question to the king|qui solutionem regi annuntiet]]. Arioch speaks as though he had found Daniel by his own search and diligence, wishing by this to please the king, after the manner of servants, who, when they bring good news, want it to seem their own and to have it put down to themselves. Sometimes, however, a man is said to find not only what he seeks but also what comes his way unexpectedly or by chance, as those who find a treasure unawares.

paras.t: Respondit rex et dixit Danieli, cujus nomen erat Balthasar : Putasne vere potes mihi indicare somnium quod vidi, et interpretationem ejus ? Quæ multum læta sunt, vix creduntur; similiter quæ valde difficilia : ideo rex somnium et interpretationem ejus vehementissime scire desiderans, eaque sibi insinuari difficile esse perpendens, prima facie vix credidit Arioch. Ob hoc Danielem interrogavit. Et secundum Hieronymum, servat ordinem quæstionis, ut primo somnium, et postea interpretationem quærat : ut quum somnium audierit, et quod viderat recognoverit, tunc credat et interpretationi, quæ variam recipit conjecturam.
paras.en: [[2:26|The king answered, and said to Daniel, whose name was Baltassar|Respondit rex et dixit Danieli, cujus nomen erat Balthasar]]: [[2:26|Thinkest thou indeed that thou canst tell me the dream that I saw, and the interpretation thereof?|Putasne vere potes mihi indicare somnium quod vidi, et interpretationem ejus]] Things that are very glad are hardly believed, and likewise things very difficult: so the king, desiring most vehemently to know the dream and its interpretation, and judging it hard for them to be made known to him, at first hardly believed Arioch. For this reason he questioned Daniel. And according to Jerome, he keeps the order of the question, asking first for the dream and afterwards for the interpretation: so that when he has heard the dream and recognized what he had seen, he may then believe the interpretation too, which admits of various conjecture.

paras.t: Respondit Daniel coram rege imperterrite et constanter, loquente in ipso et per ipsum Spiritu Sancto : Mysterium, id est occultum somnium, et secretam interpretationem ejus, quod rex interrogat, sapientes, magi, et arioli (verba ista exposita sunt), et aruspices nequeunt indicare regi: quasi dicat, Nec humana, nec magica arte potest agnosci. Per aruspices autem Hieronymus accipit eos qui exta inspiciunt, et ex his futura denuntiant. Secundum Albertum vero, aruspices sunt augures, qui ex his quæ in aura vel aere fiunt, divinationem promittunt, ut in volatu avium vel garritu, vel auditu tonitruorum, vel occursu bestiarum. Porro, omne quod occultum est homini, et ab hominibus ignoratur, vocari potest mysterium. Sed est Deus in cœlo : qui licet infinitus incircumscriptibilisque sit, specialiter tamen in cœlo esse et habitare asseritur, quia ibidem evidentius ac magnificentius operatur, et clarius se illic ostendit; revelans mysteria, id est, secreta manifestans, quando, ubi, quibus, quoties, et quomodo vult. His verbis, secundum Hieronymum, occulte retrahit regem a multorum cultu deorum, et ad unius Dei notitiam dirigit. Qui indicavit tibi, rex Nabuchodonosor, id est, per somnium designavit, non tamen exposuit, quæ ventura sunt in novissimis temporibus, scilicet in ultima mundi ætate, et circa sæculi finem : quoniam visio ista decursum mundi usque in finem significat; imo, secundum Hieronymum, universa somnii interpretatio ad finem mundi pertingit, in quo imago statuæ quæ cernitur, conterenda est. Præterea in hac revelatione fit mentio de regno Christi, quod ultimum est regnorum; et tempus evangelicæ legis ultimum perhibetur, Paulo dicente : Nos sumus in quos fines sæculorum devenerunt. Et in prima epistola Joannis de tempore Christi inducitur : Novissima hora est.
paras.en: [[2:27|And Daniel made answer before the king|Respondit Daniel coram rege]], fearlessly and steadfastly, the Holy Ghost speaking in him and through him: [[2:27|The secret|Mysterium]], that is, the hidden dream and its secret interpretation, [[2:27|that the king desireth to know|quod rex interrogat]], [[2:27|none of the wise men, or the philosophers, or the diviners|sapientes, magi, et arioli]] (these words have been explained), [[2:27|or the soothsayers, can declare to the king|et aruspices nequeunt indicare regi]]: as if to say, It cannot be known either by human art or by magic. By *aruspices* [soothsayers] Jerome understands those who inspect entrails and foretell the future from them. But according to Albert, *aruspices* are augurs, who promise divination from things that happen in the *aura* or air, as in the flight or chatter of birds, the hearing of thunder, or the meeting of beasts. Further, whatever is hidden from man and unknown to men can be called a mystery. [[2:28|But there is a God in heaven|Sed est Deus in cœlo]]: who, though he is infinite and cannot be circumscribed, is yet said to be and to dwell in heaven in a special way, because there he works more evidently and magnificently and shows himself more clearly; [[2:28|that revealeth mysteries|revelans mysteria]], that is, making secrets manifest, when, where, to whom, how often and in what way he wills. By these words, according to Jerome, he quietly draws the king away from the worship of many gods and directs him to the knowledge of the one God. [[2:28|who hath shewn to thee, O king Nabuchodonosor|Qui indicavit tibi, rex Nabuchodonosor]], that is, has signified by the dream, though not explained, [[2:28|what is to come to pass in the latter times|quæ ventura sunt in novissimis temporibus]], namely in the last age of the world and near the end of the world: since this vision signifies the course of the world down to the end; nay, according to Jerome, the whole interpretation of the dream reaches to the end of the world, at which the image of the statue that is seen is to be broken. Moreover, in this revelation mention is made of the kingdom of Christ, which is the last of the kingdoms; and the time of the gospel law is said to be the last, as Paul says: We are they [[1 Cor 10:11|upon whom the ends of the world are come|in quos fines sæculorum devenerunt]]. And in the first epistle of John it is said of the time of Christ: [[1 John 2:18|it is the last hour|Novissima hora est]].

paras.t: Consequenter accedit ad solutionem : in qua plus respondet quam rex interrogavit, quia enuntiat quid rex ante somnium cogitavit, quod soli Deo cognitum fuit. Somnium tuum, et visiones capitis, id est cordis seu intellectus, tui in cubili tuo, hujuscemodi sunt. Somnium et visiones pro eodem hic accipiuntur, secundum Albertum : ut somnium dicatur, per comparationem ad dormientem; visiones, quoad rerum demonstrationes. Vel pluraliter ait, Visiones, propter multa quæ continentur in somnio isto.
