Tu, rex, cogitare cœpisti in strato tuo, quid esset futurum post hæc tempora tua et gesta, videlicet de successione regum sive regnorum, et his quæ tuum concernunt imperium : secundum quod homines avidi sunt scientiæ futurorum; et qui revelat mysteria, scilicet Deus, ostendit tibi quamvis indigno, ex sua clementia, quæ ventura sunt. Secundum Hieronymum, in hoc quod dicit, Tu, rex, cogitare cœpisti, ostendit causas somnii : quod idcirco ei Deus futurorum mysteria revelaverit, quia ipse rex voluit scire ventura. Circa quod Lyra ait : Ex hoc etiam patet, quod sollicitudo præcedens in vigilia, est bene causa somniorum sequentium in dormitione. Sed hoc contingit dupliciter : Uno modo naturaliter, quando phantasmata quæ fuerunt in vigilia, revertuntur in somno, vel similia. Hoc autem non fuit hic, quia talia somnia non sunt signa futurorum, sed magis præcedentium. Alio modo supernaturaliter, quando ex sollicitudine circa aliquid futurum disponitur homo, ut de talibus fiat sibi aliqua a Deo ostensio in sequenti somno : quoniam talia convenientius fiunt in somno quam in vigilia. Insuper, secundum Hieronymum, tanta est omnipotentis Dei clementia, ut etiam Nabuchodonosor impio regi dispensationis suæ, qua mundum regit, mysteria revelarit.
paras.en: Next he comes to the solution, in which he answers more than the king asked, since he declares what the king thought before the dream, which was known to God alone. [[2:28|Thy dream, and the visions of thy head|Somnium tuum, et visiones capitis]], that is, of thy heart or understanding, [[2:28|upon thy bed, are these|tui in cubili tuo, hujuscemodi sunt]]. *Dream* and *visions* are taken here for the same thing, according to Albert: it is called a dream by comparison with the sleeper, visions as regards the showing of things. Or he says *visions* in the plural because of the many things contained in this dream. [[2:29|Thou, O king, didst begin to think in thy bed, what should come to pass hereafter|Tu, rex, cogitare cœpisti in strato tuo, quid esset futurum post hæc]], after these thy times and deeds, namely about the succession of kings or kingdoms and the things that concern thy empire, since men are eager to know the future; [[2:29|and he that revealeth mysteries|et qui revelat mysteria]], namely God, [[2:29|shewed thee|ostendit tibi]], unworthy though thou art, out of his clemency, [[2:29|what shall come to pass|quæ ventura sunt]]. According to Jerome, in saying *Thou, O king, didst begin to think*, he shows the cause of the dream: that God revealed to him the mysteries of the future because the king himself wished to know what was to come. On this Lyra says: From this it is also plain that care beforehand in waking is indeed a cause of the dreams that follow in sleep. But this happens in two ways. In one way naturally, when the images [*phantasmata*] that were present in waking, or others like them, return in sleep. But this was not so here, since such dreams are not signs of things to come but rather of things gone before. In another way supernaturally, when through care about some future thing a man is disposed to receive from God some showing about such things in the sleep that follows: since such things are more fittingly done in sleep than in waking. Moreover, according to Jerome, so great is the clemency of almighty God that he revealed the mysteries of his dispensation, by which he rules the world, even to Nabuchodonosor, an impious king.

paras.t: Mihi quoque non in sapientia quæ est in me plus quam in cunctis viventibus, id est non per sapientiam meam naturalem et studio acquisitam, in qua ego non sum cunctis viventibus doctior, quamvis per supernaturalem illuminationem excellens sim (sicque negatio cadit super hoc totum), sacramentum hoc, id est sacrum istud secretum, revelatum est : quasi dicat, Non humana virtute aut sapientia istud agnosco; sed ut interpretatio somnii tibi regi manifesta fieret, et cogitationes mentis tuæ in somno habitas, oblivionique traditas, scires. Revelatio nempe prophetica est gratia gratis data, quæ ordinatur ad aliorum utilitatem, sicut ait Apostolus : Unicuique datur manifestatio Spiritus ad utilitatem. His verbis Daniel arrogantiam vitat, humilitatem ostendit, invidentiam aliorum fugit; sapientes Babylonis excusat, innuendo quod non nisi summi Dei revelatione ista potuerunt agnosci; regem quoque honorat, dum propter illius certificationem sibi fatetur divina revelata mysteria.
paras.en: [[2:30|To me also|Mihi quoque]] [[2:30|not by any wisdom that I have more than all men alive|non in sapientia quæ est in me plus quam in cunctis viventibus]], that is, not by my natural wisdom, acquired by study, in which I am not more learned than all the living, though I excel by supernatural illumination (and so the negation falls on the whole of this), [[2:30|this secret|sacramentum hoc]], that is, this sacred hidden thing, [[2:30|is revealed|revelatum est]]: as if to say, I do not know this by human power or wisdom; [[2:30|but that the interpretation might be made manifest to the king|sed ut interpretatio somnii tibi regi manifesta fieret]], [[2:30|and thou mightest know the thought of thy mind|et cogitationes mentis tuæ]], which thou hadst in sleep and which were given over to forgetfulness. For prophetic revelation is a grace freely given [*gratia gratis data*: a gift given for the good of others, not for the holiness of the one who receives it], which is ordered to the profit of others, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 12:7|the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man unto profit|Unicuique datur manifestatio Spiritus ad utilitatem]]. By these words Daniel avoids arrogance, shows humility, and shuns the envy of others; he excuses the wise men of Babylon, hinting that these things could not be known except by the revelation of the most high God; and he honours the king too, in confessing that the divine mysteries were revealed to him for the king's assurance.

paras.t: Tu, rex, videbas visione imaginativa in somno; et ecce : hoc adverbium signat notabile esse quod dicitur; quasi statua una grandis, id est imago alicujus repræsentativa. Unde statua dicitur, quia per similitudinem ponit seu statuit id, cujus est imago. Statua illa magna et statura sublimis stabat contra te. Omnia ista per similitudines in interiori sensu regis formatas fiebant : et statua ista magna et alta apparuit, quia rei magnæ fuit indicium; in visione quoque ita apparuit, quasi staret ex opposito regis intuens eum. Et intuitus ejus erat terribilis. Ideo horribiliter apparebat, quia horribilia figurabat, videlicet regnorum successionem et debellationem, quæ non sine innumerabilium hominum occisione completæ sunt. Hujus statuæ caput ex auro optimo erat, secundum apparentiam non confictam, sed alicujus veri significativam. Pectus autem et brachia de argento. Porro venter et femora ex ære, etc. Omnia ista sic somnialiter visa sunt, nec Prophetæ expositionem anticipare oportet : ipse enim sanctus Daniel omnia ista consequenter exponit in textu, idcirco textum transilio usque ibi : Hoc ergo est somnium.
paras.en: [[2:31|Thou, O king, sawest|Tu, rex, videbas]] in an imaginative vision in sleep, [[2:31|and behold|et ecce]]: this adverb marks that what is said is noteworthy; [[2:31|there was as it were a great statue|quasi statua una grandis]], that is, an image representing something. It is called a *statue* [*statua*] because by likeness it sets up or establishes [*statuit*] that of which it is the image. [[2:31|this statue, which was great and high, tall of stature, stood before thee|Statua illa magna et statura sublimis stabat contra te]]. All these things were done by likenesses formed in the king's inner sense: and this statue appeared great and tall because it was the sign of a great thing; in the vision too it appeared as though it stood opposite the king, looking at him. [[2:31|and the look thereof was terrible|Et intuitus ejus erat terribilis]]. It appeared fearful because it figured fearful things, namely the succession and overthrow of kingdoms, which were not accomplished without the slaughter of countless men. [[2:32|The head of this statue was of fine gold|Hujus statuæ caput ex auro optimo erat]], in an appearance not feigned but signifying something true. [[2:32|but the breast and the arms of silver|Pectus autem et brachia de argento]], [[2:32|and the belly and the thighs of brass|Porro venter et femora ex ære]], etc. All these things were seen thus in the dream, and there is no need to anticipate the Prophet's explanation: for holy Daniel himself explains them all in order in the text; and so I pass over the text as far as the words: [[2:36|This is the dream|Hoc ergo est somnium]].

paras.t: Deinceps expositionem annectit. Interpretationem quoque ejus dicemus coram te, rex. Tu rex regum es : primo, quoniam multos reges devicit, eisque imperavit; secundo, quoniam tempore suo non fuit ei in terra æqualis. Hinc etiam in Ezechiele Nabuchodonosor vocatur rex regum. Et Deus cœli, regnum istud quod habes, scilicet Chaldæorum, et fortitudinem qua aliis prævales, et imperium quo pluribus præsides, et gloriam, id est famam, excellentiam, gloriationem quoque de crebris victoriis, dedit tibi. Omnia enim bona, Dei sunt dona, et ex specialibus causis providentia Dei promovit eum ad ista, sicut et Cyro contulit monarchiam, secundum quod ipsemet Cyrus loquitur : Omnia regna terræ dedit mihi Deus cœli. Et omnia, scilicet loca seu habitacula, in quibus habitant filii hominum, et bestiæ agri, volucres quoque cœli, dedit in manu, id est potestate tua, et sub ditione, id est jussione tua universa constituit : id est, omnem tibi terram cum hominibus ac brutis subjecit. Quod totum intelligendum est synecdochice ac hyperbolice, ponendo partem pro toto : ita quod hic est sermo per excessum dictus ad majorem expressionem faciendam, ad designandum quod valde multis nationibus imperavit, et irrationabilia variis modis possedit; non quod bruta ferocia sibi miraculose fuerint mansuefacta, sicut sanctis hominibus. Hinc frequenter per Jeremiam Dominus loquitur : Quia non solum homines, sed et bestias terræ dedi ei, scilicet Nabuchodonosor regi.
paras.en: Next he adds the explanation. [[2:36|we will also tell the interpretation thereof before thee, O king|Interpretationem quoque ejus dicemus coram te, rex]]. [[2:37|Thou art a king of kings|Tu rex regum es]]: first, because he conquered many kings and ruled over them; second, because in his time he had no equal on earth. Hence in Ezechiel too Nabuchodonosor is called king of kings[[Ezech 26:7||]]. [[2:37|and the God of heaven|Et Deus cœli]], [[2:37|a kingdom|regnum istud]] which thou hast, namely that of the Chaldeans, [[2:37|and strength|et fortitudinem]] by which thou prevailest over others, [[2:37|and power|et imperium]] by which thou presidest over many, [[2:37|and glory|et gloriam]], that is, fame, excellence, and glorying too in frequent victories, [[2:37|hath given thee|dedit tibi]]. For all good things are gifts of God, and for special reasons the providence of God advanced him to these things, just as it also bestowed the monarchy on Cyrus, as Cyrus himself says: [[1 Esd 1:2|The Lord the God of heaven hath given to me all the kingdoms of the earth|Omnia regna terræ dedit mihi Deus cœli]]. [[2:38|And all|Et omnia]], namely places or dwellings, [[2:38|wherein the children of men, and the beasts of the field do dwell|in quibus habitant filii hominum, et bestiæ agri]]: [[2:38|he hath also given the birds of the air into thy hand|volucres quoque cœli, dedit in manu]], that is, into thy power, [[2:38|and hath put all things under thy power|et sub ditione]], that is, thy command: that is, he has subjected to thee the whole earth with men and brute beasts. All this is to be understood by synecdoche and hyperbole, putting the part for the whole: so that here the speech is made by excess, for the sake of greater expression, to signify that he ruled very many nations and possessed the irrational creatures in various ways; not that fierce beasts were miraculously tamed for him, as for holy men. Hence the Lord often says through Jeremias: Not only men, but also [[Jer 28:14|I have given him the beasts of the earth|bestias terræ dedi ei]][[Jer 27:6||]], namely to King Nabuchodonosor.

paras.t: Tu es ergo caput aureum, id est, tu, o rex, et regnum tuum Babylonium, designatur per aureum caput statuæ quam vidisti : quia ceteros reges nunc excedis, sicut aurum reliqua metalla, et propter divitias quas in tuo imperio congregasti. Et rursus, quemadmodum caput primum est inter corporis membra, sic inter quatuor regna, per statuam secundum diversas ejus partes signata, regnum tuum Chaldæum est primum.
paras.en: [[2:38|thou, therefore, art the head of gold|Tu es ergo caput aureum]], that is, thou, O king, and thy Babylonian kingdom are signified by the golden head of the statue that thou sawest: because thou now surpassest the other kings, as gold surpasses the other metals, and because of the riches that thou hast gathered in thy empire. And again, as the head is first among the members of the body, so among the four kingdoms signified by the statue in its different parts, thy Chaldean kingdom is the first.

paras.t: Et post te consurget regnum aliud minus te, argenteum, hoc est regnum Medorum atque Persarum : quod occiso Balthasar filio filii Nabuchodonosor regis invaluit, et post mortem Darii unum regnum effectum est, Cyro utrumque regnum tenente : cujus tamen regnum minus fuit regno Nabuchodonosor regis, habuitque se ad illud sicut argentum ad aurum. Hoc itaque regnum signatum est per pectus et brachia argentea : nam et ideo duo brachia argentea visa sunt, quia (ut dictum est) regnum Persarum atque Medorum primo fuerunt duo regna divisa ; sed quoniam postea unum regnum sunt facta, hinc brachia ista in uno pectore argenteo videbantur. Et regnum aliud tertium æreum, quod imperabit universæ terræ. Hoc fuit regnum Græcorum sive Macedonum pro tempore Alexandri Magni. Tunc enim Alexander pene toti orienti prævaluit, et usque ad fines terræ pervenit; multi quoque solo ejus terrore dejecti, sponte subdiderunt se ei : non tamen simpliciter cunctis terræ provinciis imperavit et regnis, sed in hoc est hyperbolica quædam locutio. Quemadmodum autem æs durius est argento et auro, sic regnum istud præcedentibus fuit robustius. Quod etiam comparatum est æri, quod optime sonat, quoniam Græci sonoritate eloquentiæ intendebant : eratque regnum hoc ubique famosum propter potentiam, sapientiam, eloquentiamque Græcorum, quando et Aristoteles dixit : Sumus ergo nos Græci digni universum mundum gubernare. Hoc itaque regnum significatum est per ventrem et femora statuæ æreæ.
paras.en: [[2:39|And after thee shall rise up another kingdom, inferior to thee, of silver|Et post te consurget regnum aliud minus te, argenteum]], that is, the kingdom of the Medes and Persians: which grew strong when Balthasar, the son of the son of King Nabuchodonosor, was slain[[Dan 5:30||]], and after the death of Darius[[Dan 5:31||]] was made one kingdom, Cyrus holding both kingdoms; yet his kingdom was less than the kingdom of King Nabuchodonosor, and stood to it as silver to gold. This kingdom, then, was signified by the silver breast and arms: and two silver arms were seen for this reason, that (as has been said) the kingdom of the Persians and that of the Medes were at first two separate kingdoms; but since they were afterwards made one kingdom, these arms were seen on one silver breast. [[2:39|and another third kingdom of brass, which shall rule over all the world|Et regnum aliud tertium æreum, quod imperabit universæ terræ]]. This was the kingdom of the Greeks or Macedonians in the time of Alexander the Great. For then Alexander prevailed over nearly the whole East and reached the ends of the earth; and many, overthrown by the mere terror of him, submitted to him of their own accord: yet he did not rule absolutely over all the provinces and kingdoms of the earth, but there is a kind of hyperbole in this. And as brass is harder than silver and gold, so this kingdom was stronger than those before it. It is also compared to brass, which rings out very well, because the Greeks gave themselves to sonorous eloquence; and this kingdom was famous everywhere for the power, wisdom and eloquence of the Greeks, at the time when Aristotle too said: We Greeks, then, are worthy to govern the whole world. This kingdom, then, was signified by the brazen belly and thighs of the statue.

paras.t: Et regnum quartum, scilicet Romanorum imperium, erit velut ferreum. Cujus ratio subditur : Quomodo ferrum comminuit et domat omnia tangibilia, sibi in materia communicantia, seu cuncta metalla ; sic comminuet et conteret, id est destruet, omnia hæc regna præfata. Romani enim, præsertim tempore Julii atque Pompeii et Octaviani, monarchiam sortiti sunt, omniumque regnorum gentem et gloriam devicerunt, ac plurimos occiderunt. Unde hoc regnum signatum est per ferreas tibias statuæ hujus ; et per duas statuæ tibias intelligi potest, quod regnum hoc postea divisum est in regnum Romanorum et Constantinopolitanum imperium.
paras.en: [[2:40|And the fourth kingdom|Et regnum quartum]], namely the empire of the Romans, [[2:40|shall be as iron|erit velut ferreum]]. The reason is added: [[2:40|As iron breaketh into pieces, and subdueth all things|Quomodo ferrum comminuit et domat omnia]] that can be touched [*tangibilia*], that share with it in matter, or all metals; [[2:40|so shall that break|sic comminuet]] [[2:40|and destroy|et conteret]], that is, lay waste, [[2:40|all these|omnia hæc]] kingdoms aforesaid. For the Romans, especially in the time of Julius, Pompey and Octavian, obtained the monarchy, overcame the people and the glory of all the kingdoms, and killed very many. Hence this kingdom was signified by the iron legs of this statue; and by the statue's two legs it can be understood that this kingdom was afterwards divided into the kingdom of the Romans and the empire of Constantinople.

paras.t: Porro, quia vidisti pedum et digitorum qui erant in pede, secundum Albertum, partem testeam figuli, et partem ferream, id est unam partem terream, ut est testa formata a figulo, aliam partem de ferro : designat videlicet, quod regnum divisum erit : id est, primo erit fortissimum atque durissimum tanquam ferrum, sed per intestina bella, civiumque discordias intra se et contra se, dividetur ac debile fiet : quod Augustinus in libris de Civitate Dei clarissime docet impletum. Nam et Julius quum vicisset occidentem, et Pompeius victo oriente, contra se invicem gravissime præliabantur : imo causa quod Romanum imperium ita deperiit, fuit Romanorum infelix ac detestanda ambitio. Quod tamen, id est quæ divisio, de plantario ferri orietur, id est de fortitudine Romani imperii, ex qua dissensio orta est : in qua divisione, una pars Romanorum facta est debilis, alia fortis ac prævalens : nam et Julius tandem fugavit Pompeium. Planta autem statuæ ferrea apparebat, sed digiti de ea prodeuntes, partim testei, partim ferrei visi sunt. Robur autem et opulentia Romanorum, fuit eis occasio ambitionis et dissensionis : nam ceteris superatis, contra se invicem bellare cœperunt. Et istud consequenter in textu subjungitur.
paras.en: [[2:41|And whereas thou sawest the feet, and the toes|Porro, quia vidisti pedum et digitorum]] that were on the foot, according to Albert, [[2:41|part of potter's clay, and part of iron|partem testeam figuli, et partem ferream]], that is, one part of earth, like a pot formed by a potter, the other part of iron: this signifies, namely, that [[2:41|the kingdom shall be divided|regnum divisum erit]]: that is, at first it will be very strong and very hard like iron, but through civil wars and the discords of its citizens within itself and against itself it will be divided and become weak; and Augustine, in his books On the City of God, shows most clearly that this was fulfilled. For Julius, when he had conquered the West, and Pompey, having conquered the East, fought most grievously against each other: indeed the reason why the Roman empire so came to ruin was the unhappy and detestable ambition of the Romans. [[2:41|but yet|Quod tamen]], that is, this division, [[2:41|it shall take its origin from the iron|de plantario ferri orietur]] [*de plantario ferri*: literally "from the seed-bed of the iron"; Denis connects it with *planta*, the sole of the foot], that is, from the strength of the Roman empire, from which the dissension arose: in which division one part of the Romans was made weak, the other strong and prevailing; for Julius at length put Pompey to flight. Now the sole [*planta*] of the statue appeared of iron, but the toes coming forth from it were seen to be partly of earthenware, partly of iron. And the strength and wealth of the Romans was to them the occasion of ambition and dissension: for when the rest had been overcome, they began to make war on one another. And this is added next in the text.

paras.t: Secundum quod vidisti, o Nabuchodonosor, ferrum mixtum, id est junctum, testæ et luto : in pede equidem statuæ tria hæc videbantur, planta existente ferrea, digitis ejus terreis seu lutosis. Aliqui autem textum sic legunt, Ferrum mixtum testæ ex luto : ut sit sensus, quod testa fuit ex luto formata. Et digitos pedum vidisti ex parte ferreos, et ex parte fictiles, id est testeos : sicut expositum est, ita quod aliqui digiti erant ferrei, aliqui testei ; ex parte regnum erit solidum, et ex parte contritum. Hoc significatum est per prædicta, quod imperium istud pro parte erit robustum, præsertim in suo processu non longe a principio, et postea debile ; item quod una pars populi ejus vincetur ab alia. Quod autem vidisti ferrum mixtum testæ ex luto formatæ : quæ mixtio fuit per contactum, non autem mixtio proprie dicta ; commiscebuntur quidem humano semine, id est, ipsi Romani per connubia prolificabunt, ut contra adversarios augeantur, sed non adhærebunt sibi, per caritatem et pacem, filiis patrum discordiam sequentibus, sicut ferrum misceri non potest testæ, mixtione proprie dicta, per quam ex mixtibilibus fit aliquid formaliter unum : et ista intestina dissensio eorum qui corporaliter cohabitabant, figurabatur per conjunctionem ferri et testæ, quæ non nisi superficialiter miscebantur, seu potius jungebantur, quia jam dictum est quod misceri non queunt.
paras.en: [[2:41|according as thou sawest|Secundum quod vidisti]], O Nabuchodonosor, [[2:41|the iron mixed|ferrum mixtum]], that is, joined, [[2:41|with the miry clay|testæ et luto]]: for in the foot of the statue these three were seen, the sole being of iron, and its toes of earth or clay. Some, however, read the text thus: *Ferrum mixtum testæ ex luto* [iron mixed with earthenware made of clay], so that the sense is that the earthenware was formed of clay. [[2:42|And as the toes of the feet were part of iron, and part of clay|Et digitos pedum vidisti ex parte ferreos, et ex parte fictiles]], that is, of earthenware, as has been explained, so that some toes were of iron, some of earthenware: [[2:42|the kingdom shall be partly strong, and partly broken|ex parte regnum erit solidum, et ex parte contritum]]. By the foregoing it was signified that this empire will be partly sturdy, especially in its course not long after its beginning, and afterwards weak; and also that one part of its people will be conquered by another. [[2:43|And whereas thou sawest the iron mixed with miry clay|Quod autem vidisti ferrum mixtum testæ ex luto]] formed (a mixing that was by contact, not mixing properly so called): [[2:43|they shall be mingled indeed together with the seed of man|commiscebuntur quidem humano semine]], that is, the Romans will beget offspring through marriages, so as to grow in number against their adversaries, [[2:43|but they shall not stick fast one to another|sed non adhærebunt sibi]] by charity and peace, the sons following the discord of their fathers, [[2:43|as iron cannot be mixed with clay|sicut ferrum misceri non potest testæ]] by mixing properly so called, by which something formally one is made out of things that can be mixed: and this internal dissension of men who lived together bodily was figured by the joining of iron and earthenware, which were mixed only on the surface, or rather joined, since, as has been said already, they cannot be mixed.

paras.t: In diebus autem regnorum illorum, id est decursis temporibus regnorum de quibus jam mentio facta est, adhuc durante regno Romano; vel pluraliter dicit, Regna, propter partes Romani regni præfatas; suscitabit, id est, promovebit et faciet, Deus cæli regnum quod in æternum non dissipabit, id est regnum atque Ecclesiam Christi, de quo angelus dixit ad Virginem : Regnabit in domo Jacob in æternum, et regni ejus non erit finis. Et Isaias : Multiplicabitur, inquit, ejus imperium, et pacis non erit finis. Regnum quippe et status Ecclesiæ a tempore Christi incepit, et usque in finem mundi durabit, deinde in cœlis perficietur. Hic enim inchoatur, et in patria perpetuatur. Duplex autem est regimen populi regni Christi, puta Ecclesiæ, scilicet spirituale et sæculare, seu divinum atque civile ; et Christus per suos vicarios, prælatos, ac principes regnat in Christianis, in quorum cordibus spiritualiter regnat in via per gratiam, in patria vero per gloriam. Et regnum ejus populo alteri non tradetur, id est, hostium manibus non tradetur. Quamvis enim Christus plebem fidelem permiserit et permittit, ac potissime permissurus sit tempore Antichristi ab impiis impugnari, partimque vinci ac trucidari, nunquam tamen permittit hanc in toto exstingui; imo eidem promisit : Ego vobiscum sum cunctis diebus usque ad consummationem sæculi. Aliqui autem referunt clausulam istam ad populum Christi, quantum ad statum ejus in Ecclesia triumphanti, eo quod regnum Christi potissime sit in cœlo, ubi cives sunt immortales.
paras.en: [[2:44|But in the days of those kingdoms|In diebus autem regnorum illorum]], that is, when the times of the kingdoms already mentioned have run their course, while the Roman kingdom still lasts; or he says *kingdoms* in the plural because of the parts of the Roman kingdom spoken of above; [[2:44|will set up|suscitabit]], that is, will advance and make, [[2:44|the God of heaven|Deus cæli]] [[2:44|a kingdom that shall never be destroyed|regnum quod in æternum non dissipabit]], namely the kingdom and Church of Christ, of which the angel said to the Virgin: [[Luke 1:32|he shall reign in the house of Jacob for ever|Regnabit in domo Jacob in æternum]], [[Luke 1:33|And of his kingdom there shall be no end|et regni ejus non erit finis]]. And Isaias: [[Is 9:7|His empire shall be multiplied|Multiplicabitur]], he says, [[Is 9:7|and there shall be no end of peace|et pacis non erit finis]]. For the kingdom and state of the Church began from the time of Christ, and will last to the end of the world, and afterwards will be made perfect in heaven: for here it is begun, and in the fatherland it is made everlasting. Now the government of the people of Christ's kingdom, that is, of the Church, is twofold, namely spiritual and secular, or divine and civil; and Christ reigns among Christians through his vicars, prelates and princes, and in their hearts he reigns spiritually, by grace on the way [that is, in this life] and by glory in the fatherland. [[2:44|and his kingdom shall not be delivered up to another people|Et regnum ejus populo alteri non tradetur]], that is, shall not be delivered into the hands of enemies. For although Christ has permitted and permits, and will permit above all in the time of Antichrist, the faithful people to be attacked by the impious and partly conquered and slaughtered, yet he never permits it to be wholly extinguished; nay, he promised it: [[Matt 28:20|I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the world|Ego vobiscum sum cunctis diebus usque ad consummationem sæculi]]. Some, however, refer this clause to the people of Christ as regards its state in the Church triumphant, since the kingdom of Christ is above all in heaven, where the citizens are immortal.

paras.t: Comminuet autem et consumet universa regna hæc. Regna enim præfata etiam cum Romano imperio, subdita facta sunt regno Christi atque Ecclesiæ, consumptis in eis ritibus paganismi, omnique pristino tumore ac statu superbiæ; et in fine, Antichristo occiso, omnes pene convertentur ad Christum. Postremo, in finali judicio omnis terrena ac inimica potestas tolletur, et omnia Christo plenissime subjicientur. Hinc enim Christi Ecclesiæ promissum est a Michæa : Exaltabitur manus tua super hostes tuos, et omnes inimici tui peribunt; et ab Isaia, Gens et regnum quod non servierit tibi, peribit. Denique de Christi Apostolis prædictum fuit atque impletum est : Constitues eos principes super omnem terram. Et ipsum stabit in vigore virtutum, et gratia Dei ad divina erectum, in æternum, nunc inchoative per dona gratiæ, et in futuro completive per dona gloriæ : sicut et Christus eis promisit, Gaudium vestrum nemo tollet a vobis.
paras.en: [[2:44|and it shall break in pieces, and shall consume all these kingdoms|Comminuet autem et consumet universa regna hæc]]. For the kingdoms aforesaid, together with the Roman empire too, were made subject to the kingdom of Christ and of the Church, the rites of paganism being consumed in them, with all their former swelling and proud state; and at the end, when Antichrist has been slain, nearly all will be converted to Christ. Lastly, at the final judgment all earthly and hostile power will be taken away, and all things will be most fully subjected to Christ. For hence it was promised to the Church of Christ by Micheas: [[Mich 5:9|Thy hand shall be lifted up over thy enemies, and all thy enemies shall be cut off|Exaltabitur manus tua super hostes tuos, et omnes inimici tui peribunt]]; and by Isaias: [[Is 60:12|the nation and the kingdom that will not serve thee, shall perish|Gens et regnum quod non servierit tibi, peribit]] [the margin gives Is. ix, 12; the words are Is 60:12]. Lastly, it was foretold of the Apostles of Christ, and fulfilled: [[Ps 44:17|thou shalt make them princes over all the earth|Constitues eos principes super omnem terram]]. [[2:44|and itself shall stand|Et ipsum stabit]] in the vigour of the virtues, and raised up by the grace of God to divine things, [[2:44|for ever|in æternum]]: now in its beginning, through the gifts of grace, and hereafter in its completion, through the gifts of glory; as Christ also promised them: [[John 16:22|your joy no man shall take from you|Gaudium vestrum nemo tollet a vobis]].

paras.t: Secundum quod vidisti, id est, eo modo cuncta comminuet, et durabit, prout in visione tibi ostensum est, scilicet, quod de monte abscissus est lapis sine manibus. Lapis iste est Christus ob suam immobilem firmitatem. De quo ait Psalmista : Lapidem quem reprobaverunt ædificantes, hic factus est in caput anguli. Et in Zacharia de ipso habetur : Super lapidem unum oculi septem sunt. De quo per Isaiam Dominus ait : Ecce ego mittam in Sion lapidem probatum, angularem, pretiosum, in fundamento fundatum. Mons autem intelligitur Synagoga, quantum ad sanctos Patriarchas, reges et Prophetas, de quibus natus est Christus. Vel mons est virgo Maria, propter altissimam ejus excellentiam in omni sanctitate et gratia : de quo monte abscissus est, id est prodiit, Christus, sine manibus, id est absque operatione, ope, semine, coituque humanis, virtute et operatione Spiritus Sancti, qui in Zacharia protestatur : Ecce ego cælabo sculpturam ejus, id est, corpus ejus in utero virginali formabo.
paras.en: [[2:45|According as thou sawest|Secundum quod vidisti]], that is, he will break all things in pieces and will endure in the way that was shown thee in the vision, namely, [[2:45|that the stone was cut out of the mountain without hands|quod de monte abscissus est lapis sine manibus]]. This stone is Christ, because of his immovable firmness. Of him the Psalmist says: [[Ps 117:22|The stone which the builders rejected; the same is become the head of the corner|Lapidem quem reprobaverunt ædificantes, hic factus est in caput anguli]]. And in Zacharias it is said of him: [[Zach 3:9|upon one stone there are seven eyes|Super lapidem unum oculi septem sunt]]. Of him the Lord says through Isaias: [[Is 28:16|Behold I will lay a stone in the foundations of Sion, a tried stone, a corner stone, a precious stone, founded in the foundation|Ecce ego mittam in Sion lapidem probatum, angularem, pretiosum, in fundamento fundatum]]. The mountain is understood as the Synagogue, as regards the holy Patriarchs, kings and Prophets of whom Christ was born. Or the mountain is the Virgin Mary, because of her most lofty excellence in all holiness and grace: from which mountain Christ was cut out, that is, came forth, without hands, that is, without human working, help, seed or intercourse, by the power and working of the Holy Ghost, who declares in Zacharias: [[Zach 3:9|behold I will grave the graving thereof|Ecce ego cælabo sculpturam ejus]], that is, I will form his body in the virginal womb.

paras.t: Et comminuit testam, et ferrum, et æs, et argentum, et aurum, id est, universa mundi regna sibi subjiciet, adversariosque prosternet, quemadmodum ab Isaia prædictum est : Ad eum venient, et confundentur omnes qui repugnant ei. Qui enim modo Christo non subjiciuntur per fidem et obedientiam, in æternum sunt perituri. Ideo supra in descriptione somnii textus habet : Tunc contrita sunt pariter ferrum et testa, æs, argentum et aurum, videlicet regna omnia per hæc designata, et redacta sunt quasi in favillam æstivæ areæ, id est in favillam stipulæ, quæ relinquitur in area æstivali, domo succensa, juxta illud Isaiæ : Erit fortitudo vestra ut favilla stuppæ, et opus vestrum quasi scintilla ; et succendetur utrumque simul; quæ rapta sunt vento, id est, prædicta cito concussa et mota sunt, sicut de impiis dicit Psalmista : Deus meus, pone illos ut rotam, et sicut stipulam ante faciem venti. Nullusque locus inventus est eis, id est, ipsa de locis suis sublata sunt, juxta illud : Quæsivi eum, scilicet impium, et non est inventus locus ejus. Et in Job : Vidi impios Domino flante periisse. Lapis autem qui percusserat statuam, id est Christus, qui mundanam potestatem et regnum terrenum prostravit, factus est mons magnus, id est universis prælatus, Rex regum et Dominus dominantium factus quoad naturam assumptam, omni sanctitate excellens. De quo scriptum est in Isaia : Erit mons domus Domini in vertice montium. Et implevit universam terram majestate sua et gloria, id est, regimen ejus totum mundum occupavit : juxta illud in Psalmo, Replebitur majestate ejus omnis terra; et in Malachia, A solis ortu usque ad occasum, magnum est nomen meum in gentibus, dicit Dominus ; rursusque in Psalmo, Reminiscentur et convertentur ad Dominum universi fines terræ.
paras.en: [[2:45|and broke in pieces the clay, and the iron, and the brass, and the silver, and the gold|Et comminuit testam, et ferrum, et æs, et argentum, et aurum]], that is, he will subject to himself all the kingdoms of the world and lay low his adversaries, as was foretold by Isaias: [[Is 45:25|they shall come to him, and all that resist him shall be confounded|Ad eum venient, et confundentur omnes qui repugnant ei]]. For those who are not now subject to Christ by faith and obedience will perish for ever. Therefore above, in the description of the dream, the text has: [[2:35|Then was the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver, and the gold broken to pieces together|Tunc contrita sunt pariter ferrum et testa, æs, argentum et aurum]], namely all the kingdoms signified by them, [[2:35|and became like the chaff of a summer's threshing floor|et redacta sunt quasi in favillam æstivæ areæ]], that is, into the ashes of the stubble that is left on a summer threshing floor when it has been burnt [the print has *domo succensa*, "the house being set on fire"], according to that of Isaias: [[Is 1:31|your strength shall be as the ashes of tow, and your work as a spark: and both shall burn together|Erit fortitudo vestra ut favilla stuppæ, et opus vestrum quasi scintilla ; et succendetur utrumque simul]]; [[2:35|and they were carried away by the wind|quæ rapta sunt vento]], that is, the things aforesaid were quickly shaken and moved, as the Psalmist says of the wicked: [[Ps 82:14|O my God, make them like a wheel; and as stubble before the wind|Deus meus, pone illos ut rotam, et sicut stipulam ante faciem venti]]. [[2:35|and there was no place found for them|Nullusque locus inventus est eis]], that is, they were taken away from their places, according to that: [[Ps 36:36|I sought him|Quæsivi eum]], namely the wicked man, [[Ps 36:36|and his place was not found|et non est inventus locus ejus]]. And in Job: [[Job 4:8|I have seen|Vidi impios]] the wicked [[Job 4:9|Perishing by the blast of God|Domino flante periisse]]. [[2:35|but the stone that struck the statue|Lapis autem qui percusserat statuam]], that is, Christ, who laid low worldly power and the earthly kingdom, [[2:35|became a great mountain|factus est mons magnus]], that is, set over all, made King of kings and Lord of lords as regards the nature he assumed, excelling in all holiness. Of this it is written in Isaias: [[Is 2:2|the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of mountains|Erit mons domus Domini in vertice montium]]. [[2:35|and filled the whole earth|Et implevit universam terram]] with his majesty and glory, that is, his rule has taken hold of the whole world: according to that in the Psalm, [[Ps 71:19|the whole earth shall be filled with his majesty|Replebitur majestate ejus omnis terra]] [the margin gives Ps. lxxxi, 19; the words are Ps 71:19]; and in Malachias, [[Mal 1:11|from the rising of the sun even to the going down, my name is great among the Gentiles|A solis ortu usque ad occasum, magnum est nomen meum in gentibus]], [[Mal 1:11|saith the Lord|dicit Dominus]]; and again in the Psalm, [[Ps 21:28|All the ends of the earth shall remember, and shall be converted to the Lord|Reminiscentur et convertentur ad Dominum universi fines terræ]].

paras.t: Præterea, sicut Hieronymus refert, quæ de lapide et potentissimo Christi regno jam dicta sunt, Judæi impiusque Porphyrius male exponunt de populo Israel : quem in fine sæculorum volunt esse fortissimum, et omnia regna conterere, et in æternum regnare. Advertendum quoque, quia ut Scholastica refert historia, Josephus super hæc verba de lapide dicit : Significavit etiam Daniel regi de lapide, quod mihi non placuit indicare. Josephus enim quum esset Judæus, noluit indicare destructionem Judæorum factam tempore Christi.
paras.en: Moreover, as Jerome relates, what has been said of the stone and of the most mighty kingdom of Christ the Jews and the impious Porphyry wrongly explain of the people of Israel, which they will have to be most mighty at the end of the ages, to break all kingdoms in pieces, and to reign for ever. It is to be noted also that, as the Scholastic History relates, Josephus says on these words about the stone: Daniel also told the king about the stone, which it has not pleased me to set out. For Josephus, being a Jew, did not wish to set out the destruction of the Jews that came about in the time of Christ.

paras.t: Deus magnus, cujus magnitudinis non est finis, cujus comparatione totum universum est quasi pulvis exiguus. Et magnitudo Dei quid est, nisi infinita perfectio ejus, ipsumque esse divinum, plenum, purum, immensum? Ostendit regi, tibi scilicet Nabuchodonosor, quæ ventura sunt postea, id est post te, prout scire optasti. Et verum est somnium quod vidisti, id est veri significativum, et fidelis interpretatio ejus, id est vera expositio quam audisti.
paras.en: [[2:45|the great God|Deus magnus]], [[Ps 144:3|of his greatness there is no end|cujus magnitudinis non est finis]], in comparison with whom the whole universe is [[Is 40:15|as a little dust|quasi pulvis exiguus]]. And what is the greatness of God but his infinite perfection, the divine being itself, full, pure, immense? [[2:45|hath shewn the king|Ostendit regi]], namely thee, Nabuchodonosor, [[2:45|what shall come to pass hereafter|quæ ventura sunt postea]], that is, after thee, as thou didst desire to know. [[2:45|and the dream is true|Et verum est somnium]] that thou sawest, that is, it signifies what is true, [[2:45|and the interpretation thereof is faithful|et fidelis interpretatio ejus]], that is, the explanation thou hast heard is true.

paras.t: Tunc rex Nabuchodonosor cecidit in faciem suam, humiliando se Deo cœli, cujus majestatem ex præinductis pensavit; tantaque admiratione repletus est ac stupore, quod se dejecit attonitus, et Danielem adoravit, et hostias et incensa, scilicet holocausta, præcepit ut sacrificarent ei. Contra hunc locum Porphyrius probare volens hoc volumen non a Daniele editum, sed ab alio quodam confictum, primo sic arguit : Nunquam accidere poterat, ut rex superbissimus hominem a se captum adoraret ; secundo, quod minus credibile est quod divinum ei cultum impenderet ; tertio, quia Daniel quum fuerit sanctus, non permisisset sibi adorationem, hostias et incensa impendi. Sed ista facillime dissolvuntur. Primo, quod gentilium error fuit, omne quod supra hominem aliquid apparet aut agit, Deum putare : sicut et barbari, viso quod Paulus apostolus non læderetur a vipera, dixerunt eum esse deum. Lycaonicenses quoque voluerunt ei ac Barnabæ sacrificare, quemadmodum in Actibus Apostolorum narratur. Secundo, quod adoratio hic accipitur pro reverentia magna seu adoratione duliæ, qua in Scripturis sæpe aliqui etiam sancti, quosdam homines vel angelos adorasse leguntur, ut Abraham tres angelos. Tertio, quod rex tanto stupore fuit impletus, ut vix sciret quid faceret. Quarto, quod Deum adoravit in Daniele, quemadmodum Alexander rex in pontifice Judæorum adoravit Deum eorum : ut hic refert Hieronymus; secundum quem etiam dici potest, quod Deo in Daniele sacrificari præcepit, sicut et verba sequentia insinuare videntur : statim namque majestatem Dei professus est. Denique licet hic scribitur quod jussit sacrificari Danieli, non tamen quod illud factum sit, aut Daniel istud permiserit : imo credendum est, quod non permisit sibi sacrificari ut Deo.
paras.en: [[2:46|Then king Nabuchodonosor fell on his face|Tunc rex Nabuchodonosor cecidit in faciem suam]], humbling himself before the God of heaven, whose majesty he weighed from what had gone before; and he was filled with such wonder and amazement that he threw himself down astonished, [[2:46|and worshipped Daniel|et Danielem adoravit]], [[2:46|and commanded that they should offer in sacrifice to him victims and incense|et hostias et incensa, scilicet holocausta, præcepit ut sacrificarent ei]], the victims being burnt offerings. Against this passage Porphyry, wishing to prove that this book was not written by Daniel but made up by someone else, argues first thus: It could never have happened that a most proud king should worship a man whom he had taken captive; second, what is less credible, that he should pay him divine worship; third, that Daniel, being holy, would not have allowed worship, victims and incense to be offered to him. But these objections are very easily answered. First, it was the error of the gentiles to take for a god whatever appears or acts as something above man: as the barbarians too, seeing that the apostle Paul was not hurt by the viper, said that he was a god[[Acts 28:6||]]. The Lycaonians also wished to sacrifice to him and to Barnabas[[Acts 14:12||]], as is told in the Acts of the Apostles [the margin gives Acts xxviii, 3–6 and xiv, 10–12]. Second, adoration is taken here for great reverence, or the adoration of dulia [that is, the honour given to a creature for its excellence, as distinct from latria, the worship due to God alone], with which in the Scriptures even some saints are often read to have adored certain men or angels, as Abraham adored the three angels[[Gen 18:2||]]. Third, the king was so filled with amazement that he scarcely knew what he was doing. Fourth, he adored God in Daniel, as King Alexander adored the God of the Jews in their high priest, as Jerome here relates; according to whom it can also be said that he commanded sacrifice to be offered to God in Daniel, as the words that follow seem to suggest, for he at once confessed the majesty of God. Lastly, although it is written here that he commanded sacrifice to be offered to Daniel, it is not written that this was done, or that Daniel allowed it: nay, it is to be believed that he did not allow sacrifice to be offered to him as to God.

paras.t: Loquens ergo rex ait Danieli : Vere Deus vester, quem colitis vos, Judæi, Deus deorum est, et Dominus regum. Ex suo effectu Deum Israel altissimum esse cognovit : quia illud revelavit Danieli quod dii Chaldæorum ac aliorum suis non valuerunt revelare cultoribus. Hinc subditur : revelans mysteria, his qui cum Psalmista dicere possunt : Incerta et occulta sapientiæ tuæ manifestasti mihi; quoniam potuisti aperire sacramentum hoc, id est somnium et ejus mysterium declarare ex instructione divina. Ipse quoque Porphyrius fassus est, quod Deus Hebræorum sit pater et rex deorum, quem et numina perhorrescunt. Et Jethro auditis a Moyse mirabilibus Dei, ait in Exodo : Nunc cognovi quoniam magnus Dominus super omnes deos. Hæc demum conjunctio, Quoniam, etc., si referatur ad id quod ait rex, Vere Deus vester, Deus deorum est : potius dicit signum causæ, quam causam, vel dicit causam a posteriori.
paras.en: [[2:47|And the king spoke to Daniel, and said|Loquens ergo rex ait Danieli]]: [[2:47|Verily, your God|Vere Deus vester]], whom you Jews worship, [[2:47|is the God of gods, and Lord of kings|Deus deorum est, et Dominus regum]]. From its effect he knew the God of Israel to be most high: because he revealed to Daniel what the gods of the Chaldeans and of others could not reveal to their worshippers. Hence is added: [[2:47|and a revealer of hidden things|revelans mysteria]] to those who can say with the Psalmist: [[Ps 50:8|the uncertain and hidden things of thy wisdom thou hast made manifest to me|Incerta et occulta sapientiæ tuæ manifestasti mihi]] [the margin gives Ps. i, 8; the words are Ps 50:8]; [[2:47|seeing thou couldst discover this secret|quoniam potuisti aperire sacramentum hoc]], that is, couldst declare the dream and its mystery by divine instruction. Porphyry himself, too, confessed that the God of the Hebrews is the father and king of the gods, before whom even the divinities tremble. And Jethro, when he had heard from Moses the wonders of God, says in Exodus: [[Ex 18:11|Now I know, that the Lord is great above all gods|Nunc cognovi quoniam magnus Dominus super omnes deos]] [the margin gives Exod. xviii without a verse]. Lastly, this conjunction *Quoniam* [seeing], etc., if it is referred to what the king says, *Verily your God is the God of gods*, expresses rather a sign of the cause than the cause, or expresses a cause a posteriori [that is, reasoning from the effect back to the cause].

paras.t: Tunc rex Danielem in sublime extulit, id est, magnifice exaltavit verbis, signis, factis et donis, et munera multa et magna dedit ei. Et in hoc calumniator Ecclesiæ, inimicusque Christi Porphyrius reprehendit libri hujus auctorem, cur Propheta munera ista accepit. Cui respondendum, quod Daniel munera ista non ex cupiditate suscepit, sed ad consolationem populi sui capti ac spoliati. Sic enim et Joseph a rege Ægypti, et Mardochæus ab Assuero rege dignitatibus atque muneribus sublimati noscuntur. Et constituit eum super omnes provincias Babylonis, id est Babyloni Chaldææ metropoli subditas, principem secundum post regem : sicut et Pharao posuit Joseph Ægypto præpositum, Absque tui, inquiens, oris imperio nullus manum aut pedem movebit in omni terra Ægypti; et præfectum, quantum ad auctoritatis ac potestatis eminentiam, et magistrum, quantum ad judiciorum discretionem ordinationemque legum, super cunctos sapientes Babylonis, magos videlicet, ariolos sive aruspices.
paras.en: [[2:48|Then the king advanced Daniel to a high station|Tunc rex Danielem in sublime extulit]], that is, exalted him magnificently by words, signs, deeds and gifts, [[2:48|and gave him many and great gifts|et munera multa et magna dedit ei]]. And in this Porphyry, the slanderer of the Church and enemy of Christ, finds fault with the author of this book, asking why the Prophet accepted these gifts. To him it must be answered that Daniel accepted these gifts not out of covetousness but for the consolation of his people, captive and despoiled. For so too Joseph is known to have been raised up with dignities and gifts by the king of Egypt[[Gen 41:43||]], and Mardochai by King Assuerus[[Esth 8:2||]][[Esth 8:15||]]. [[2:48|and he made him governor over all the provinces of Babylon|Et constituit eum super omnes provincias Babylonis]], that is, those subject to Babylon, the chief city of Chaldea, as prince second after the king: just as Pharao too set Joseph over Egypt, saying: [[Gen 41:44|without thy commandment no man shall move hand or foot in all the land of Egypt|Absque tui, inquiens, oris imperio nullus manum aut pedem movebit in omni terra Ægypti]]; [[2:48|and chief|et præfectum]], as regards eminence of authority and power, [[2:48|of the magistrates|et magistrum]] [Denis reads *præfectum et magistrum*, "prefect and master", where the Vulgate has *præfectum magistratuum*], as regards discernment in judgments and the ordering of laws, [[2:48|over all the wise men of Babylon|super cunctos sapientes Babylonis]], namely the magicians, diviners or soothsayers.

paras.t: Daniel autem postulavit a rege licentiam faciendi quod subditur : et constituit auctoritate regis, super opera provinciæ Babylonis, Sidrach, Misach et Abdenago: id est, socios suos tres viros sapientes et virtuosos præfecit publicis provinciarum Babylonis operibus, unicuique certas partes terrarum committens, in die bonorum memor malorum, et sociis suis servans fidelitatem, eos suæ prosperitatis consortes efficiens qui suæ adversitatis atque periculi fuerunt participes : quod item Deo ordinante ac miserante peractum est, ad consolationem Judæorum per Babyloniæ provincias dispersorum. Ipse autem Daniel mansit in foribus regis : ab ejus latere non discedens, ut eum in favore Judæorum teneret, et ne quis inter regem et se seu populum Judæorum captum, discordias seminaret.
paras.en: [[2:49|And Daniel requested of the king|Daniel autem postulavit a rege]] leave to do what follows: [[2:49|and he appointed|et constituit]] by the king's authority [[2:49|Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago, over the works of the province of Babylon|super opera provinciæ Babylonis, Sidrach, Misach et Abdenago]]: that is, he set his three companions, wise and virtuous men, over the public works of the provinces of Babylon, committing to each certain parts of the land, mindful in the day of good things of evil things[[Ecclus 11:27||]], and keeping faith with his companions, making those partners in his prosperity who had shared his adversity and danger: and this too was done by God's ordering and mercy, for the consolation of the Jews scattered through the provinces of Babylonia. [[2:49|but Daniel himself was in the king's palace|Ipse autem Daniel mansit in foribus regis]] [literally "remained at the king's doors"; a printed note gives the reading *erat*, "was", for *mansit*]: not leaving his side, so as to keep him in favour towards the Jews, and so that no one might sow discord between the king and himself, or the captive people of the Jews.

paras.t: Legitur autem S. Franciscus quasi similem habuisse visionem, quam et Deus ei exposuit. Vidit enim statuam superius auream, in medio argenteam, inferius cupream. Juxta quod, quæ de statua Nabuchodonosor dicta sunt, ad statum Ecclesiæ seu cujuscumque religionis possunt referri : ut per auream statuæ portionem designetur status militantis Ecclesiæ, quantum ad ejus principium, quando fervor divini amoris, devotioque interna cum omni virtutum excellentia in plebe viguit christiana, potissime in religiosis; per partem vero argenteam, status in quo, caritatis ardore tepescente, claritas scientiæ et studium Scripturarum fulserunt; porro, per ferream partem, status ille miserrimus, in quo cordis duritia prævalet, suntque homines amantes se ipsos, qui excluso divino amore, carnali ac sæculari affectione repleti sunt.
paras.en: It is read, moreover, that St Francis had a vision somewhat like this one, which God also explained to him. For he saw a statue of gold above, of silver in the middle, and of copper below. Accordingly, what has been said of Nabuchodonosor's statue can be applied to the state of the Church or of any religious order: so that by the golden portion of the statue is signified the state of the Church militant in its beginning, when the fervour of divine love and inward devotion, with all excellence of the virtues, flourished in the Christian people, above all in religious; by the silver part, the state in which, as the ardour of charity grew lukewarm, the brightness of learning and the study of the Scriptures shone forth; and by the iron part, that most wretched state in which hardness of heart prevails, and men are lovers of themselves, who shut out divine love and are filled with carnal and worldly affection.

3.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI TERTII : NABUCHODONOSOR REX FECIT STATUAM AUREAM.
3.title_en: Explanation of the third chapter: King Nabuchodonosor made a statue of gold.

paras.t: PRÆSENTI capitulo tertia visio Danielis, id est a Daniele descripta, inducitur : et quamvis res gesta hic recitetur, visio tamen vocatur, propter angeli apparitionem in ea contentam.
paras.en: In the present chapter the third vision of Daniel is brought forward, that is, one described by Daniel: and although it is a deed done that is related here, it is nevertheless called a vision because of the appearance of the angel contained in it.

paras.t: Nabuchodonosor rex fecit, id est, per artifices fieri jussit, statuam auream, altitudine cubitorum sexaginta, latitudine cubitorum sex. Circa quod dicit Hieronymus : Velox oblivio veritatis, ut qui dudum servum Dei Danielem quasi Deum adoraverat, nunc statuam sibi fieri jubet, ut ipse adoretur in statua. Ex quibus elicitur, quod rex fecit hanc statuam ut ipse repræsentaretur per eam. Ideo quoque fecit eam tam magnam, ut intuentibus stuporem incuteret et terrorem, cultusque divinus sibi in ea reverentialius impenderetur. An autem statua ista fuerit totaliter aurea aut superficie tenus tantum, et an fuerit concava aut plena seu solida, non est adeo certum, quamvis aliqui dicant, quod non nisi exterius fuerat aurea. Denique per id quod dicitur, Altitudine sexaginta cubitorum, quidam affirmant describi altitudinem basis supra quam posita erat, non statuæ : aliter latitudo non corresponderet, quæ sex cubitorum fuisse conscribitur. Istud textui consonum non videtur, quia eodem modo locutionis, altitudo et latitudo statuæ hujus describitur : ideo sicut per id quod dicitur, Latitudine cubitorum sex, insinuatur statuæ latitudo; ita per id quod dicitur, Altitudine sexaginta cubitorum, non basis, sed statuæ altitudo exprimitur. Argumentum quoque nil cogit. Quemadmodum enim præfata altitudo, humani corporis altitudinem vehementer excedit, ita et latitudo illa latitudinem hominis : quæ duorum palmorum esse debet, secundum Albertum. Præterea, hujus Nabuchodonosor indicibilem pompam, secutus est alius eo posterior Nabuchodonosor, de quo in libro Judith habetur : qui jussit Holoferni conterere deos populorum, ut ipse solus a gentibus superatis haberetur ut deus.
paras.en: [[3:1|King Nabuchodonosor made|Nabuchodonosor rex fecit]], that is, ordered to be made by craftsmen, [[3:1|a statue of gold, of sixty cubits high, and six cubits broad|statuam auream, altitudine cubitorum sexaginta, latitudine cubitorum sex]]. Of this Jerome says: Swift is the forgetting of the truth, that he who but lately had adored Daniel, the servant of God, as a god, now commands a statue to be made for himself, that he himself may be adored in the statue. From this it is gathered that the king made this statue so that he himself might be represented by it. And he made it so large for this reason too, that it might strike those who beheld it with amazement and terror, and that divine worship might be paid to him in it with greater reverence. But whether this statue was wholly of gold or only on the surface, and whether it was hollow or full, that is, solid, is not so certain, although some say that it was golden only on the outside. Lastly, from the words [[3:1|of sixty cubits high|Altitudine sexaginta cubitorum]], some assert that it is the height of the base on which the statue stood that is described, not that of the statue: otherwise the breadth, which is written to have been six cubits, would not be in proportion. This does not seem consonant with the text, because the height and the breadth of this statue are described in the same manner of speech; therefore, just as by the words [[3:1|six cubits broad|Latitudine cubitorum sex]] the breadth of the statue is indicated, so by the words [[3:1|of sixty cubits high|Altitudine sexaginta cubitorum]] the height not of the base but of the statue is expressed. Nor does the argument compel anything. For just as the said height far exceeds the height of a human body, so too does that breadth exceed the breadth of a man, which, according to Albert, should be two palms. Moreover, the unspeakable pomp of this Nabuchodonosor was followed by another Nabuchodonosor later than he, of whom we read in the book of Judith: he commanded Holofernes to destroy the gods of the peoples, so that he alone might be held as a god by the conquered nations[[Jdt 3:13||]].

paras.t: Et statuit eam in campo Duran provinciæ Babylonis. Sicut in primi expositione capitulo patuit, Sennaar, Duran et Babylon, ejusdem loci nomina. Campus autem hic latissimus erat, ideo ibi statuit eam, ut plures circa eam congregarentur, et videretur a pluribus. Quumque statuam erexisset, circumsepivit campum, ut in Scholastica historia legitur. Unde pro Duran, Septuaginta transtulerunt, περίβολον, quod interpretatur conclusum. Albertus etiam dicit verisimile esse, quod vallavit eam vallo aqua pleno.
paras.en: [[3:1|and he set it up in the plain of Dura, of the province of Babylon|Et statuit eam in campo Duran provinciæ Babylonis]]. As was made clear in the exposition of the first chapter[[Dan 1:2||]], Sennaar, Duran and Babylon are names of the same place. Now this plain was very broad, and so he set the statue up there, that many might be gathered about it and that it might be seen by many. And when he had erected the statue, he fenced the plain round, as we read in the Scholastic History [the biblical history of Peter Comestor]. Hence for Duran the Septuagint translated *peribolon*, which is interpreted "enclosed". Albert too says it is likely that he surrounded it with a dyke full of water.

paras.t: Itaque Nabuchodonosor rex misit ad congregandos satrapas, qui erant quasi senatores seu nobiles barones, magistratus, qui officia curiæ ordinabant, seu ad consiliarios, et judices, quorum fuit causas audire ac determinare, duces exercitus seu militum, scilicet Cerethi et Phelethi. Cerethi autem dicuntur quasi vivificantes, quoniam cives vivificabant, id est, in vita servabant. Phelethi vero dicuntur mortificantes, quasi qui pessimos trucidabant. Et tyrannos, id est strenuos inter milites vel tributorum regalium exactores, et præfectos, id est præpositos, seu eos qui singulis præerant villis, omnesque principes regionum Babyloni subditarum : qui principes erant præsides provinciarum; ut convenirent ad dedicationem, id est consecrationem, statuæ, quæ sancta ac divina fuit pronuntianda, quam erexerat Nabuchodonosor rex. Secundum Hieronymum, excelsa periculis suis stant, id est, majori periculo expositi sunt altiores. Unde Glossa apertius ait, Excelsa periculosius stant. Insuper, secundum Hieronymum, citius corruunt quæ sublimia sunt. Principes et majores congregati sunt, ut per eos seducantur minores. Qui enim divites sunt et potentes, dum timent carere divitiis atque potentia, facilius supplantantur peccatis; et seductis magistratibus, subditi pereunt exemplo majorum.
paras.en: [[3:2|Then Nabuchodonosor, the king, sent to call together|Itaque Nabuchodonosor rex misit ad congregandos]] [[3:2|the nobles|satrapas]], who were as it were senators or noble barons, [[3:2|the magistrates|magistratus]], who ordered the offices of the court, or to the counsellors, [[3:2|and the judges|et judices]], whose office it was to hear and decide causes, [[3:2|the captains|duces]] of the army or of the soldiers, namely the Cerethi and Phelethi. Now the Cerethi are so called as being "life-givers", because they kept the citizens alive, that is, preserved them in life; but the Phelethi are called "slayers", as those who put the worst men to death. [[3:2|the rulers|Et tyrannos]], that is, the valiant among the soldiers, or the collectors of the royal tributes, [[3:2|and governors|et præfectos]], that is, overseers, or those who were set over the several towns, [[3:2|and all the chief men of the provinces|omnesque principes regionum]] subject to Babylon, which princes were the governors of the provinces; [[3:2|to come to the dedication|ut convenirent ad dedicationem]], that is, the consecration, [[3:2|of the statue|statuæ]], which was to be proclaimed holy and divine, [[3:2|which king Nabuchodonosor had set up|quam erexerat Nabuchodonosor rex]]. According to Jerome, high things stand by their own perils, that is, the higher men are exposed to the greater danger. Hence the Gloss says more plainly: High things stand more perilously. Moreover, according to Jerome, the things that are lofty fall the sooner. The princes and greater men were gathered together, so that through them the lesser might be led astray. For those who are rich and powerful, while they fear to lose their riches and power, are the more easily tripped up by sins; and when the magistrates have been led astray, the subjects perish by the example of their betters.

paras.t: Denique, secundum Albertum, hanc statuam spiritualiter erigunt avari, qui aurum venerantur ut deum, quia Apostolus avaritiam vocat idolorum servitutem. Hæretici quoque et schismatici, qui fulgore eloquentiæ sæcularis falsum dogma componunt, auream faciunt statuam, vel potius deauratam, et quantum in se est, persuasione sua compellunt homines ut cadentes adorent idolum falsitatis.
paras.en: Lastly, according to Albert, this statue is spiritually set up by the covetous, who venerate gold as a god, for the Apostle calls covetousness [[Eph 5:5|a serving of idols|idolorum servitutem]][[Col 3:5||]]. Heretics and schismatics too, who compose a false doctrine with the glitter of worldly eloquence, make a golden statue, or rather a gilded one, and as far as in them lies compel men by their persuasion to fall down and adore the idol of falsehood.

paras.t: Tunc congregati sunt satrapæ, et ceteri jam præfati, ad dedicationem statuæ. Stabant autem in conspectu statuæ quam erexerat rex. Et præco clamabat valenter, grandi scilicet voce : Vobis dicitur, id est, ex parte regis præcipitur, populis, et tribubus, in quas dividitur populus, et linguis, id est diversarum linguarum nationibus ;
paras.en: [[3:3|Then|Tunc]] [[3:3|the nobles|satrapæ]] and the others already named [[3:3|were gathered together|congregati sunt]] [[3:3|to the dedication of the statue|ad dedicationem statuæ]]. [[3:3|And they stood before the statue which king Nabuchodonosor had set up|Stabant autem in conspectu statuæ quam erexerat rex]] [the margin gives the reading *posuerat* for Denis's *erexerat*; both mean "had set up"]. [[3:4|Then a herald cried with a strong voice|Et præco clamabat valenter]], that is, with a loud voice: [[3:4|To you it is commanded|Vobis dicitur]], that is, it is ordered on the king's behalf, [[3:4|O nations|populis]], [[3:4|tribes|et tribubus]], into which a people is divided, [[3:4|and languages|et linguis]], that is, to the nations of diverse tongues;

paras.t: in hora qua audieritis sonitum tubæ et fistulæ. Fistula est instrumentum musicum ligneum, multa habens foramina, quæ sonum modulatum emittit. Et citharæ et sambucæ. Sambuca dicitur quasi buccina parva, a sam, quod est sol, et bucca : quia non fit nisi in æstate. Et psalterii, id est instrumenti musici quod decem chordis super concavum extensis perficitur, juxta illud : In psalterio decem chordarum psallite ei. Et symphoniæ, quæ erat in cantibus sacerdotum, secundum Albertum. Aliqui tamen accipiunt pro instrumento oblongo, quod digitis tangitur, et a cæcis solet portari. Communiter vero sumitur symphonia pro melodia in generali. Et universi generis musicorum, quæ hic in speciali non exprimuntur. Quæ omnia ibi resonabant, ut ex tantis melodiis cor populi molliretur et accenderetur ad statuæ venerationem. Diversæ siquidem melodiæ diversas causant in anima affectiones. Unde et David quum arcam Dei transferret, musicis usus est instrumentis, ut legitur secundo Regum volumine. Cadentes adorate statuam auream, quam constituit Nabuchodonosor rex.
paras.en: [[3:5|That in the hour that you shall hear the sound of the trumpet, and of the flute|in hora qua audieritis sonitum tubæ et fistulæ]]. The flute [*fistula*, a pipe] is a wooden musical instrument with many holes, which gives out a modulated sound. [[3:5|and of the harp|Et citharæ]], [[3:5|of the sackbut|et sambucæ]]. The sackbut [*sambuca*] is so called as being a little trumpet [*buccina*], from *sam*, which means "sun", and *bucca* [the cheek or mouth], because it is only made in summer. [[3:5|and of the psaltery|Et psalterii]], that is, of the musical instrument which is made up of ten strings stretched over a hollow body, according to that: [[Ps 32:2|sing to him with the psaltery, the instrument of ten strings|In psalterio decem chordarum psallite ei]]. [[3:5|and of the symphony|Et symphoniæ]], which belonged to the chants of the priests, according to Albert. Some, however, take it for an oblong instrument which is played with the fingers and is commonly carried about by the blind [apparently the hurdy-gurdy, called *symphonia* in Denis's day]. But commonly *symphonia* is taken for melody in general. [[3:5|and of all kind of music|Et universi generis musicorum]], which are not named here one by one. All these sounded there, so that by so many melodies the heart of the people might be softened and kindled to the veneration of the statue. For diverse melodies cause diverse affections in the soul. Hence David too, when he was bringing over the ark of God, made use of musical instruments, as we read in the second volume of Kings[[2 Kings 6:5||]]. [[3:5|ye fall down and adore the golden statue which king Nabuchodonosor hath set up|Cadentes adorate statuam auream, quam constituit Nabuchodonosor rex]].

paras.t: Si quis autem non prostratus adoraverit statuam, eadem hora mittatur in fornacem ignis ardentis. Dira comminatio, ut terror pœnarum eos compellat quos ratio prohibet.
paras.en: [[3:6|But if any man shall not fall down and adore|Si quis autem non prostratus adoraverit]] the statue, [[3:6|he shall the same hour be cast into a furnace of burning fire|eadem hora mittatur in fornacem ignis ardentis]]. A dire threat, so that the terror of punishment might compel those whom reason forbids.

paras.t: Post hæc ergo statim ut audierint omnes populi sonitum tubæ, etc., cadentes omnes populi, tribus et linguæ, id est in terram se prosternentes, in reverentiam idoli, seu regis in idolo, adoraverunt statuam auream : non quod universi populi illic tunc erant; sed est distributio pro generibus singulorum, quia cum majoribus aliqui de subditis, de singulis locis regi subjectis venerunt.
paras.en: [[3:7|Upon this, therefore, at the time when all the people heard the sound of the trumpet|Post hæc ergo statim ut audierint omnes populi sonitum tubæ]], etc., [[3:7|all the nations, tribes, and languages fell down|cadentes omnes populi, tribus et linguæ]], that is, prostrating themselves on the ground in reverence for the idol, or for the king in the idol, [[3:7|and adored the golden statue|adoraverunt statuam auream]]: not that all the peoples were there at that time; but it is a distribution over the kinds of individuals [that is, "all" means some of every kind, not every single one], since along with the greater men some of their subjects came from each of the places subject to the king.

paras.t: Statimque in ipso tempore accedentes viri Chaldæi, accusaverunt Judæos : quibus invidebant, eo quod in regni negotiis sibi erant prælati. Hinc passionibus agitati, celeriter aggressi sunt regem. Passio namque rationis judicium non exspectat.
paras.en: [[3:8|And presently at that very time some Chaldeans came|Statimque in ipso tempore accedentes viri Chaldæi]] [[3:8|and accused the Jews|accusaverunt Judæos]], whom they envied because they had been set over them in the affairs of the kingdom. Stirred, then, by their passions, they went quickly to the king. For passion does not wait for the judgment of reason.

paras.t: Dixeruntque Nabuchodonosor regi, ejus benevolentiam captando, ut magis placerent et impetrarent intentum : Rex, in æternum vive, nunc in sæculo isto, et postea cum immortalibus diis.
paras.en: [[3:9|And said to king Nabuchodonosor|Dixeruntque Nabuchodonosor regi]], courting his goodwill, that they might please him the more and obtain what they intended: [[3:9|O king, live for ever|Rex, in æternum vive]], now in this world, and afterwards with the immortal gods.

paras.t: Tu, rex, posuisti decretum, ut omnis homo præter te, qui audierit sonitum tubæ, fistulæ et citharæ, etc. Littera plana est.
paras.en: [[3:10|Thou, O king, hast made a decree, that every man|Tu, rex, posuisti decretum, ut omnis homo]] besides thee, [[3:10|that shall hear the sound of the trumpet, the flute, and the harp|qui audierit sonitum tubæ, fistulæ et citharæ]], etc. The letter is plain.

paras.t: Sunt ergo viri Judæi, quos constituisti super opera regionis Babyloniæ, quia de tua licentia Daniel eos præfecit publicis operibus provinciarum Babylonis : ut dictum est in fine capituli præcedentis; Sidrach, Misach et Abdenago. Viri isti contempserunt decretum tuum : deos tuos non colunt, et statuam non adorant. Tanquam dicant : O rex, ingrati sunt tibi, et reddunt mala pro bonis, injuriam et contemptum pro honore eis a te impenso; captivos, principes fecisti populi tui, et tamen rebelles sunt tibi. Quidam hoc loco deos et statuam pro eodem accipiunt, sicut in Exodo de vitulo conflatili dixerunt filii Israel, Isti sunt dii tui. Sed quoniam dictum est, quod rex in statua jussit se adorari, et ultra hoc, ipsemet idola adoravit, convenientius pro diversis accipiuntur. Noverunt enim Chaldæi, quod viri isti non nisi Deum Israel colerent.
paras.en: [[3:12|Now there are certain Jews, whom thou hast set over the works of the province of Babylon|Sunt ergo viri Judæi, quos constituisti super opera regionis Babyloniæ]], for by thy leave Daniel set them over the public works of the provinces of Babylon, as was said at the end of the preceding chapter[[Dan 2:49||]]: [[3:12|Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago|Sidrach, Misach et Abdenago]]. [[3:12|these men, O king, have slighted thy decree|Viri isti contempserunt decretum tuum]]: [[3:12|they worship not thy gods, nor do they adore the golden statue|deos tuos non colunt, et statuam non adorant]]. As if they said: O king, they are ungrateful to thee, and return evil for good, injury and contempt for the honour shown them by thee; captives as they were, thou hast made them princes of thy people, and yet they rebel against thee. Some take *gods* and *statue* here for the same thing, as in Exodus the children of Israel said of the molten calf: [[Ex 32:8|These are thy gods|Isti sunt dii tui]][[Ex 32:4||]]. But since it has been said that the king commanded himself to be adored in the statue, and that besides this he himself adored idols, they are more fittingly taken for different things. For the Chaldeans knew that these men worshipped none but the God of Israel.

paras.t: Tunc rex Nabuchodonosor in furore, id est impetu furioso, et ira, quæ est appetitus vindictæ, præcepit ut adducerentur coram se Sidrach, Misach et Abdenago, volens eis dare locum respondendi et excusandi : sicut in Actibus scribitur Apostolorum : Non est consuetudo Romanis condemnare aliquem, nisi præsentes habeat accusatores, et locum accipiat respondendi ad abluenda crimina. Qui confestim adducti sunt in conspectu regis. Accusatores enim eorum avidissimi erant condemnationis ipsorum : ideo festinabant eos adducere.
paras.en: [[3:13|Then Nabuchodonosor in fury|Tunc rex Nabuchodonosor in furore]], that is, with furious impetuosity, [[3:13|and in wrath|et ira]], which is the appetite for revenge, [[3:13|commanded that Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago should be brought|præcepit ut adducerentur coram se Sidrach, Misach et Abdenago]] before him, wishing to give them room to answer and excuse themselves, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles: [[Acts 25:16|it is not the custom of the Romans to condemn any man, before that he who is accused have his accusers present and have liberty to make his answer, to clear himself of the things laid to his charge|Non est consuetudo Romanis condemnare aliquem, nisi præsentes habeat accusatores, et locum accipiat respondendi ad abluenda crimina]]. [[3:13|who immediately were brought before the king|Qui confestim adducti sunt in conspectu regis]]. For their accusers were most eager for their condemnation, and so they hurried to bring them.

paras.t: Pronuntiansque rex verba accusationis audita, ait eis : Verene, id est anne vere, o Sidrach, Misach et Abdenago, deos meos non colitis, et statuam auream quam constitui, non adoratis? Ex hoc apparet, quod dii et statua non accipiuntur hic pro eodem, præsertim quoniam statuam, in qua se ipsum jussit adorari, deos suos non nominaret.
paras.en: [[3:14|And Nabuchodonosor, the king, spoke|Pronuntiansque rex]] the words of the accusation he had heard, [[3:14|to them, and said|ait eis]]: [[3:14|Is it true|Verene]], that is, is it truly so, [[3:14|O Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago, that you do not worship my gods, nor adore the golden statue that I have set up?|o Sidrach, Misach et Abdenago, deos meos non colitis, et statuam auream quam constitui, non adoratis?]] From this it appears that *gods* and *statue* are not taken here for the same thing, especially since he would not call the statue in which he commanded himself to be adored his gods.

paras.t: Nunc ergo si estis parati, quacumque hora audieritis sonitum tubæ, etc., prosternite vos humiliter coram idolo, et adorate statuam : quod si non adoraveritis eam, eadem hora mittemini in fornacem ignis ardentis. Quamvis in furore jussit eos adduci, tamen his verbis dat spatium pœnitendi, et priori offensæ ignoscit, dummodo vel secunda vice admoniti acquiescant : quod si noluerint, pœnalissimam mortem minatur. Ignis namque est magis activus, et activa sua proprietate, puta calore, magis affligit. Ex quo patet quod non libenter, imo valde invite pueros istos interemisset, quoniam sibi carissimi erant, potissime propter Danielem. Unde et eis visis, ad pietatem flexus videtur, licet cum furore mandavit eos sibi adduci.
paras.en: [[3:15|Now, therefore, if you be ready, at what hour soever, you shall hear the sound of the trumpet|Nunc ergo si estis parati, quacumque hora audieritis sonitum tubæ]], etc., [[3:15|prostrate yourselves|prosternite vos]] humbly before the idol, [[3:15|and adore the statue|et adorate statuam]]: [[3:15|but if you do not adore|quod si non adoraveritis]] it, [[3:15|you shall be cast the same hour into the furnace of burning fire|eadem hora mittemini in fornacem ignis ardentis]]. Although he commanded them to be brought in fury, yet by these words he gives them room for repentance and pardons the former offence, provided that, warned at least a second time, they comply; but if they will not, he threatens a most painful death. For fire is the more active, and by its active property, that is, by heat, it afflicts the more. From this it is plain that he would have put these youths to death not willingly, but very unwillingly, since they were most dear to him, above all for Daniel's sake. Hence on seeing them he seems to have been moved to pity, although he had ordered them brought before him in fury.

paras.t: Et quis est Deus qui eripiat, id est, eripere possit, vos de manu mea? Mira instabilitas et excæcatio regis hujus, quod de Deo Hebræorum, quem dudum Deum deorum et Dominum regum confessus est, nunc tam blasphemanter ac impie loquitur, quasi non sit homine mortali potentior. Simili quoque modo Sennacherib rex Assyriorum, dixit per nuntios ad Ezechiam : Non te seducat Deus tuus, quia non poterit te liberare de manu hac.
paras.en: [[3:15|and who is the God that shall deliver|Et quis est Deus qui eripiat]], that is, can deliver, [[3:15|you out of my hand|vos de manu mea]]? Wondrous is the instability and blindness of this king, that he now speaks so blasphemously and impiously of the God of the Hebrews, whom he lately confessed to be [[Dan 2:47|the God of gods, and Lord of kings|Deum deorum et Dominum regum]], as though he were no mightier than a mortal man. In like manner Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, said through messengers to Ezechias: [[4 Kings 19:10|Let not thy God deceive thee|Non te seducat Deus tuus]], for he will not be able to deliver thee out of this hand[[2 Par 32:14||]][[2 Par 32:15||]].

paras.t: Respondentes Sidrach, Misach et Abdenago, dixerunt regi voce secura et corde non territo, non timentes eum qui corpus occidit, sed eum qui potestatem habet corpus et animam mittere in gehennam : Non oportet nos de hac re, scilicet, quis sit Deus qui possit nos de tuis eripere manibus, respondere tibi sermonibus, quoniam factis comprobandum est magis quam verbis. Hoc dicunt tanquam de divina protectione securi. Vel, secundum Hieronymum, sensus est : Non debes audire verba nostra, quorum jam ipsis rebus probabis fortitudinem atque constantiam. Rursusque sensus est : Quæstio tua, qua quæris an deos tuos ac statuam adoremus, et quis sit Deus qui valeat nos liberare, ita absurda est, ut responsione indigna sit. Quid enim stultius, quam idola, inanimataque colere, et de summi Dei omnipotentia dubitare?
paras.en: [[3:16|Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago, answered|Respondentes Sidrach, Misach et Abdenago]], [[3:16|and said to king|dixerunt regi]] with an untroubled voice and an unterrified heart, not fearing him who kills the body, but him who has power to cast body and soul into hell[[Matt 10:28||]]: [[3:16|We have no occasion|Non oportet nos]] [[3:16|concerning this matter|de hac re]], namely, who is the God that can deliver us from thy hands, [[3:16|to answer thee|respondere tibi]] in words, since it must be proved by deeds rather than by words. They say this as men secure of the divine protection. Or, according to Jerome, the sense is: Thou oughtest not to hear our words, whose fortitude and constancy thou wilt presently prove by the deeds themselves. And again the sense is: Thy question, in which thou askest whether we adore thy gods and the statue, and who is the God that can deliver us, is so absurd that it is unworthy of an answer. For what is more foolish than to worship idols and lifeless things, and to doubt the omnipotence of the most high God?
