paras.t: Benedicite, cœli, Domino, omnes scilicet orbes cœlestes: ex quorum magnitudinis, pulchritudinis, causalitatis, sphæricitatis, coordinationis ac multiplicis proprietatis consideratione, omnipotentia, sapientia et bonitas Dei admirabiliter collaudantur. De quibus in Job dicitur: Tu forsitan cum Deo fabricatus es cœlos, qui solidissimi quasi ære fusi sunt. Isaias quoque ad contemplationem Dei ex consideratione eorum adhortans: Levate, inquit, in excelsum oculos vestros, et videte quis creavit hæc.
paras.en: [[3:59|O ye heavens, bless the Lord|Benedicite, cœli, Domino]]: that is, all the heavenly spheres; for from considering their greatness, beauty, causality, roundness, coordination and many properties, the almighty power, wisdom and goodness of God are wonderfully praised. Of them it is said in Job: [[Job 37:18|Thou perhaps hast made the heavens with him, which are most strong, as if they were of molten brass|Tu forsitan cum Deo fabricatus es cœlos, qui solidissimi quasi ære fusi sunt]] [the margin gives Job xxxviii, 18; the words are Job 37:18; Denis has *with God* for *with him*]. Isaias too, urging us to the contemplation of God from considering them, says: [[Is 40:26|Lift up|Levate]], he says, [[Is 40:26|your eyes on high, and see who hath created these things|in excelsum oculos vestros, et videte quis creavit hæc]].

paras.t: Benedicite, aquæ omnes quæ super cœlos sunt, Domino. Hoc loco apertissime dicuntur aquæ consistere super cœlos, et consonat illud Genesis: Dixit quoque Deus: Fiat firmamentum in medio aquarum, et dividat aquas ab aquis. Et fecit Deus firmamentum, divisitque aquas quæ erant sub firmamento, ab his quæ erant super firmamentum; vocavitque Deus firmamentum cœlum. Itemque in Psalmo: Laudate eum, cœli cœlorum; et aquæ omnes quæ super cœlos sunt, laudent nomen Domini. Quæ licet prima facie videantur forsitan naturali rationi et dictis philosophorum contraria, tamen ut scribit Augustinus super Genesim, major est scripturæ illius Geneseos auctoritas, quam omnis humani intellectus perspicacitas sive capacitas.
paras.en: [[3:60|O all ye waters that are above the heavens, bless the Lord|Benedicite, aquæ omnes quæ super cœlos sunt, Domino]]. In this place it is said most plainly that there are waters above the heavens, and that saying of Genesis agrees with it: [[Gen 1:6|And God said: Let there be a firmament made amidst the waters: and let it divide the waters from the waters|Dixit quoque Deus: Fiat firmamentum in medio aquarum, et dividat aquas ab aquis]]. [[Gen 1:7|And God made a firmament, and divided the waters that were under the firmament, from those that were above the firmament|Et fecit Deus firmamentum, divisitque aquas quæ erant sub firmamento, ab his quæ erant super firmamentum]]; [[Gen 1:8|And God called the firmament, Heaven|vocavitque Deus firmamentum cœlum]]. And likewise in the Psalm: [[Ps 148:4|Praise him, ye heavens of heavens: and let all the waters that are above the heavens|Laudate eum, cœli cœlorum; et aquæ omnes quæ super cœlos sunt]], [[Ps 148:5|Praise the name of the Lord|laudent nomen Domini]]. And though these things may perhaps seem at first sight contrary to natural reason and to the sayings of the philosophers, yet, as Augustine writes on Genesis, the authority of that scripture of Genesis is greater than all the keenness or reach of the human understanding.

paras.t: Unde et Thomas in prima parte, quæstione 68, de ista loquens materia, ait: Certissime ergo sciamus esse aquas super cœlos; sed quæ vel quales aquæ, non est adeo certum. Origenes enim per aquas has intelligit spirituales substantias; sed hoc non placet Basilio. Sunt ergo ibi corporales aquæ; sed quales, diversimode traditur. Si enim dicamus firmamentum esse cœlum sidereum, tunc illæ aquæ possunt dici illius naturæ, cujus est hoc cœlum. Unde qui dicunt cœlum esse de natura elementorum, dicere possunt aquas illas esse elementares. Qui autem asserunt cœlum esse specialis naturæ, affirmant has aquas non esse elementares, sed naturæ cœlestis: et sic per aquas intelligitur nona sphæra, quæ est sine stellis; et aqueum dicitur, propter diaphaneitatem, sicut cœlum Beatorum vocatur empyreum, id est igneum, propter splendorem. Qui autem ponunt aquas elementares super cœlum, ut Beda, Cassiodorus et alii multi, dicere possunt quod non sint graves, sed subtiles; nec fluidæ, sed ad instar glaciei firmæ ac duræ: unde a quibusdam cœlum crystallinum dicuntur. Et aliqui ponunt ibi aquas ad temperandum calorem cœlestium corporum, quæ dicunt esse de natura ignis: et ut ait Augustinus, hujus experimentum quidam sumpserunt, quod Saturnus est maxime frigidus ob vicinitatem ad aquas illas.
paras.en: Hence Thomas too, in the First Part, question 68, speaking of this matter, says: Let us then know most certainly that there are waters above the heavens; but what waters, or of what kind, is not so certain. For Origen understands by these waters spiritual substances; but this does not please Basil. There are therefore bodily waters there; but of what kind is handed down in different ways. For if we say that the firmament is the starry heaven, then those waters can be said to be of the same nature as this heaven. Hence those who say that the heaven is of the nature of the elements can say that those waters are elemental. But those who assert that the heaven is of a special nature affirm that these waters are not elemental but of a heavenly nature; and so by the waters is understood the ninth sphere, which is without stars; and it is called watery because of its transparency, just as the heaven of the Blessed is called empyrean, that is, fiery, because of its splendour. And those who place elemental waters above the heaven, as Bede, Cassiodorus and many others do, can say that they are not heavy but subtle, and not fluid but firm and hard like ice; hence some call them the crystalline heaven. And some place waters there to temper the heat of the heavenly bodies, which they say are of the nature of fire; and, as Augustine says, some have taken as proof of this that Saturn is extremely cold because of its nearness to those waters.

paras.t: Denique Albertus scribit hoc loco: Aquæ istæ quæ super cœlos sunt, ut dicit Augustinus, in minutissimis guttis ibi suspensæ sunt: et quidam autumant inde rorem descendere. Vel forte melius dicitur, ait Albertus, quod aquæ nomen est primum materiæ, in Genesi: Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas. Et ratione perspicuitatis, sunt in cœlo crystallino; ratione humiditatis et fluiditatis, in cœlo inferiori, puta aerio. De ista difficultate tractat Magister, secundo Sententiarum; et doctores multa ibi conscribunt. Communius autem tenetur, quod per aquas has intelligatur cœlum crystallinum seu aqueum, scilicet nona sphæra, non propter naturam, sed similitudinem aquæ in diaphaneitate.
paras.en: Lastly, Albert writes on this place: These waters which are above the heavens, as Augustine says, are suspended there in the tiniest drops; and some think that the dew comes down from them. Or perhaps, says Albert, it is better said that *waters* is the first name of matter, in Genesis: [[Gen 1:2|the spirit of God moved over the waters|Spiritus Domini ferebatur super aquas]]. And by reason of their transparency they are in the crystalline heaven; by reason of their moistness and fluidity, in the lower heaven, that is, the air. The Master treats of this difficulty in the second book of the *Sentences*, and the doctors write much there. But it is more commonly held that by these waters is understood the crystalline or watery heaven, namely the ninth sphere, not because of its nature but because of its likeness to water in transparency.

paras.t: Moraliter vero per aquas quæ super cœlos sunt, quidam intelligunt perspicuas seu illuminatas mentes Sanctorum, in quibus velut in speculo resplendent divina.
paras.en: Morally, by the waters that are above the heavens some understand the clear, that is, enlightened minds of the Saints, in which divine things shine back as in a mirror.

paras.t: Benedicite, omnes virtutes Domini, Domino. Per virtutes quidam intelligunt hic orbium motores cœlestium, qui a philosophis intelligentiæ, a theologis angeli asseruntur. Et ut Thomas in Summa contra gentiles opinatur, sunt de medio ordine mediæ hierarchiæ, puta de choro Virtutum: idcirco nunc Virtutes vocantur. De quibus fertur in Psalmo: Laudate eum, omnes virtutes ejus; et, Benedicite Domino, omnes virtutes ejus, ministri ejus qui facitis voluntatem ejus. Denique, secundum divinum Dionysium, sicut omnes supernæ mentes angeli, ita et virtutes vocantur propter vigorem, agilitatem, efficaciamque agendi quidquid eis divinitus commendatur sive præcipitur.
paras.en: [[3:61|O all ye powers of the Lord, bless the Lord|Benedicite, omnes virtutes Domini, Domino]]. By *powers* [*virtutes*, which is also the name of the choir of the Virtues] some understand here the movers of the heavenly spheres, who are called intelligences by the philosophers and angels by the theologians. And, as Thomas holds in the *Summa contra Gentiles*, they are of the middle order of the middle hierarchy, that is, of the choir of the Virtues; and so they are now called Virtues. Of them it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 148:2|praise ye him, all his hosts|Laudate eum, omnes virtutes ejus]]; and, [[Ps 102:21|Bless the Lord, all ye his hosts: you ministers of his that do his will|Benedicite Domino, omnes virtutes ejus, ministri ejus qui facitis voluntatem ejus]]. Lastly, according to the divine Dionysius, just as all the heavenly minds are called angels, so too they are called virtues, because of their vigour, swiftness and power to accomplish whatever is entrusted or commanded to them by God.

paras.t: Itaque locus iste multipliciter potest exponi. Primo, de angelicis mentibus, sicut prætactum est. Secundo, de viribus causativis cœlestium corporum, quæ sunt potestates causales per creationem insitæ cœlestibus cunctis corporibus, per quas agunt et influunt in elementa et mixta, secundum quod Aristoteles ait: Sol et homo generant hominem. Sunt enim cœlestia corpora, per virtutes hujusmodi, instrumentaliter causæ motuum et alterationum, generationum et corruptionum in inferioribus istis: ut etiam beatus Dionysius ait quarto capitulo de Divinis nominibus, præsertim de sole loquens ibidem; consonatque verbo Philosophi, asserentis quod accessus solis in obliquo circulo, puta zodiaco, est causa generationis et renovationis in inferioribus seu terræ nascentibus; recessus vero ejus in circulo isto, est causa corruptionis et arefactionis illorum, sicut ad oculum est videre. Unde Peripatetici ponunt quatuor causas universales, summas, primarias: quarum altissima Deus est; secunda est intelligentia; tertia, anima nobilis (cœlestia etenim corpora animata dixerunt, quorum animas nobiles nuncupabant); quarta est natura, vis seu virtus insita cœlestibus corporibus. Hinc ait Albertus: In orbibus cœlorum virtutes sunt moventes et instaurantes naturam (scilicet inferiorum per individuorum procreationem, in quorum successione continua species perpetuatur), quas hic ad Dei laudem inducit. — Tertio potest exponi de virtutibus imperialibus, quas ponit Damascenus, ab eis cœlos moveri affirmans. Quarto, de omnium naturalium seu creatarum rerum ac specierum naturalibus viribus sive potentiis, per quas ad operationes sibi connaturales ac debitas exstant idoneæ. Nullum enim naturalium propria caret operatione, secundum Damascenum: alioqui frustra esset, quum ens non queat suum attingere finem, nisi per propriam actionem seu motum. Has virtutes putavit Rabbi Moyses in Scripturis angelos nuncupari: in quo tamen erravit, putans angelicas mentes seu separatas substantias, non esse plures quam sunt orbes cœlestes, prout Albertus et Thomas suis locis de ipso enarrant.
paras.en: So this place can be explained in several ways. First, of the angelic minds, as was touched on above. Secondly, of the causative forces of the heavenly bodies, which are causal powers implanted by creation in all the heavenly bodies, by which they act upon and pour their influence into the elements and compound bodies; according to what Aristotle says: The sun and a man beget a man. For the heavenly bodies, through such powers, are instrumentally the causes of the motions and alterations, the generations and corruptions, in these lower things; as blessed Dionysius also says in the fourth chapter of *On the Divine Names*, speaking there especially of the sun. And this agrees with the saying of the Philosopher, who asserts that the approach of the sun in the oblique circle, that is, the zodiac, is the cause of generation and renewal in the lower things, that is, in what springs from the earth; while its withdrawal in that circle is the cause of their corruption and withering, as one can see with one's own eyes. Hence the Peripatetics posit four universal, highest and first causes: of which the highest is God; the second is the intelligence; the third, the noble soul (for they said the heavenly bodies were animate, and called their souls noble souls); the fourth is nature, the force or power implanted in the heavenly bodies. Hence Albert says: In the spheres of the heavens are the powers that move and renew nature (that is, the nature of the lower things, through the begetting of individuals, in whose continual succession the species is perpetuated), and these he here brings in to the praise of God. Thirdly, it can be explained of the imperial powers which the Damascene posits, affirming that the heavens are moved by them. Fourthly, of the natural forces or powers of all natural or created things and species, by which they are fitted for the operations that are connatural and due to them. For no natural thing lacks its own operation, according to the Damascene; otherwise it would exist in vain, since a being cannot reach its end except by its own action or motion. Rabbi Moyses thought these powers are called angels in the Scriptures; but in this he erred, thinking that the angelic minds, or separated substances, are no more in number than the heavenly spheres, as Albert and Thomas relate of him in their places.

paras.t: Benedicite, sol et luna, Domino. Hæc sunt duo luminaria cœli illustrantia terram, de quibus dicitur in Genesi: Fecit Deus duo luminaria magna. In quorum, præsertim in solis diligenti consideratione, divina majestas mirabiliter conspicitur et relucet. Nempe, ut quarto de Divinis nominibus capitulo loquitur Dionysius, sol iste visibilis, evidens est imago divinæ bonitatis, quæ est sol æternus et intellectualis, sol sapientiæ atque justitiæ: imo in magnitudine, velocitate, claritate, causalitate, influentia et efficientia solis, divinæ potestatis ac sapientiæ eminentiam satis admirari non possumus. Et dicitur sol, quasi solus omnibus lucens, quia non solum luna, sed cetera quoque astra ac planetæ, secundum plures philosophos, lumen sortiuntur ab eo. Hinc et signifer ille S. Franciscus, considerando intuendoque fratrem solem, non mediocriter delectabatur in Creatore altissimo. De hac re in Ecclesiastico legitur: Species cœli in visione gloriæ, sol in adspectu, vas admirabile, opus Excelsi, radios igneos efflans. Magnus Dominus qui fecit illum, et in sermonibus ejus festinavit iter. Et luna in omnibus in tempore suo, ostensio temporis et signum ævi; mensis secundum nomen est ejus, crescens mirabiliter in consummatione, vas castrorum in excelsis, in firmamento cœli resplendens gloriose.
paras.en: [[3:62|O ye sun and moon, bless the Lord|Benedicite, sol et luna, Domino]]. These are the two lights of heaven that give light to the earth, of which it is said in Genesis: [[Gen 1:16|God made two great lights|Fecit Deus duo luminaria magna]]. In the careful consideration of them, and especially of the sun, the divine majesty is wonderfully seen and shines forth. For, as Dionysius says in the fourth chapter of *On the Divine Names*, this visible sun is a clear image of the divine goodness, which is the eternal and intellectual sun, the sun of wisdom and of justice; indeed, in the greatness, swiftness, brightness, causality, influence and working of the sun we cannot wonder enough at the eminence of the divine power and wisdom. And it is called *sol*, as it were *solus* [alone] giving light to all, because not only the moon but the other stars and planets too, according to many philosophers, receive their light from it. Hence that standard-bearer St Francis, considering and gazing on brother sun, took no small delight in the most high Creator. Of this we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 43:1|the beauty of heaven with its glorious shew|Species cœli in visione gloriæ]], [[Ecclus 43:2|The sun when he appeareth|sol in adspectu]], [[Ecclus 43:2|an admirable instrument, the work of the most High|vas admirabile, opus Excelsi]], [[Ecclus 43:4|breathing out fiery vapours|radios igneos efflans]]. [[Ecclus 43:5|Great is the Lord that made him, and at his words he hath hastened his course|Magnus Dominus qui fecit illum, et in sermonibus ejus festinavit iter]]. [[Ecclus 43:6|And the moon in all in her season, is for a declaration of times and a sign of the world|Et luna in omnibus in tempore suo, ostensio temporis et signum ævi]]; [[Ecclus 43:8|The month is called after her name, increasing wonderfully in her perfection|mensis secundum nomen est ejus, crescens mirabiliter in consummatione]], [[Ecclus 43:9|Being an instrument of the armies on high, shining gloriously in the firmament of heaven|vas castrorum in excelsis, in firmamento cœli resplendens gloriose]].

paras.t: Spiritualiter autem sol significat intellectum veri et boni, ac rationis fulgorem super ceteras vires ei subjectas, quæ illuminantur ab ea ne ruant, errantes in lubrico vitiorum. Luna designat inferiorem animæ portionem, ut ab animæ suprema portione, directione virtuosa, perfusam eique subditam. Et quia electi horum habent utrumque, idcirco in Apocalypsi de Ecclesia scribitur: Mulier amicta sole, et luna sub pedibus ejus.
paras.en: Spiritually, the sun signifies the understanding of the true and the good, and the brightness of reason over the other powers subject to it, which are enlightened by it lest they fall, straying on the slippery ground of vices. The moon denotes the lower part of the soul, as filled by the highest part of the soul with virtuous direction and subject to it. And because the elect have both of these, it is written in the Apocalypse of the Church: [[Apoc 12:1|A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet|Mulier amicta sole, et luna sub pedibus ejus]].

paras.t: Benedicite, stellæ cœli, Domino. Magnificentiam enim sui Creatoris multipliciter repræsentant sua pulchritudine, motione, causalitate, pluralitate, situ, influxu et ordine. Parvæ quidem videntur, sed minima major asseritur tota terra, quoniam remotissime distant a nobis. Propter quod in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Species cœli gloria stellarum, mundum illuminans in excelsis Dominus. — Stellæ autem designant virtuosos sapientia præditos, qui verbo, exemplo, fama seu moribus, aliis lucent: qui sunt velut lucerna lucens et ardens, quemadmodum ad Philippenses scribit Apostolus: Omnia facite sine murmurationibus, ut sitis sine querela et simplices filii Dei in medio nationis pravæ atque perversæ, inter quos lucetis sicut luminaria mundi, verbum vitæ continentes. Hinc infra scribitur: Qui multos erudiunt ad justitiam, fulgebunt quasi stellæ in perpetuas æternitates.
paras.en: [[3:63|O ye stars of heaven, bless the Lord|Benedicite, stellæ cœli, Domino]]. For they represent the magnificence of their Creator in many ways: by their beauty, motion, causality, number, position, influence and order. They seem small indeed, but the smallest of them is said to be greater than the whole earth, since they are very far distant from us. For this reason it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 43:10|The glory of the stars is the beauty of heaven; the Lord enlighteneth the world on high|Species cœli gloria stellarum, mundum illuminans in excelsis Dominus]]. The stars, moreover, denote virtuous men endowed with wisdom, who give light to others by word, example, good name or conduct; who are as it were [[John 5:35|a burning and a shining light|lucerna lucens et ardens]], as the Apostle writes to the Philippians: [[Phil 2:14|do ye all things without murmurings|Omnia facite sine murmurationibus]], [[Phil 2:15|That you may be blameless and sincere children of God|ut sitis sine querela et simplices filii Dei]] [[Phil 2:15|in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation: among whom you shine as lights in the world|in medio nationis pravæ atque perversæ, inter quos lucetis sicut luminaria mundi]], [[Phil 2:16|Holding forth the word of life|verbum vitæ continentes]]. Hence it is written below: [[12:3|they that instruct many to justice, as stars for all eternity|Qui multos erudiunt ad justitiam, fulgebunt quasi stellæ in perpetuas æternitates]].

1.t: Quoniam deficiente electis humano auxilio, adesse solet divinum, subjungitur : Angelus autem Domini descendit, per visibilem operationem, secundum Albertum, imo et vere realiter intravit cum Azaria, inter hos tres principali, ut dictum est, et sociis ejus Anania et Misaele, in fornacem. Angelus quippe est definitive in loco; et secundum Damascenum, illic est ubi operatur. Et excussit flammam ignis de fornace usque ad spatium quadraginta novem cubitorum, ut paulo ante expositum est. Angelici quippe spiritus plenum habent dominium super materiam inferiorum, quantum ad motum localem, secundum doctores. Denique non ita excussit flammam ignis de fornace, quod in fornace ignis non manserit, quum infra in isto dicatur capitulo, Ecce ego video viros quatuor ambulantes in medio ignis; sed partem ignis ejecit. Et fecit medium fornacis, ubi ignis fortissimus fuit, quasi ventum roris flantem, id est dulciter pueros refrigerantem : ut per rorem esset exstinctivus, et per ventum refrigerativus, secundum Albertum. Verumtamen non fuit ignis ille nec ardor ejus exstinctus, nisi quoad hoc, quod actio ejus suspensa fuit a corporibus puerorum. Sicque angelus dicitur medium fornacis fecisse quasi ventum roris, quoniam virtute divina cooperante principaliter, et administrante angelo, pueri isti ita suaviter sentiebant ibidem, ac si in vento roris adductivo fuissent. Aliqui tamen dixerunt, quod ignis omnino excussus fuit, et angelus refrigerativa apposuit, ita quod in fornace non manserit ardor. Sed, ut tactum est, illud stare non potest.
1.en: Since, when human help fails the elect, divine help is wont to be at hand, there follows: [[3:49|But the angel of the Lord went down|Angelus autem Domini descendit]], by a visible working, according to Albert; nay, he truly and really entered [[3:49|with Azarias|cum Azaria]], the chief among these three, as has been said, [[3:49|and his companions|et sociis ejus]] Ananias and Misael, [[3:49|into the furnace|in fornacem]]. For an angel is in a place definitively [that is, by being wholly present within it, not by filling it with dimensions as a body does]; and according to Damascene, he is there where he works. [[3:49|And he drove the flame of the fire out of the furnace|Et excussit flammam ignis de fornace]] to the distance of forty-nine cubits, as was explained a little before. For the angelic spirits have full dominion over the matter of the lower things as regards local motion, according to the doctors. Yet he did not so drive the flame of the fire out of the furnace that no fire remained in the furnace, since further on in this chapter it is said, [[3:92|Behold, I see four men|Ecce ego video viros quatuor]] [[3:92|walking in the midst of the fire|ambulantes in medio ignis]]; but he cast out part of the fire. [[3:50|And made the midst of the furnace|Et fecit medium fornacis]], where the fire was fiercest, [[3:50|like the blowing of a wind bringing dew|quasi ventum roris flantem]], that is, sweetly cooling the youths: so that by the dew it should be quenching, and by the wind cooling, according to Albert. Nevertheless that fire and its heat were not quenched, except in this, that its action was held back from the bodies of the youths. And so the angel is said to have made the midst of the furnace like a wind of dew, because, by the divine power working principally and the angel ministering, these youths felt as pleasant there as if they had been in a wind bringing dew. Some, however, have said that the fire was wholly driven out, and that the angel applied cooling things, so that no heat remained in the furnace. But, as has been touched on, that cannot stand.

1.t: Et non tetigit eos omnino ignis. Si in medio ignis ambulaverunt, quomodo ignis eos non tetigit, a quo undique circumdabantur? Verumtamen non tetigit, id est, actionem suam in eis non exercuit, nec afflixit. Unde Albertus exponit : Non tetigit, tactu physico ad nocumentum. Sic nempe habetur in lege, quod novacula Nazaræorum caput non tangeret, id est, non raderet : solus namque contactus non erat prohibitus. Et per Zachariam Dominus ait electis : Qui tetigerit vos, tanget pupillam oculi mei. Qui tetigerit, id est, tangendo afflixerit. Hinc expositorie subditur : neque contristavit, nec quidquam molestiæ intulit : quum tamen ignis sit maxime activus et afflictivus, secundum Philosophum, ita quod pœna ignis dicitur maxima.
1.en: [[3:50|And the fire touched them not at all|Et non tetigit eos omnino ignis]]. If they walked in the midst of the fire, how did the fire not touch them, when it surrounded them on every side? Yet it did not *touch* them, that is, it did not exercise its action on them, nor afflict them. Hence Albert explains: It did not touch them with a physical touch, to do harm. So indeed we have it in the Law that the razor should not touch the head of the Nazarites[[Num 6:5||]][[Judg 13:5||]], that is, should not shave it: for mere contact was not forbidden. And through Zacharias the Lord says to the elect: [[Zach 2:8|he that toucheth you, toucheth the apple of my eye|Qui tetigerit vos, tanget pupillam oculi mei]]. *He that toucheth*, that is, afflicteth by touching. Hence there is added by way of explanation: [[3:50|nor troubled them, nor did them any harm|neque contristavit, nec quidquam molestiæ intulit]]: though fire is most active and most afflicting, according to the Philosopher, so that the pain of fire is called the greatest.

1.t: Circa hoc Lyra prolixam efficit quæstionem, qualiter factum sit illud; sed faciliter respondetur, quod per omnipotentiam Dei, qui non solum per angelos, sed et per homines instrumentaliter aliquid ministerii adhibentes facit miracula : omni enim naturæ creatæ indita exstat divinitus obedientialis potentia, per quam Deo creatori in omnibus quæ contradictionem non implicant, ad nutum obedit, ut Scotus declarat. Ægidius quoque de Roma in libro de Sacramento altaris, de hoc subtiliter scribit, præsertim sexto et septimo capitulis, inter cetera dicens, quod qualitates duplicem comparationem habent : unam ad subjectum, secundum quam dant sibi esse tale; aliam ad objectum sive ad exteriora, secundum quam sunt principia actionum, et ratio seu causa agendi : utputa calor per comparationem ad subjectum, dat esse calidum; prout vero comparatur ad calefactibile, est calefaciendi principium. Itaque per divinam virtutem fieri valet, ut qualitas primam habeat comparationem habitudinemque absque secunda ; sicque igni erit ratio quod calidus sit in se ipso, non autem ut per ipsum calefaciat aliud : quemadmodum in Sacramento altaris, corpus Christi per propriam quantitatem habet extensionem, situm et ordinem partium ad se invicem et in toto, non autem per comparationem ad locum.
1.en: On this Lyra raises a lengthy question, how this came about; but the answer is easy: by the omnipotence of God, who works miracles not only through angels but also through men, who apply some ministry as instruments. For there is divinely implanted in every created nature an obediential potency [that is, a capacity in a creature to be raised by God to effects beyond its natural powers], by which it obeys God the Creator at His nod in all things that do not imply a contradiction, as Scotus declares. Giles of Rome, too, writes subtly of this in his book on the Sacrament of the Altar, especially in the sixth and seventh chapters, saying among other things that qualities have a twofold relation: one to their subject, by which they give it to be such; the other to an object, or to things outside, by which they are principles of actions and the reason or cause of acting. Heat, for example, in relation to its subject, gives it to be hot; but as it is related to what can be heated, it is the principle of heating. And so it can come about by the divine power that a quality has the first relation and bearing without the second; and thus the fire will have what makes it hot in itself, but not what makes it heat something else by it: just as in the Sacrament of the Altar the body of Christ, by its own quantity, has extension, position, and order of its parts to one another and in the whole, but not by relation to place.

1.t: Præterea, quoniam singularia beneficia Dei, et potissime magna evidentissimaque miracula, provocant beneficiatos bonos et gratos ad præcipuam laudem Altissimi, hinc devotissima gratiarum actio trium virorum istorum subjungitur. Tunc hi tres pari beneficio provocati, quasi ex uno ore, id est consona concordique voce ex interiori voluntatis concordia, caritate, pace, et gratia. Ex quo Augustinus ostendit et admonet, quam concorditer psallentes in choro, debeant Deum laudare humiliter et modeste, non præcipitanter aut festinanter. Laudabant, glorificabant et benedicebant Deum in fornace, qui corpora eorum servavit illæsa, et corda fecit igne amoris flammantia. Porro laus Deo debetur ratione suæ virtutis ac bonitatis; glorificatio, ratione suæ claritatis ac celsitudinis; benedictio, ratione suæ liberalitatis. Ideo dicit Albertus : Laudabant præconio virtutis, glorificabant demonstratione claritatis, benedicebant in gratiarum actione. Ad hujuscemodi consonam Dei honorificentiam hortatur nos Paulus ad Romanos : Deus solatii det vobis id ipsum sapere in alterutrum, secundum Jesum Christum, ut unanimes uno ore honorificetis Deum et Patrem Domini nostri Jesu Christi. Et Petrus in sua Canonica : Unanimes in oratione omnes estote. Nempe ut asserit Glossa, Os divisum nil impetrat; nec dubium quin in dissonantia psallentium Deo, dæmon tripudiet.
1.en: Moreover, since God's singular benefits, and above all great and most evident miracles, move the good and grateful who receive them to special praise of the Most High, there follows the most devout thanksgiving of these three men. [[3:51|Then these three|Tunc hi tres]], moved by an equal benefit, [[3:51|as with one mouth|quasi ex uno ore]], that is, with a voice in harmony and accord, from an inward accord of will, from charity, peace and grace. From this Augustine shows, and warns, how harmoniously those who sing psalms in choir ought to praise God, humbly and modestly, not headlong or hurriedly. [[3:51|praised and glorified and blessed God, in the furnace|Laudabant, glorificabant et benedicebant Deum in fornace]], who kept their bodies unharmed and made their hearts flame with the fire of love. Now praise is owed to God by reason of His power and goodness; glorifying, by reason of His brightness and loftiness; blessing, by reason of His liberality. So Albert says: They praised by proclaiming His power, glorified by showing forth His brightness, blessed in giving thanks. To honour God thus in harmony Paul exhorts us in Romans: Now the God [[Rom 15:5|of comfort grant you to be of one mind, one towards another, according to Jesus Christ|solatii det vobis id ipsum sapere in alterutrum, secundum Jesum Christum]]: [[Rom 15:6|That with one mind and with one mouth you may glorify God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.|ut unanimes uno ore honorificetis Deum et Patrem Domini nostri Jesu Christi]] And Peter in his Epistle: [[1 Pet 3:8|be ye all of one mind|Unanimes in oratione omnes estote]] [Denis reads "be ye all of one mind in prayer"; *in prayer* is not in 1 Pet 3:8]. For, as the Gloss asserts, a divided mouth obtains nothing; and no doubt the devil dances for joy at the discord of those singing psalms to God.

1.t: Dicentes : Benedictus es, Domine Deus patrum nostrorum. Quomodo Deus sublimis atque omnipotens dicitur benedictus, superius tactum est. Etenim benedictus est, utpote in se ipso felix, bonus et sanctus, omnique bono nomine superdignus, ac jugiter benedicendus, bene ac reverentialiter exprimendus, totiusque boni origo, et omnis doni causa fontana; benedictus in se atque in omni suo effectu ac opere, quia in omnibus virtuose est agens. Porro per patres suos, intelligunt specialiter Patriarchas ac Vates veteris Testamenti, quorum se Deus universorum specialiter Deum esse perhibuit, et effectu ostendit per singularem suam providentiam, pietatem, gratiamque ad eos : ex quibus incarnari Filius Dei elegit, dicente Apostolo ad Hebræos : Nusquam angelos apprehendit, sed semen Abrahæ apprehendit. Unde in Deuteronomio Moyses populo Israel ait : En Domini Dei tui cœlum est et cœli cœlorum, terra et omnia quæ in eis sunt : et tamen patribus tuis conglutinatus est Dominus, et amavit eos, elegitque semen eorum post eos. Unde propter singularia Dei beneficia Israelitis collata, ex singulari ejus pietate ac providentia circa Israeliticum populum procedentia, fertur in Psalmo : Qui annuntiat verbum suum Jacob, etc. Etenim circa illos perhibetur omnipotens omnium Dominator singularem providentiam gerere, quos singulari gratia in ultimum dirigit finem. Et quanto circa aliquem gratiosius clementiusque se habet, tanto singulariorem circa eum providentiam habere censetur.
1.en: [[3:51|saying|Dicentes]]: [[3:52|Blessed art thou, O Lord, the God of our fathers|Benedictus es, Domine Deus patrum nostrorum]]. How the sublime and almighty God is called blessed was touched on above. For He is blessed, as being in Himself happy, good and holy, more than worthy of every good name, and ever to be blessed, to be spoken of well and with reverence, the origin of all good and the fountain-cause of every gift; blessed in Himself and in all His effects and works, because in all things He acts with power. Now by *their fathers* they mean especially the Patriarchs and Prophets of the Old Testament, of whom God, the God of all, declared Himself to be in a special way the God, and showed it in deed by His singular providence, kindness and grace towards them: from whom the Son of God chose to become incarnate, as the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 2:16|nowhere doth he take hold of the angels: but of the seed of Abraham he taketh hold|Nusquam angelos apprehendit, sed semen Abrahæ apprehendit]]. Hence in Deuteronomy Moses says to the people of Israel: [[Deut 10:14|Behold heaven is the Lord's thy God, and the heaven of heaven, the earth and all things that are therein.|En Domini Dei tui cœlum est et cœli cœlorum, terra et omnia quæ in eis sunt]] [[Deut 10:15|And yet the Lord hath been closely joined to thy fathers, and loved them and chose their seed after them|et tamen patribus tuis conglutinatus est Dominus, et amavit eos, elegitque semen eorum post eos]]. Hence, because of the singular benefits of God bestowed on the Israelites, proceeding from His singular kindness and providence towards the people of Israel, it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 147:8|Who declareth his word to Jacob|Qui annuntiat verbum suum Jacob]], etc. [the margin gives Ps. cxlvii, 19, the Hebrew numbering; in the Vulgate the verse is Ps 147:8]. For the almighty Ruler of all is said to exercise a singular providence over those whom He directs by singular grace to their last end. And the more graciously and mercifully He deals with anyone, the more singular the providence He is held to have over him.

1.t: Et laudabilis, ob tuam bonitatem, virtutem et sanctitatem. Laus enim debetur virtuti, sicut et honor : sed laus consistit in verbis, honor in actibus. Est namque exhibitio reverentiæ, in signum testimoniumque virtutis. Et sicut virtus et sanctitas Dei in infinitum cunctis præeminet, sic ipse superbeatissimus Deus infinite laudabilior est, quam eum aliqua possit creatura laudare, juxta illud Ecclesiastici : Glorificantes Dominum quantumcumque potueritis, supervalebit adhuc, etc. Itaque etsi incessabiliter laudibus Dei intenti fuerimus etiam mente devota, non inaniter gloriemur, nec præsumamus quasi quid magni egerimus; sed pensantes omne nostrum præconium atque obsequium infinite a dignitate ac laudabilitate altitudinis Dei nostri deficere, ipsum humillime deprecemur ut per pietatem suam immensam, laudes nostras acceptare dignetur : potissime quia et quidquid in eis boni est, ipsius est donum; quidquid vero defectuositatis admixtum, id prorsus est nostrum.
1.en: [[3:52|and worthy to be praised|Et laudabilis]], for Thy goodness, power and holiness. For praise is owed to virtue, as is honour too; but praise consists in words, honour in deeds. For honour is a showing of reverence, as a sign and testimony of virtue. And as the power and holiness of God infinitely surpass all things, so this most supremely blessed God is infinitely more worthy of praise than any creature can praise Him, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 43:32|Glorify the Lord as much as ever you can, for he will yet far exceed|Glorificantes Dominum quantumcumque potueritis, supervalebit adhuc]], etc. And so, even if we have been intent on God's praises without ceasing, and with a devout mind, let us not glory vainly, nor presume as though we had done something great; but, weighing that all our praise and service falls infinitely short of the dignity and praiseworthiness of the height of our God, let us most humbly beseech Him that of His immense kindness He deign to accept our praises: above all because whatever good is in them is His gift, while whatever of defect is mixed in is wholly ours.

1.t: Et gloriosus. Secundum quod gloria multis modis accipitur, sic et Deus multipliciter gloriosus asseritur. Est enim gloriosus, id est plenus gloria, sive per gloriam intelligatur jucunditas, sive felicitas, sive excellentia, seu majestas, aut clara cum laude notitia, aut fama præinclyta. Et absolute loquendo, ipse solus plenus est istis, utpote plenitudine infinita. Interdum etiam sumitur gloria Dei pro magnifico aliquo ejus effectu, ut quum Ezechiel scribit : Egressa est gloria Domini a limine templi, etc. Hujuscemodi quoque effectibus Deus causaliter plenus est. Denique Moyses in Deuteronomio Deum esse gloriosum protestans, disseruit : Nisi timueritis nomen Domini gloriosum atque terribile, augebit plagas tuas. Et superexaltatus : quoniam universis et singulis simul acceptis incomparabiliter et immense melior altiorque consistit. Siquidem finiti ad infinitum nulla est comparatio. Ideo cantat Psalmista : Magnus Dominus et laudabilis nimis, et magnitudinis ejus non est finis. In sæcula utique universa, id est omnium spatio sæculorum, generationum seu temporum. Sæculum autem variis modis accipitur, prout in libro suo Damascenus eloquitur.
1.en: [[3:52|and glorified|Et gloriosus]] [the Latin is *gloriosus*, "glorious"]. As glory is taken in many ways, so God too is said to be glorious in many ways. For He is glorious, that is, full of glory, whether by glory is understood delight, or happiness, or excellence, or majesty, or bright knowledge joined with praise, or renown of great fame. And, speaking absolutely, He alone is full of these, with an infinite fullness. Sometimes too the glory of God is taken for some magnificent effect of His, as when Ezechiel writes: [[Ezech 10:18|And the glory of the Lord went forth from the threshold of the temple|Egressa est gloria Domini a limine templi]], etc. Of such effects too God is full as their cause. Lastly Moses in Deuteronomy, declaring God to be glorious, said: Unless you [[Deut 28:58|fear his glorious and terrible name|timueritis nomen Domini gloriosum atque terribile]], [[Deut 28:59|The Lord shall increase thy plagues|augebit plagas tuas]]. [[3:52|and exalted above all|Et superexaltatus]]: because He is incomparably and immeasurably better and higher than all things together and each one of them. For between the finite and the infinite there is no comparison. Therefore the Psalmist sings: [[Ps 144:3|Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised: and of his greatness there is no end.|Magnus Dominus et laudabilis nimis, et magnitudinis ejus non est finis]] [[3:52|for ever|In sæcula]], that is, through all the ages, that is, for the whole span of all ages, generations or times. Now *age* [*sæculum*] is taken in various ways, as Damascene sets out in his book.

1.t: Et benedictum nomen gloriæ tuæ. Si nomen pro nomine nominato, id est re significata per nomen nominans, accipiatur (sicut et in Actibus quum Petrus affirmat, Non est aliud nomen sub cœlo datum hominibus, in quo oporteat nos salvos fieri; et Isaias, Ecce, inquit, nomen Domini venit de longinquo; et in Psalmo, Sit nomen Domini benedictum), sic benedictum nomen gloriæ Dei, nil aliud est nisi Deus gloriosus ac benedictus, qui proprie Deus et pater atque rex gloriæ appellatur, propter incomparabilem suam majestatem, excellentiam, voluptatem, et perfectionem in se et in suis operibus. Apostolus enim ait ad Ephesios : Pater gloriæ det vobis spiritum sapientiæ. Et Stephanus in Actibus : Deus gloriæ apparuit patri nostro Abrahæ. Rursus, gloria sumitur pro objecto gloriæ, vel representativo, vel ostensivo gloriæ : ut quum ait Scriptura, Filius sapiens gloria patris; et Paulus, Mulier, inquit, gloria est viri, et vir gloria Dei dicitur.
1.en: [[3:52|and blessed is the holy name of thy glory|Et benedictum nomen gloriæ tuæ]]. If *name* is taken for the name named, that is, for the thing signified by the naming name (as in the Acts, when Peter affirms, [[Acts 4:12|there is no other name under heaven given to men, whereby we must be saved|Non est aliud nomen sub cœlo datum hominibus, in quo oporteat nos salvos fieri]]; and Isaias, [[Is 30:27|Behold|Ecce]], he says, [[Is 30:27|the name of the Lord cometh from afar|nomen Domini venit de longinquo]]; and in the Psalm, [[Ps 112:2|Blessed be the name of the Lord|Sit nomen Domini benedictum]] [the margin gives Ps. cxiii, 2, the Hebrew numbering; in the Vulgate it is Ps 112:2]), then the blessed name of the glory of God is nothing else but God glorious and blessed, who is properly called the God and Father and King of glory, for His incomparable majesty, excellence, delight and perfection in Himself and in His works. For the Apostle says to the Ephesians: [[Eph 1:17|the Father of glory, may give unto you the spirit of wisdom|Pater gloriæ det vobis spiritum sapientiæ]]. And Stephen in the Acts: [[Acts 7:2|The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham|Deus gloriæ apparuit patri nostro Abrahæ]]. Again, glory is taken for the object of glory, that which represents or shows forth glory: as when Scripture says, A wise son is the glory of his father[[Prov 10:1||]][[Prov 13:1||]] [the margin gives Prov. x, 1 and xiii, 1; neither verse has *glory*: they read "maketh the father glad" and "heareth the doctrine of his father"]; and Paul: [[1 Cor 11:7|the woman|Mulier]], he says, [[1 Cor 11:7|is the glory of the man|gloria est viri]], and man is called the [[1 Cor 11:7|glory of God|gloria Dei]].

1.t: Porro si nomen pro nomine nominante sumatur, istud benedictum asseritur propter rei significatæ per ipsum sanctitatem atque virtutem. Tunc specialiter de hoc nomine Domini tetragrammaton explanatur, quod secundum Rabbi Moysen impositum est ad significandam divinam essentiam absolutissime in se ipsa, videlicet secundum intrinsecas suas proprietates absque respectu ad creaturas. Alia autem Dei nomina imponuntur a divinis operibus, ut Elohim in Hebræo, seu Deus in Latino, quod imponitur a generali Dei providentia atque regimine, unde aliis per participationem quamdam communicatur, quemadmodum in Exodo : Si latet fur, dominus domus applicabitur ad deos, id est judices. Et multo plus alia quædam Dei nomina aliis communicantur. Nomen autem Domini tetragrammaton, Deo appropriatur, et de eo solummodo dicitur, sanctum : quia essentialiter purum, virtuosum, firmum et supermundissimum, si de nomine nominato sumatur. Nomen autem nominans, sanctum est, sicut et benedictum, et laudabile, et superexaltatum in omnibus sæculis : quia universis quæ unquam fuerunt, sunt aut erunt, incomparabiliter et immense exstat præstantius atque sublimius. Ex quo apparet, quod de nomine nominato hæc clausula intelligatur.
1.en: But if *name* is taken for the naming name, it is said to be blessed because of the holiness and power of the thing signified by it. Then it is explained especially of the Lord's name, the Tetragrammaton, which according to Rabbi Moses [Maimonides] was given to signify the divine essence most absolutely in itself, that is, according to its intrinsic properties, without respect to creatures. But the other names of God are given from the divine works, as *Elohim* in Hebrew, or *Deus* in Latin, which is given from God's general providence and government; whence it is shared with others by a kind of participation, as in Exodus: [[Ex 22:8|If the thief be not known, the master of the house shall be brought to the gods|Si latet fur, dominus domus applicabitur ad deos]], that is, the judges. And certain other names of God are shared with others much more. But the Lord's name, the Tetragrammaton, is proper to God, and is said of Him alone: [[3:52|holy|sanctum]], because it is essentially pure, powerful, firm and most supremely clean, if it is taken of the name named. But the naming name is holy, as it is also blessed, [[3:52|and worthy to be praised and exalted above all, in all ages|et laudabile, et superexaltatum in omnibus sæculis]]: because it stands incomparably and immeasurably more excellent and sublime than all things that ever were, are or shall be. From which it appears that this clause is to be understood of the name named.

1.t: Benedictus es in templo sancto gloriæ tuæ. Quando hæc verba dicebantur, templum Jerusalem fuit destructum. Quidam tamen de ipso hæc verba exponunt, quod ipsum vocetur templum sanctum gloriæ Dei, quia in eo Deus gloriam et excellentiam gratiæ suæ patribus declaravit. De quo ait Psalmista : Replebimur in bonis domus tuæ; sanctum est templum tuum, mirabile in æquitate. De quo et illud Habacuc exponitur a quibusdam : Dominus in templo sancto suo : in quo fuit Deus benedictus, qui omni loco et tempore benedictus est. Aliqua tamen loca sibi specialiter deputantur propter specialem suam operationem in eis : in quibus et benedictus est in se ipso, et in suo effectu, quoniam in omnibus irreprehensibiliter agit, videlicet sapienter, sancte et virtuose, imo clementer et juste, dicente Propheta : Justus Dominus in omnibus viis suis, et sanctus in omnibus operibus suis. Ex quibus verbis sequentia quoque facilius patent : et superlaudabilis, quia infinite laudabilior quam comprehendere, aut laudibus exsequi valeamus, sicut expositum est, et supergloriosus in sæcula.
1.en: [[3:53|Blessed art thou in the holy temple of thy glory|Benedictus es in templo sancto gloriæ tuæ]]. When these words were said, the temple of Jerusalem had been destroyed. Some, however, explain these words of it: that it is called the holy temple of God's glory because in it God declared to the fathers the glory and excellence of His grace. Of it the Psalmist says: [[Ps 64:5|We shall be filled with the good things of thy house; holy is thy temple|Replebimur in bonis domus tuæ; sanctum est templum tuum]], [[Ps 64:6|Wonderful in justice|mirabile in æquitate]]. Of it too that saying of Habacuc is explained by some: [[Hab 2:20|the Lord is in his holy temple|Dominus in templo sancto suo]]: in which God was blessed, who is blessed in every place and time. Yet some places are assigned to Him in a special way because of His special working in them: in which He is blessed both in Himself and in His effect, since in all things He acts blamelessly, that is, wisely, holily and with power, nay mercifully and justly, as the Prophet says: [[Ps 144:17|The Lord is just in all his ways: and holy in all his works.|Justus Dominus in omnibus viis suis, et sanctus in omnibus operibus suis]] From these words what follows is also more easily clear: [[3:53|and exceedingly to be praised|et superlaudabilis]], because He is infinitely more worthy of praise than we can grasp or carry out in praises, as has been explained, [[3:53|and exalted above all for ever|et supergloriosus in sæcula]] [the Latin is *supergloriosus*, "exceedingly glorious"].

1.t: Benedictus es in throno regni tui. Thronus iste est judiciaria sedes incircumscriptibilis Dei : quæ sedes intelligi potest, vel divina auctoritas, seu potestas judicativa dominativaque omnium, quæ est ipsemet Deus excelsus, qui nullibi verius est quam in se ipso; vel thronus hic, est cœlum empyreum, in quo Deus specialiter esse et residere perhibetur, tanquam in summa aula ac supremo palatio unde cuncta gubernat. Hinc in Apocalypsi loquitur Christus : Qui vicerit, dabo ei sedere mecum in throno meo, sicut et ego vici, et sedi cum Patre meo in throno ejus. Ceterum Deus secundum se ipsum nullam habet limitationem, habitudinem aut specialitatem ad locum, sed in se ipso ac propria suæ substantiæ puritate, illocalis, intemporalis, interminabilisque consistit, nec ab aliquo tangitur, neque alicui commiscetur. Præterea regnum Dei, est Ecclesia mi[litans] et triumphans, ubi per dona gratiæ et gloriæ in suorum cordibus regnat; vel totus mundus, secundum Albertum, quem ut rex summus dispensat, juxta illud in Job : Quem constituit alium super terram? aut quem posuit super orbem quem fabricatus est? Et in Psalmo : Regnum tuum regnum omnium sæculorum. Sicque Deo potissime competit illud Proverbiorum : Rex qui sedet in solio judicii, dissipat omne malum intuitu suo.
1.en: [[3:54|Blessed art thou on the throne of thy kingdom|Benedictus es in throno regni tui]]. This throne is the judgment seat of the uncircumscribable God: which seat may be understood either as the divine authority, or the power of judging and ruling all things, which is the most high God Himself, who is nowhere more truly than in Himself; or this throne is the empyrean heaven, in which God is said to be and dwell in a special way, as in the highest hall and supreme palace from which He governs all things. Hence in the Apocalypse Christ says: [[Apoc 3:21|To him that shall overcome, I will give to sit with me in my throne: as I also have overcome and am set down with my Father in his throne.|Qui vicerit, dabo ei sedere mecum in throno meo, sicut et ego vici, et sedi cum Patre meo in throno ejus]] But God in Himself has no limitation, relation or particular bearing towards place; but in Himself and in the very purity of His substance He abides without place, without time, without end, neither touched by anything nor mingled with anything. Further, the kingdom of God is the Church militant and triumphant, where He reigns in the hearts of His own by the gifts of grace and glory; or the whole world, according to Albert, which He orders as the supreme King, according to that in Job: [[Job 34:13|What other hath he appointed over the earth? or whom hath he set over the world which he made?|Quem constituit alium super terram? aut quem posuit super orbem quem fabricatus est?]] And in the Psalm: [[Ps 144:13|Thy kingdom is a kingdom of all ages|Regnum tuum regnum omnium sæculorum]]. And so that of Proverbs belongs to God above all: [[Prov 20:8|The king, that sitteth on the throne of judgment, scattereth away all evil with his look.|Rex qui sedet in solio judicii, dissipat omne malum intuitu suo]]

1.t: Postremo per thronum intelligi potest angelicorum spirituum ordo, præsertim chorus infimus supremæ hierarchiæ angelicæ : cujus spiritus Throni vocantur, ab inhabitatione ac insidentia tranquillissima Dei, secundum beatissimum Dionysium Angelicæ hierarchiæ capitulo septimo. Cui expositioni consonat illud Augustini tertio libro de Trinitate : In angelicis spiritibus summa atque plenissima amicitia copulatis, et in unam voluntatem quodam spirituali caritatis igne conflatis, tanquam in excelsa et sancta et secreta sede præsidens Deus velut in domo sua et in templo suo, inde se quibusdam ordinatissimis creaturæ motibus, primo spiritualibus, deinde carnalibus et corporalibus per cuncta diffundit, et utitur omnibus ad incommutabile arbitrium sententiæ suæ.
1.en: Lastly, by the throne may be understood an order of the angelic spirits, especially the lowest choir of the highest angelic hierarchy, whose spirits are called Thrones from God's indwelling and most tranquil sitting upon them, according to the most blessed Dionysius in the seventh chapter of the *Angelic Hierarchy*. With this explanation agrees that saying of Augustine in the third book *On the Trinity*: In the angelic spirits, joined by the highest and fullest friendship and fused into one will by a certain spiritual fire of charity, God presiding as in a lofty, holy and secret seat, as in His house and in His temple, pours Himself out from there through all things by certain most ordered movements of creatures, first spiritual, then fleshly and bodily, and uses all things for the unchangeable decision of His will.

1.t: De hoc throno legitur in Ecclesiastico : Unus est Altissimus, creator omnium omnipotens, rex potens et metuendus nimis, sedens super thronum; et in Psalmo, Sedisti super thronum, qui judicas justitiam; in Sapientia quoque, Mitte illam, puta sapientiam, de cœlis sanctis tuis, et a sede magnitudinis tuæ.
1.en: Of this throne we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 1:8|There is one most high Creator Almighty, and a powerful king, and greatly to be feared, who sitteth upon his throne|Unus est Altissimus, creator omnium omnipotens, rex potens et metuendus nimis, sedens super thronum]]; and in the Psalm, [[Ps 9:5|thou hast sat on the throne, who judgest justice|Sedisti super thronum, qui judicas justitiam]]; in Wisdom too, [[Wis 9:10|Send her|Mitte illam]], that is, wisdom, [[Wis 9:10|out of thy holy heaven, and from the throne of thy majesty|de cœlis sanctis tuis, et a sede magnitudinis tuæ]].

1.t: Benedictus es qui intueris luce seu oculo supersplendidissimæ sapientiæ tuæ, universa et singula perfectissime ac distinctissime cognoscentis : secundum illud ad Hebræos, Omnia nuda et aperta sunt oculis ejus; abyssos, id est Oceanum, omniumque aquarum profunda, et pelagi ima; vel, Abyssos, id est absconditas partes terræ, secundum Albertum, prout in Ecclesiastico fertur : Oculi Domini multo plus lucidiores sunt super solem, circumspicientes omnes vias hominum, et profundum abyssi. Quidam per abyssos intelligunt angelos reprobos de cœlo projectos, forte propter caliginem impiamque profunditatem mentis eorum.
1.en: [[3:55|Blessed art thou that beholdest|Benedictus es qui intueris]] by the light or eye of Thy most supremely resplendent wisdom, which knows all things together and each one most perfectly and most distinctly: according to that to the Hebrews, [[Heb 4:13|all things are naked and open to his eyes|Omnia nuda et aperta sunt oculis ejus]]; [[3:55|the depths|abyssos]], that is, the Ocean, and the deeps of all waters, and the bottom of the sea; or, *The depths*, that is, the hidden parts of the earth, according to Albert, as is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 23:28|the eyes of the Lord are far brighter than the sun, beholding round about all the ways of men, and the bottom of the deep|Oculi Domini multo plus lucidiores sunt super solem, circumspicientes omnes vias hominum, et profundum abyssi]]. Some understand by *the depths* the reprobate angels cast down from heaven, perhaps because of the darkness and impious depth of their minds.

1.t: Et sedes super Cherubim. Secundum Gregorium, Deus proprie super Thronos, qui sunt de tertio ordine primæ hierarchiæ angelicæ, residet; sed propter vicinitatem eorum ad Cherubim, qui sunt medius ordo hierarchiæ præfatæ, etiam super Cherubim sedere describitur, juxta illud Psalmi : Qui sedes super Cherubim, manifestare. Aliqui vero ad litteram per Cherubim intelligunt imagines Cherubim in tabernaculo Moysis, quæ in Exodo appellantur Cherubim gloriæ obumbrantia propitiatorium, de quo Dominus loquebatur ad Moysen. Sicque super Cherubim illa unde apparuit, affirmatur sedisse, sicut in templo dicitur habitasse. Itaque super angelicas mentes de ordine Cherubim sedet Deus, præsidens illis : super quos etiam sedere dicitur, quoniam illorum scientiæ, quamvis altæ, supereminet infinite, ita quod eum comprehendere nequeunt. Propter quod quidam Sanctorum leguntur dixisse, quod Cherubim Deum non audent adspicere, quem tamen avidissime, jucundissime, inavertibiliterque adspiciunt. Talis ergo modus loquendi extensus, pie sumendus est, ut sit sensus : Non audent Deum adspicere, id est, majestatem ipsius plenarie perscrutari, seu comprehendere non præsumunt, sed terminis ac legibus sibi divinitus præstitutis contenti sunt, ut divinus Dionysius docet. His demum expositio Alberti concordat, dicentis : Sedes, id est quiescis, super Cherubim, id est plenitudinem scientiæ. Non enim discurris super scita ut nos, scilicet ratiocinando; nec scientia tua causatur a scitis, sed est causa scitorum : et sicut pertingis ubique faciendo, sic et videndo : secundum illud Sapientiæ, Attingit a fine usque ad finem fortiter; et Job, Scio quia omnia potes, et nulla te latet cogitatio.
1.en: [[3:55|and sittest upon the cherubims|Et sedes super Cherubim]]. According to Gregory, God properly rests upon the Thrones, who are of the third order of the first angelic hierarchy; but because of their nearness to the Cherubim, who are the middle order of that hierarchy, He is also described as sitting upon the Cherubim, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 79:2|Thou that sittest upon the cherubims, shine forth|Qui sedes super Cherubim, manifestare]] [the margin gives Ps. lxxxix, 2; the verse is Ps 79:2]. Others, however, understand by the Cherubim, literally, the images of the Cherubim in the tabernacle of Moses, which in Exodus are called Cherubim of glory overshadowing the propitiatory, from which the Lord spoke to Moses[[Ex 25:20||]][[Ex 25:22||]] [the margin gives Exod. xxv, 19–22; the words "cherubims of glory overshadowing the propitiatory" are those of Heb 9:5]. And so He is affirmed to have sat upon those Cherubim from which He appeared, as He is said to have dwelt in the temple. So God sits upon the angelic minds of the order of the Cherubim, presiding over them; and He is also said to sit upon them because He infinitely surpasses their knowledge, high though it is, so that they cannot comprehend Him. For this reason some of the Saints are read to have said that the Cherubim dare not look upon God, whom yet they behold most eagerly, most joyfully and without turning away. Such a stretched way of speaking, then, is to be taken devoutly, so that the sense is: They dare not look upon God, that is, they do not presume to search out or comprehend His majesty fully, but are content with the bounds and laws set for them by God, as the divine Dionysius teaches. With these, lastly, the explanation of Albert agrees, who says: [[3:55|sittest|Sedes]], that is, Thou restest, [[3:55|upon the cherubims|super Cherubim]], that is, upon the fullness of knowledge. For Thou dost not run over things known as we do, that is, by reasoning; nor is Thy knowledge caused by the things known, but it is the cause of the things known: and as Thou reachest everywhere by making, so also by seeing; according to that of Wisdom, [[Wis 8:1|She reacheth|Attingit]] [[Wis 8:1|from end to end mightily|a fine usque ad finem fortiter]]; and Job, [[Job 42:2|I know that thou canst do all things, and no thought is hid from thee.|Scio quia omnia potes, et nulla te latet cogitatio.]] [the margin gives Job xliii, 2; the verse is Job 42:2].

1.t: Benedictus es in firmamento cœli, id est in firmamento quod dicitur cœlum, de quo in Genesi: Fiat firmamentum in medio aquarum; et item, Vocavit Deus firmamentum cœlum. Quod dicitur firmamentum, quoniam firmat omnia in se contenta, quorum est locus communis. Locus autem est conservativus locati, secundum Philosophum: qui etiam dicit, quod motus cœli est velut vita quædam, virtus et conservatio inferiorum. Unde in firmamento est Deus, tanquam principalis motor, rector, atque influxor in inferiora: qui licet non sit proximus motor cœlestium orbium in genere causæ efficientis, seu efficienter moventis, est tamen motor primus et summus in genere causæ finalis, quoniam movet sicut desideratum seu bonum optatum movet desiderium et optantem, secundum meliores philosophos, tam Peripateticos quam Platonicos.
1.en: [[3:56|Blessed art thou in the firmament of heaven|Benedictus es in firmamento cœli]], that is, in the firmament which is called heaven, of which it is said in Genesis: [[Gen 1:6|Let there be a firmament made amidst the waters|Fiat firmamentum in medio aquarum]]; and again, [[Gen 1:8|God called the firmament, Heaven|Vocavit Deus firmamentum cœlum]]. It is called the firmament because it makes firm [*firmat*] all things contained in it, of which it is the common place. Now a place preserves what is placed in it, according to the Philosopher, who also says that the motion of the heaven is as it were a kind of life, power and preservation for the things below. Hence God is in the firmament as its chief mover, ruler, and one who pours his influence into the things below. And though he is not the proximate mover of the heavenly spheres in the order of efficient cause, that is, as moving them by acting on them, he is nevertheless the first and highest mover in the order of final cause, since he moves them as the thing desired, or the good longed for, moves the one who desires and longs for it, according to the better philosophers, Peripatetics and Platonists alike.

1.t: Consequenter tres viri isti omnes creaturas per ordinem provocant et invitant ad Dei præconium. Quo enim quis in Dei amore plus ardet, eo intensius ipsum ab universis laudari, amari ac honorari desiderat. Propterea libro primo de Doctrina christiana loquitur Augustinus: Quanto quis in amore Dei ferventior est, tantum agit quibus potest modis, ut Deus a pluribus diligatur; rursus, quo aliquis Deum sincerius contemplatur, eo se ipsum plus parvi pendit atque humiliat, ac per hoc laudem qua ipse Deum laudat, insufficientiorem existimat, et ideo eum a cunctis magnifice laudari cupit, et ut valet procurat.
1.en: Next these three men call upon and invite all creatures, in order, to the praise of God. For the more ardently anyone burns with the love of God, the more intensely he desires that God be praised, loved and honoured by all. Hence Augustine says in the first book of *On Christian Doctrine*: The more fervent anyone is in the love of God, the more he strives, by whatever means he can, that God be loved by more people. Again, the more purely someone contemplates God, the less he esteems himself and the more he humbles himself; and so he reckons the praise with which he himself praises God all the more insufficient, and therefore he longs for God to be magnificently praised by all, and brings it about as far as he can.

1.t: Sed antequam sequens canticum exponatur, sciendum quod præinducta ab aliquibus aliter elucidantur. Quum enim dicitur, Benedictus es in templo sancto gloriæ tuæ: per templum, Christi humanitatem accipiunt, quia ut ait Apostolus ad Colossenses, In Christo habitat omnis plenitudo Divinitatis corporaliter. Propter quod, ut aiunt, dicitur in Apocalypsi de cœlesti Jerusalem: Templum non vidi in ea; Dominus enim Deus templum illius est et Agnus. Per thronum vero intelligunt beatam Virginem, Deo ratione maternitatis speciali modo conjunctam, in cujus gremio sedit Christus, quando a Magis adorabatur. Has autem expositiones non litterales, sed mysticas reor seu spirituales: sicut et per templum intelligi potest Ecclesia, fidelisque anima, imo et templum materiale, in quo Christus sacramentaliter ac realiter continetur, seu est in utraque suæ personæ natura.
1.en: But before the song that follows is explained, it should be known that the verses before it are explained differently by some. For where it is said, [[3:53|Blessed art thou in the holy temple of thy glory|Benedictus es in templo sancto gloriæ tuæ]], they take the temple to be the humanity of Christ, since, as the Apostle says to the Colossians, [[Col 2:9|in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead corporeally|In Christo habitat omnis plenitudo Divinitatis corporaliter]]. For this reason, they say, it is said in the Apocalypse of the heavenly Jerusalem: [[Apoc 21:22|I saw no temple therein. For the Lord God Almighty is the temple thereof, and the Lamb|Templum non vidi in ea; Dominus enim Deus templum illius est et Agnus]]. By the throne[[3:54||]] they understand the Blessed Virgin, joined to God in a special way by reason of her motherhood, in whose lap Christ sat when he was adored by the Magi. But I take these expositions to be not literal but mystical or spiritual; just as by the temple may be understood the Church and the faithful soul, and indeed also the material temple, in which Christ is contained sacramentally and really, that is, is present in both natures of his person.

1.t: Benedicite, omnia opera Domini, Domino, laudate et superexaltate eum in sæcula. Circa hoc ait Glossa, et sunt verba Hieronymi: Omnis creatura non voce, sed opere laudat Deum, quia ex creaturis Creator intelligitur, et in singulis operibus atque effectibus magnificentia Dei monstratur. Insuper advertendum, quod quamvis hoc verum sit de creatura irrationali, seu non intellectuali, intellectuales tamen creaturæ vocibus mentis et oris Dominum benedicunt. Nam et angeli, quamvis in propria natura non nisi mentalibus verbis utantur, in corporibus tamen assumptis verba sensibiliter proferunt. Dæmones quoque quandoque, quamvis invite, Deum verbis extollunt, quemadmodum in Marco legitur: Spiritus immundi quum Christum videbant, procidebant ei, dicentes: Tu es Filius Dei. Hoc autem cunctis commune est creaturis, quod Deum benedicunt, laudant et superexaltant dupliciter. Primo materialiter, quoniam sunt materia laudis sui Creatoris, in quantum sunt bonæ, et divina in eis relucet perfectio, juxta illud Genesis: Vidit Deus cuncta quæ fecerat, et erant valde bona; et in Sapientiæ libro, A magnitudine speciei creaturæ, poterit creator horum cognoscibiliter videri. Quibus consentiens Paulus ad Romanos fatetur: Invisibilia Dei per ea quæ facta sunt, intellecta conspiciuntur, sempiterna quoque virtus ejus et divinitas. Secundo, hoc faciunt per suas operationes naturales, in quarum industria seu ordinato processu, motu et ordine, divina sapientia non mediocriter commendatur, sicut et in naturalibus eorum proprietatibus, viribus, plumis, pilis, coloribus et figuris.
1.en: [[3:57|All ye works of the Lord, bless the Lord: praise and exalt him above all for ever|Benedicite, omnia opera Domini, Domino, laudate et superexaltate eum in sæcula]]. On this the Gloss says (and the words are Jerome's): Every creature praises God, not with its voice but by its work, because the Creator is understood from his creatures, and the magnificence of God is shown in each of his works and effects. It should be noted besides that, though this is true of irrational or non-intellectual creatures, intellectual creatures bless the Lord with the voices of the mind and of the mouth. For the angels too, though in their own nature they use only mental words, yet in bodies they have assumed utter words that can be heard. The demons too sometimes extol God in words, though unwillingly, as we read in Mark: [[Mark 3:11|the unclean spirits, when they saw him, fell down before him|Spiritus immundi quum Christum videbant, procidebant ei]], saying: [[Mark 3:12|Thou art the Son of God|Tu es Filius Dei]]. Now it is common to all creatures that they bless, praise and exalt God above all in two ways. First, materially, because they are the matter of their Creator's praise, inasmuch as they are good and the divine perfection shines in them, according to that saying of Genesis: [[Gen 1:31|God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good|Vidit Deus cuncta quæ fecerat, et erant valde bona]]; and in the book of Wisdom, [[Wis 13:5|by the greatness of the beauty, and of the creature, the creator of them may be seen, so as to be known thereby|A magnitudine speciei creaturæ, poterit creator horum cognoscibiliter videri]]. Agreeing with these, Paul declares to the Romans: [[Rom 1:20|the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made. His eternal power also and divinity|Invisibilia Dei per ea quæ facta sunt, intellecta conspiciuntur, sempiterna quoque virtus ejus et divinitas]]. Secondly, they do it by their natural operations, in whose skill, that is, in their ordered course, motion and order, the divine wisdom is commended in no small measure, as it is also in their natural properties, powers, feathers, hairs, colours and shapes.

1.t: Postremo quod ait, Opera Domini, Domino, dupliciter sumitur. Primo, de effectibus seu creaturis Dei in natura productis: sic enim omnes creaturæ, etiam naturæ rerum, dicuntur opera Dei, quemadmodum ait Scriptura: Opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli; et iterum, Manus Domini fecit hæc omnia. Secundo, de operibus virtutum, quæ efficit Deus in bonis, juxta illud Isaiæ: Omnia opera nostra operatus es in nobis. In quibus operibus nobis a Deo collatis, omnipotentia atque clementia ejus ostenditur. Sic namque ait Psalmista: Mirabilis Deus in sanctis suis; et Apostolus, Gratias, inquit, ago Deo super inenarrabili dono ejus.
1.en: Lastly, what he says, [[3:57|works of the Lord, bless the Lord|Opera Domini, Domino]], is taken in two ways. First, of the effects or creatures of God produced in nature: for in this way all creatures, and also the natures of things, are called the works of God, as Scripture says: [[Ps 101:26|the heavens are the works of thy hands|Opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli]]; and again, [[Job 12:9|the hand of the Lord hath made all these things|Manus Domini fecit hæc omnia]] [the margin gives Deut. xxxii, 27, where the enemies say, "Our mighty hand, and not the Lord, hath done all these things"; Denis's wording is closer to Job 12:9]. Secondly, of the works of the virtues which God brings about in the good, according to that saying of Isaias: [[Is 26:12|thou hast wrought all our works for us|Omnia opera nostra operatus es in nobis]]. In these works, bestowed on us by God, his almighty power and his mercy are shown. For so the Psalmist says: [[Ps 67:36|God is wonderful in his saints|Mirabilis Deus in sanctis suis]]; and the Apostle: [[2 Cor 9:15|Thanks|Gratias]], he says, [[2 Cor 9:15|be to God for his unspeakable gift|ago Deo super inenarrabili dono ejus]].

1.t: Circa hoc oritur quæstio (benedicere enim videtur esse majoris, dicente Apostolo ad Hebræos, Sine ulla contradictione, quod minus est, a majore benedicitur), quomodo creaturæ benedicere Creatorem monentur. Et respondendum est, quod duplex est benedictio, utpote consecrationis aut perfectivæ collationis, de qua veritatem habet instantia: sic enim Deus benedicit creatis. Unde Gregorius ait: Benedictio Dei, est collatio munerum ejus, et multiplicatio eorumdem. Prælati quoque tanquam medii inter Deum et subditos aut subjecta, benedicunt eis hoc modo. Alia est benedictio laudis, seu gratiarum actionis, de qua modo est mentio: quomodo Simeon justus Deum legitur benedixisse; et David testatur, Benedicam Dominum in omni tempore.
1.en: Here a question arises (for to bless seems to belong to the greater, since the Apostle says to the Hebrews, [[Heb 7:7|without all contradiction, that which is less is blessed by the better|Sine ulla contradictione, quod minus est, a majore benedicitur]]): how are creatures bidden to bless the Creator? And the answer is that blessing is of two kinds. One is the blessing of consecration, or of a bestowal that perfects; and of this the objection holds true, for it is in this way that God blesses the things he has made. Hence Gregory says: The blessing of God is the bestowal of his gifts, and their multiplication. Prelates too, as standing between God and their subjects or the things under them, bless them in this way. The other is the blessing of praise, or of thanksgiving, which is the one meant here: in this way we read that Simeon the just blessed God[[Luke 2:28||]]; and David testifies, [[Ps 33:2|I will bless the Lord at all times|Benedicam Dominum in omni tempore]].

1.t: Laudate et superexaltate eum in sæcula. Eisdem modis Deum laudant et superexaltant, quibus et benedicunt. Asseritque Albertus: Laudant, quia virtus Dei in ipsis monstratur; superexaltant, quia Creator supereminere proprietatibus creaturæ monstratur. Omnibus nempe recte considerantibus dant causam, præbent materiam, excitant mentem ad Creatoris præconia, atque ad agnoscendum quod ipse sit universis sine mensura sublimior. Causa equidem in suo relucet effectu, et creatura est quasi radius quidam sui creatoris. Nam agens producit sibi simile, secundum philosophos. Ideo in omni creato bonitas, sapientia, et omnipotentia Dei apparet. Quamvis autem Laudare et Benedicere accipi soleant pro eodem, quoniam tamen in cantico isto distincte exprimuntur, potest benedictio ad gratiarum actionem referri, laus ad simplicem commendationem; vel unum istorum ad præconium Dei sine comparatione ejus ad creaturas, aliud ad præconium ejus per comparationem ad eas: juxta quem modum laudat eum S. Dionysius in libro de Divinis nominibus, ubi de Dei tractat nominibus, secundum processum influentiæ Dei ad creaturas.
1.en: [[3:57|praise and exalt him above all for ever|Laudate et superexaltate eum in sæcula]]. They praise and exalt God above all in the same ways in which they bless him. And Albert asserts: They praise him, because the power of God is shown in them; they exalt him above all, because the Creator is shown to stand far above the properties of the creature. For to all who consider rightly they give occasion, supply matter, and stir the mind to the praises of the Creator, and to acknowledge that he is beyond measure higher than all things. For a cause shines forth in its effect, and a creature is as it were a ray of its creator; since an agent produces what is like itself, according to the philosophers. Therefore the goodness, wisdom and almighty power of God appear in every created thing. Now though *to praise* and *to bless* are usually taken for the same thing, yet since they are expressed separately in this song, blessing can be referred to thanksgiving and praise to simple commendation; or one of them to the praise of God without comparing him with creatures, the other to his praise by comparison with them. It is in this way that St Dionysius praises him in the book *On the Divine Names*, where he treats of the names of God according to the going forth of God's influence to creatures.

1.t: Generali exhortatione præmissa, viri hi ad particularia descendunt creata, et quod dixerunt in summa, exsequuntur per partes, a superioribus inchoantes, in quibus major est similitudo primi opificis, secundum quod Plato fatetur: Fluens a primo bonitas, forma est in proximis, imago in distantibus, et velut obscura reflexio in ultimis. Primo ergo invitant naturam angelicam in rerum ordinibus [Deo] propinquiorem, prout duodecimo Confessionum loquitur Augustinus: Duo fecisti, o Domine: unum prope te, scilicet angelum; aliud prope nihil, puta materiam. Invitant autem angelicos spiritus, non quod ipsi nostra admonitione indigeant, aut a Dei benedictione, laude et superexaltatione unquam desistant; sed verba hæc, congratulando quia sic faciunt, magis quam exhortando ut sic faciant, rite sunt exponenda, sicut et illud in Psalmo: Laudate eum, omnes angeli ejus; et, Benedicite Domino, angeli ejus, potentes virtute; et, Lauda, Jerusalem, Dominum, si de Jerusalem cœlesti explanetur.
1.en: Having given the general exhortation first, these men come down to particular created things, and what they said in sum they carry out part by part, beginning from the higher, in which there is a greater likeness to the first Maker, according to what Plato declares: Goodness flowing from the first is a form in the nearest things, an image in the more distant, and as it were a dim reflection in the last. First, then, they invite the angelic nature, which in the order of things is nearer to God, as Augustine says in the twelfth book of the *Confessions*: Thou hast made two things, O Lord: one near to thee, namely the angel; the other near to nothing, namely matter. Now they invite the angelic spirits not because these need our admonition, or ever cease from blessing, praising and exalting God above all; rather these words are rightly to be explained as rejoicing with them because they do so, more than as urging them to do so; as is also that in the Psalm: [[Ps 148:2|Praise ye him, all his angels|Laudate eum, omnes angeli ejus]]; and, [[Ps 102:20|Bless the Lord, all ye his angels: you that are mighty in strength|Benedicite Domino, angeli ejus, potentes virtute]]; and, [[Ps 147:1|Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem|Lauda, Jerusalem, Dominum]], if it is explained of the heavenly Jerusalem.

1.t: Benedicite, angeli Domini, Domino. Angelus, secundum magnum Dionysium, quandoque est nomen cœlestis spiritus de infimo choro; interdum pro omni cœlesti spiritu sumitur, sicut et nunc. Propter quod ait Albertus: Omnes cœlestes spiritus vocat angelos, propter hoc quod ad minus per descensum et influentiam illuminationum mittuntur: quæ illuminationes a superioribus ad medios, et a mediis ad inferiores descendunt. Unde ad Hebræos dicit Apostolus: Nonne omnes sunt administratorii spiritus? Laudate et superexaltate eum. Hos actus angeli intellectualiter ac jucundissime prosequuntur tanto præclarius, affectuosius atque felicius, quo increatam lucem seu divinam essentiam limpidius ac subtilius contemplantur, majestatis Dei sui immensitatem profundius intuentes, reverentialius admirantes, perfectius honorantes. In sæcula, id est jugiter per omne ævum: juxta illud Psalmi: Beati qui habitant in domo tua, Domine; in sæcula sæculorum laudabunt te. Et in Apocalypsi: Servi Dei videbunt faciem ejus, et regnabunt in sæcula sæculorum.
1.en: [[3:58|O ye angels of the Lord, bless the Lord|Benedicite, angeli Domini, Domino]]. *Angel*, according to the great Dionysius, is sometimes the name of a heavenly spirit of the lowest choir; at other times it is taken for every heavenly spirit, as it is here. For this reason Albert says: He calls all the heavenly spirits angels, because they are sent at least by way of the descent and outpouring of illuminations; and these illuminations come down from the higher to the middle ones, and from the middle to the lower. Hence the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 1:14|Are they not all ministering spirits|Nonne omnes sunt administratorii spiritus]]? [[3:58|praise and exalt him|Laudate et superexaltate eum]]. The angels carry out these acts intellectually and most joyfully, the more gloriously, lovingly and happily, the more clearly and keenly they contemplate the uncreated light, that is, the divine essence, gazing more deeply into the immensity of the majesty of their God, wondering at it more reverently, honouring it more perfectly. [[3:58|for ever|In sæcula]], that is, continually through every age; according to that saying of the Psalm: [[Ps 83:5|Blessed are they that dwell in thy house, O Lord: they shall praise thee for ever and ever|Beati qui habitant in domo tua, Domine; in sæcula sæculorum laudabunt te]].
