[[4:22|till thou know|Donec scias]] by experience of due chastisement: know, I say, firmly and perfectly, [[4:22|that the most High ruleth|quod dominetur Excelsus]], that is, God most high, in comparison with whom all things are low, [[4:22|over the kingdom of men|super regnum hominum]], that is, that he presides over all kingdoms as the supreme, first and almighty ruler: according to that of the Psalm, [[Ps 94:4|in his hand are all the ends of the earth|In manu ejus sunt omnes fines terræ]]; [[4:22|and giveth it to whomsoever he will|et cuicumque voluerit, det illud]], justly putting down one and raising up another at his pleasure.

paras.t: Quod autem vigil et sanctus præcepit, ut germen radicum ejus, id est arboris, relinqueretur : sic enim superius dixit, Attamen germen radicum ejus in terra dimittite : id (inquam) significat, quod regnum tuum tibi manebit, id est, te exspectabit, et illud recipies, postquam cognoveris, vexatione tibi intellectum præstante, et corde tuo per humilitatem ac supernam illuminationem disposito, potestatem esse cœlestem, id est, esse unam summam ac primam virtutem increatam et independentem, in cœlis regnantem, et terrestria moderantem, providentiam universorum habentem. Itaque per germen radicum arboris, designatur possibilitas redeundi ad regnum.
paras.en: [[4:23|But whereas|Quod autem]] the watcher and holy one [[4:23|he commanded|præcepit]], [[4:23|that the stump of the roots thereof, that is, of the tree, should be left|ut germen radicum ejus, id est arboris, relinqueretur]] (for so he said above, [[4:20|but leave the stump of the roots thereof in the earth|Attamen germen radicum ejus in terra dimittite]] [the margin gives v. 12, which says the same; the words are those of v. 20]): that, I say, signifies that [[4:23|thy kingdom shall remain to thee|regnum tuum tibi manebit]], that is, shall await thee, and thou shalt receive it again, [[4:23|after thou shalt have known|postquam cognoveris]], affliction giving thee understanding, and thy heart being made ready by humility and heavenly enlightenment, [[4:23|that power is from heaven|potestatem esse cœlestem]], that is, that there is one supreme and first power, uncreated and independent, reigning in heaven and governing earthly things, having providence over all. So by the stump of the roots of the tree is signified the possibility of returning to the kingdom.

paras.t: Nunc exponenda sunt quædam superius transilita. Succidite arborem, et præcidite ramos ejus, id est, regem Nabuchodonosor de regno propellite, et dilatationem sui imperii tollite. Et excutite folia ejus, id est, verba ejus magnifica et ornatum, ostendite vana, et dispergite fructus ejus, id est, opes ipsius auferte ab eo. Aliqui etiam dicunt, quod divitiæ regni Babylonici, durante regis insania, a pluribus rapiebantur. Et fugiant bestiæ quæ subter eam sunt, id est, subditi, inferiores, rusticani et simplices, de regis jugo recedant ; et volucres, id est divites, potentes, et in dignitatibus constituti, de ramis ejus, scilicet Nabuchodonosor, abeant, sub latitudine suæ potestatis non amplius se tuendo. Cor ejus ab humano commutetur, id est, mens seu ratio ejus ab aliorum mente varietur, ita quod in amentiam transferatur. Ratione enim a brutis secernimur : dum ergo usu rationis privamur, brutales efficimur. Et cor feræ detur ei, videlicet judicio rationis nudato.
paras.en: Now some things passed over above are to be explained. [[4:11|Cut down the tree, and chop off the branches thereof|Succidite arborem, et præcidite ramos ejus]], that is, drive King Nabuchodonosor out of his kingdom, and take away the breadth of his empire. [[4:11|shake off its leaves|Et excutite folia ejus]], that is, show his grand words and his adornment to be vain, [[4:11|and scatter its fruits|et dispergite fructus ejus]], that is, take his wealth away from him. Some also say that the riches of the Babylonian kingdom, while the king's madness lasted, were plundered by many. [[4:11|let the beasts fly away that are under it|Et fugiant bestiæ quæ subter eam sunt]], that is, let the subjects, the lower sort, the country folk and the simple, withdraw from the king's yoke; [[4:11|and the birds|et volucres]], that is, the rich, the powerful and those set in dignities, [[4:11|from its branches|de ramis ejus]], that is, of Nabuchodonosor, let them go away, no longer sheltering under the breadth of his power. [[4:13|Let his heart be changed from man's|Cor ejus ab humano commutetur]], that is, let his mind or reason be made different from the mind of others, so that it is turned into madness. For by reason we are set apart from the brutes: when therefore we are deprived of the use of reason, we become brutish. [[4:13|and let a beast's heart be given him|Et cor feræ detur ei]], that is, once it is stripped of the judgement of reason.

paras.t: In sententia vigilum, id est per sententiam promulgatam per angelos, decretum est, id est, divinitus ordinatum est sic fieri : ita quod institutio seu ordinatio Dei per sententiam angelorum, innotuit mundo de regis hujus punitione præfata. Et licet unus vigil seu angelus verba inducta clamaverit, alii tamen consenserunt, aut executioni sententiæ cooperati sunt. Porro qui die ac nocte, quantum natura permittit, sanctis instant vigiliis, Dei laudibus aut actibus virtuosis vacando, cœlestium vigilum agilitatem sectantur. Hinc ait Hieronymus : Nos quoque crebris pernoctationibus imitamur officia angelorum. Et Christus in Evangelio : Beatus, inquit, servus ille, quem, quum venerit dominus ejus, et pulsaverit januam ejus, invenerit vigilantem ; et rursus, Vigilate itaque, quia nescitis qua hora Dominus vester venturus sit.
paras.en: [[4:14|by the sentence of the watchers|In sententia vigilum]], that is, by the sentence promulgated by the angels, [[4:14|This is the decree|decretum est]], that is, it has been divinely ordained that it be so: so that the institution or ordinance of God concerning the punishment of this king, foretold above, was made known to the world through the sentence of the angels. And though one watcher or angel cried out the words given, the others nevertheless agreed, or worked together in carrying out the sentence. Further, those who by day and by night, as far as nature allows, keep holy vigils, giving themselves to the praises of God or to virtuous acts, follow the alertness of the heavenly watchers. Hence Jerome says: We too, by frequent night watches, imitate the offices of the angels. And Christ in the Gospel: Blessed, he says, is that servant whom his lord, when he shall come and knock at his door, shall find watching[[Luke 12:37||]] [Denis's wording joins Luke 12:36–37, in the singular as in Matt 24:46]; and again, [[Matt 24:42|Watch ye therefore, because you know not what hour your Lord will come|Vigilate itaque, quia nescitis qua hora Dominus vester venturus sit]].

paras.t: Et sermo sanctorum : id est, eorum qui divinæ æquitati consentiunt in supernis, sermo et verbum est ut taliter fiat ; et petitio eorumdem. Sancti namque expostulant ultionem contra malignos, et Dei omnipotentiam in impiorum justa dejectione declarari precantur, juxta illud Apocalypsis : Usquequo, Domine (sanctus et verus), non judicas, et non vindicas sanguinem nostrum de his qui sunt in terra ?
paras.en: [[4:14|and the word|Et sermo]] [[4:14|of the holy ones|sanctorum]]: that is, of those on high who agree with the divine justice, it is the saying and the word that it be done so; [[4:14|and demand|et petitio]] of the same. For the saints demand vengeance against the wicked, and pray that God's almighty power be shown in the just casting down of the ungodly, according to that of the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 6:10|How long, O Lord (Holy and True), dost thou not judge and revenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?|Usquequo, Domine (sanctus et verus), non judicas, et non vindicas sanguinem nostrum de his qui sunt in terra]]

paras.t: Donec cognoscant viventes in terra, quod dominetur Excelsus, id est Deus sublimis, in regno hominum, id est, cuncta regna ejus potestati subdantur : sicut plenius dictum est super illud, Ipse transfert regna atque constituit. Et cuicumque voluerit, dabit illud. Subest enim ei, quum voluerit, posse. Ideo secundum Dei voluntatem quisque ad præsidentiam est vocandus, ut ait Gregorius ; nec debet se quisquam ingerere, neque vulpinis uti cautelis, sed rem dispositioni divinæ committere, quum ad Hebræos dicat Apostolus : Nemo sumit sibi honorem, sed qui vocatur a Deo tanquam Aaron. Et humillimum hominem constituet super eum, id est super regni principatum. Quidam per humillimum hominem intelligunt Christum, qui protestatur, Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra ; alii, regem Nabuchodonosor, qui post suam amentiam profundissime humiliavit se Deo. Generalius tamen exponi potest indeterminate, quod Deus quemcumque hominem sibi placentem ad promovendum, promoveat ad regnandum, si ita decrevit, quantumcumque ille sit vilis atque abjectus. Juxta quod dicitur primo Regum libro : Suscitat de pulvere egenum, et de stercore elevat pauperem, ut sedeat cum principibus, et solium gloriæ teneat.
paras.en: [[4:14|till the living know|Donec cognoscant viventes]] on earth, [[4:14|that the most High ruleth|quod dominetur Excelsus]], that is, God on high, [[4:14|in the kingdom of men|in regno hominum]], that is, that all kingdoms are subject to his power: as was said more fully on the words, He [[Dan 2:21|taketh away kingdoms, and establisheth them|transfert regna atque constituit]]. [[4:14|and he will give it to whomsoever it shall please him|Et cuicumque voluerit, dabit illud]]. For his power is at hand when he will[[Wis 12:18||]]. Therefore each man is to be called to high office according to God's will, as Gregory says; and no one ought to thrust himself forward, nor use the wiles of the fox, but commit the matter to the divine disposition, since the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 5:4|Neither doth any man take the honour to himself, but he that is called by God, as Aaron was|Nemo sumit sibi honorem, sed qui vocatur a Deo tanquam Aaron]]. [[4:14|and he will appoint the basest man over it|Et humillimum hominem constituet super eum]], that is, over the rule of the kingdom. Some understand by *the basest man* [that is, *humillimus*, the lowliest] Christ, who declares, [[Matt 28:18|All power is given to me in heaven and in earth|Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra]]; others, King Nabuchodonosor, who after his madness humbled himself most deeply before God. But it can be explained more generally and without restriction: that God raises to reign any man whom it pleases him to raise, if he has so decreed, however mean and abject that man may be. According to what is said in the first book of Kings: [[1 Kings 2:8|He raiseth up the needy from the dust, and lifteth up the poor from the dunghill: that he may sit with princes, and hold the throne of glory|Suscitat de pulvere egenum, et de stercore elevat pauperem, ut sedeat cum principibus, et solium gloriæ teneat]].

paras.t: Nunc visio tota exposita est ; subjungiturque consilium sancti Prophetæ, qui nil melius vidit pro rege, quam ad divinam confugere misericordissimam pietatem. Quamobrem, rex, consilium meum tibi placeat. Consilium etenim sapientium, præsertim in arduis, est quærendum atque servandum, ut in Tobia habetur : Consilium semper a sapiente perquire ; et in Proverbiis, Qui cuncta agunt consilio reguntur sapientia. Et peccata tua eleemosynis redime, ne debitor pœnæ permaneas, neque peccatis obnoxius, et iniquitates tuas misericordiis pauperum. Contraria enim curantur contrariis. Ideo decet, ut qui pauperes oppressisti, eis subvenias. Et ad impetrandum misericordiam Dei maxime confert, misericordiam pauperibus, imo et cunctis, impendere. Propter quod ait Salvator : Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur. Et iterum ait Scriptura : Sicut aqua exstinguit ignem, ita eleemosyna exstinguit peccatum ; et in Proverbiis, Per misericordiam et fidem purgantur peccata. Sed et in Tobia inde notabiliter scriptum est : Noli avertere faciem tuam ab ullo paupere : ita enim fiet, ut nec a te avertatur facies Domini. Eleemosyna ab omni peccato liberat, et non patietur animam ire in tenebras.
paras.en: Now the whole vision has been explained; and there follows the counsel of the holy Prophet, who saw nothing better for the king than to take refuge in the most merciful divine goodness. [[4:24|Wherefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to thee|Quamobrem, rex, consilium meum tibi placeat]]. For the counsel of the wise, especially in hard matters, is to be sought and kept, as is said in Tobias: [[Tob 4:19|Seek counsel always of a wise man|Consilium semper a sapiente perquire]]; and in Proverbs, [[Prov 13:10|they that do all things with counsel, are ruled by wisdom|Qui cuncta agunt consilio reguntur sapientia]]. [[4:24|and redeem thou thy sins with alms|Et peccata tua eleemosynis redime]], lest thou remain a debtor to punishment and liable for thy sins, [[4:24|and thy iniquities with works of mercy to the poor|et iniquitates tuas misericordiis pauperum]]. For contraries are cured by contraries [a maxim of the physicians, applied to the healing of the soul]. Therefore it is fitting that thou who hast oppressed the poor shouldst help them. And to obtain God's mercy it avails most to show mercy to the poor, nay, to all. Wherefore the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:7|Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy|Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur]]. And again Scripture says: As water quencheth fire, so alms quencheth sin[[Ecclus 3:33||]] [the margin notes "according to the old version", that is, an older Latin rendering; the Vulgate reads: Water quencheth a flaming fire, and alms resisteth sins]; and in Proverbs, [[Prov 15:27|By mercy and faith sins are purged away|Per misericordiam et fidem purgantur peccata]]. And in Tobias too it is notably written on this: [[Tob 4:7|turn not away thy face from any poor person: for so it shall come to pass that the face of the Lord shall not be turned from thee|Noli avertere faciem tuam ab ullo paupere : ita enim fiet, ut nec a te avertatur facies Domini]]. [[Tob 4:11|alms deliver from all sin|Eleemosyna ab omni peccato liberat]], [[Tob 4:11|and will not suffer the soul to go into darkness|et non patietur animam ire in tenebras]].

1.t: HIERONYMUS et Albertus hoc loco incipiunt capitulum quartum; quidam vero paulo ante, videlicet ibi : Nabuchodonosor rex omnibus populis ; et dicunt, quod epistola regis ibi incipiat, ad quam totum istud capitulum pertinere affirmant. In Scholastica quoque historia scribitur, quod istud capitulum sit regis epistola. Sic enim habet Historia illa : Sequitur tertia visio Danielis, quam non scripsit Daniel (scilicet populo), sed est epistola regis, quam scripsit universo regno suo, postquam de bestia restitutus est in hominem et in regnum ; in qua prædicavit mirabilia quæ apud eum fecerat Deus excelsus : quam epistolam Daniel inseruit operi suo. Itaque Daniel scripsit epistolam istam in libro isto, sed non scripsit eam ad populos : imo, secundum Hieronymum, epistola regis in Prophetæ volumine ponitur, ut non fictus ab aliquo iste liber, sed Danielis esse credatur. Porro, secundum Albertum, habita visione de regno Christi secundum potestatem qua conterit regna mundi, inducitur hic visio de eodem secundum cognitionem et viam quæ ducit ad ipsum. Hinc aliqui asserunt, quod hæc tertia visio significat Christi prædicationem contra humanam prosperitatem. Verba autem sequentia dicunt esse narrationem epistolæ, scilicet :
1.en: Jerome and Albert begin the fourth chapter at this place; but some begin it a little before, namely at the words: [[Dan 3:98|Nabuchodonosor, the king, to all peoples|Nabuchodonosor rex omnibus populis]]; and they say that the king's letter begins there, and they maintain that this whole chapter belongs to it. In the Scholastic History [the *Historia scholastica* of Peter Comestor] too it is written that this chapter is the king's letter. For that History has it thus: "There follows the third vision of Daniel, which Daniel did not write (that is, to the people), but it is a letter of the king, which he wrote to his whole kingdom after he had been restored from a beast into a man and to his kingdom; in which he proclaimed the wonders that the most high God had wrought upon him: and Daniel inserted this letter into his own work." So Daniel wrote this letter in this book, but he did not write it to the peoples: rather, according to Jerome, the king's letter is placed in the Prophet's volume so that this book may be believed to be not forged by someone, but Daniel's. Further, according to Albert, after the vision of the kingdom of Christ according to the power by which it breaks in pieces the kingdoms of the world, there is brought in here a vision of the same kingdom according to the knowledge of it and the way that leads to it. Hence some assert that this third vision signifies the preaching of Christ against human prosperity. And the words that follow, they say, are the telling of the letter, namely:

1.t: Ego Nabuchodonosor, monarcha quodammodo orientis, quietus eram a præliis, vel in lecto quiescens, in domo mea, Babylonico scilicet palatio : et quia quietus erat, ad visionis perceptionem aptior fuit. Anima enim quiescendo fit prudens. Et de Sapientia legitur in Ecclesiastico : Qui minoratur actu, percipiet illam. Sapiens quoque alius : Intrans in domum meam, conquiescam cum illa. Et florens potestate, honore, divitiis, gloria, omnique prosperitate terrena, in palatio meo.
1.en: [[4:1|I, Nabuchodonosor|Ego Nabuchodonosor]], in a manner monarch of the East, [[4:1|was at rest|quietus eram]] from battles, or resting in bed, [[4:1|in my house|in domo mea]], that is, in the palace of Babylon: and because he was at rest, he was the more fit to receive a vision. For the soul becomes wise by resting. And of Wisdom we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 38:25|he that is less in action, shall receive wisdom|Qui minoratur actu, percipiet illam]]. And another wise man: [[Wis 8:16|When I go into my house, I shall repose myself with her|Intrans in domum meam, conquiescam cum illa]]. [[4:1|And flourishing|Et florens]] in power, honour, riches, glory and every earthly prosperity, [[4:1|in my palace|in palatio meo]].

1.t: Somnium vidi, quod perterruit me. Verbum istud in superioribus fuit expositum. Insolita autem, præsertim tempore noctis visa, intuentem perterrent. Et cogitationes meæ in strato meo habitæ, et visiones capitis mei conturbaverunt me admiratione atque pavore, sollicitudine, desiderioque sciendi quid designarent. Cur autem pluraliter dicit, Visiones capitis mei, quum non nisi una visio, unumque somnium fuerit, patet ex dictis in superiori expositione, ubi sic legitur : Somnium tuum et visiones capitis tui in cubili tuo, hujusmodi sunt. Fuit quippe una visio integralis, quæ ob suas partes, pluraliter visiones vocatur. Et cur visiones dicat esse capitis sui, præallegato loco expositum est. Siquidem visio ista, imaginaria fuit et in vi imaginativa, quæ situatur in capite : in quo etiam spiritus animales et naturales, qui vehunt formas seu similitudines revelationis, puriores et lucidiores sunt, secundum Albertum : secundum quem, somnium istud insinuatur partim provenisse ex præviis cogitationibus regis, qui cœpit vigilando in lecto cogitare de sibi ac regno suo futuris ; quamvis principaliter fuerit somnium hoc divinitus inditum, secundum quod in expositione primæ visionis dictum est clarius.
1.en: [[4:2|I saw a dream that affrighted me|Somnium vidi, quod perterruit me]]. These words were explained above[[Dan 2:1||]]. Now unusual things, especially when seen at night, terrify the one who beholds them. [[4:2|and my thoughts in my bed|Et cogitationes meæ in strato meo]], the thoughts I had there, [[4:2|and the visions of my head, troubled me|et visiones capitis mei conturbaverunt me]] with wonder and dread, with anxiety and the desire to know what they meant. But why he says in the plural [[4:2|the visions of my head|Visiones capitis mei]], when there was only one vision and one dream, is clear from what was said in the exposition above, where we read thus: [[Dan 2:28|Thy dream, and the visions of thy head upon thy bed, are these|Somnium tuum et visiones capitis tui in cubili tuo, hujusmodi sunt]]. For it was one integral vision, which because of its parts is called in the plural *visions*. And why he says the visions are *of his head* was explained in the place just cited[[Dan 2:28||]]. For this vision was imaginary [that is, made of images in the imagination, neither a bodily sight nor a purely intellectual one], and in the imaginative power, which is situated in the head: in which also the animal and natural spirits [the subtle vapours that the physicians of the time held to carry sensation and life through the body], which carry the forms or likenesses of the revelation, are purer and clearer, according to Albert; and according to him it is suggested that this dream came partly from the king's previous thoughts, who began, lying awake in bed, to think about what was to come for himself and his kingdom; although this dream was chiefly put into him by God, as was said more clearly in the exposition of the first vision[[Dan 2:29||]].

1.t: Et per me, id est a proprio ore meo, positum est decretum, id est commissio, ordinatio seu præceptum, ut introducerentur in conspectu meo cuncti sapientes Babylonis : carentes sapientia quæ desursum est, quæ et bonis operibus plena est, secundum apostolum Jacobum ; sed sæculari sapientia præditi, de quibus Dominus ait : Perdam sapientiam sapientium, et prudentiam prudentium reprobabo. Denique, secundum Albertum, sapientes hic nominantur peritissimi divinationum. Et ut solutionem somnii indicarent mihi. Somniorum namque significationibus plurimum intendebant gentiles, et reges eorum de sapientium suorum consilio cuncta agebant, ut dictum est in primæ visionis commento.
1.en: [[4:3|Then I|Et per me]] (that is, by my own mouth) [[4:3|set forth a decree|positum est decretum]], that is, a commission, ordinance or command, [[4:3|that all the wise men of Babylon should be brought in before me|ut introducerentur in conspectu meo cuncti sapientes Babylonis]]: men lacking [[Jas 3:17|the wisdom that is from above|sapientia quæ desursum est]], which is also full of good works, according to the apostle James; but endowed with worldly wisdom, of whom the Lord says: [[1 Cor 1:19|I will destroy the wisdom of the wise: and the prudence of the prudent I will reject|Perdam sapientiam sapientium, et prudentiam prudentium reprobabo]][[Is 29:14||]] [the margin gives Is. xxix, 14 and 1 Cor. i, 19: the words are those of the Apostle, who is quoting Isaias]. Finally, according to Albert, the wise men named here are those most skilled in divinations. [[4:3|and that they should shew me the interpretation of the dream|Et ut solutionem somnii indicarent mihi]]. For the Gentiles paid very great heed to the meanings of dreams, and their kings did everything by the counsel of their wise men, as was said in the commentary on the first vision.

1.t: Tunc ingrediebantur arioli, magi, Chaldæi, et aruspices. Quorum significationes et distinctiones diligenter expositæ sunt in elucidatione secundi capituli. Et somnium narravi in conspectu eorum. Nunc humanius ac rationabilius habuit se, quam viso somnio primo, cujus non solum interpretationem, sed et essentiam exegit sibi a præinductis indicari hominibus. Nunc enim flagellis Dei correptus, humiliatus et emendatus, impossibilia ab illis non requisivit, sed somnium eis proposuit. Et solutionem ejus, id est somnii significationem, non indicaverunt mihi : quoniam sicut somnium supernaturale divinumque exstitit, sic expositio ejus non nisi supernaturaliter atque divinitus valuit sciri, juxta illud ad Corinthios, Quæ sunt Dei, nemo novit nisi Spiritus Dei ; et in Genesi, Numquid non Dei est interpretatio ?
1.en: [[4:4|Then came in the diviners, the wise men, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers|Tunc ingrediebantur arioli, magi, Chaldæi, et aruspices]]. What these names mean and how they differ was carefully set out in the explanation of the second chapter[[Dan 2:2||]]. [[4:4|And I told the dream before them|Et somnium narravi in conspectu eorum]]. Now he behaved more humanely and reasonably than when he had seen the first dream, of which he required the men brought in before him to tell him not only the interpretation but the dream itself. For now, chastised by the scourges of God, humbled and amended, he did not ask impossible things of them, but set the dream before them. And [[4:4|the interpretation thereof|Et solutionem ejus]], that is, the meaning of the dream, [[4:4|they did not shew me|non indicaverunt mihi]]: because, as the dream was supernatural and divine, so its exposition could be known only supernaturally and by God's gift, according to that saying to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 2:11|the things also that are of God, no man knoweth, but the Spirit of God|Quæ sunt Dei, nemo novit nisi Spiritus Dei]]; and in Genesis: [[Gen 40:8|Doth not interpretation belong to God?|Numquid non Dei est interpretatio]]

1.t: Donec collega, id est socialiter ac familiariter mihi colligatus amicitia speciali : in quo constat regem jam humiliatum, quod captivum et servum vocat collegam ; ingressus est in conspectu meo Daniel. Hæc dictio, Donec, excludit hic etiam tempus sequens, quia præfati sapientes nec post Danielis ingressum, somnium regis exponere potuerunt, nisi expositione Danielis audita. Cui nomen Balthasar Chaldaice secundum nomen dei mei, id est, eo nomine appellatus, quo deus meus : quoniam deus Nabuchodonosor, Balthasar vocabatur, secundum Glossam. Et participatione Spiritus divini, impositum est Danieli nomen divinum, quia præ ceteris divinior apparebat, prout in expositione primi capituli amplius dictum est.
1.en: [[4:5|Till their colleague|Donec collega]], that is, joined to me in fellowship and familiarity by a special friendship: in which it is plain that the king was now humbled, since he calls a captive and a slave his colleague; [[4:5|Daniel, came in before me|ingressus est in conspectu meo Daniel]]. The word *till* here shuts out the time that followed as well [that is, it does not imply that the wise men could do it afterwards], because the said wise men could not explain the king's dream even after Daniel came in, except by hearing Daniel's explanation. [[4:5|whose name is Baltassar|Cui nomen Balthasar]] in Chaldean, [[4:5|according to the name of my god|secundum nomen dei mei]], that is, called by the same name as my god: since the god of Nabuchodonosor was called Baltassar, according to the Gloss. And through his share in the divine Spirit a divine name was given to Daniel, because he appeared more godlike than the rest, as was said more fully in the exposition of the first chapter.

1.t: Qui habet spiritum deorum sanctorum in semetipso, id est, illuminatus est illo spiritu quo sancti dii sunt pleni ; vel, anima seu spiritus ejus tantæ sapientiæ est, ut deorum spiritui comparetur, estque talis ut spiritus illorum. Loquitur autem more gentilium, et falsos deos suos æstimat sanctos, futurorumque præscios. Circa quod ait Hieronymus, et habetur in Glossa : Non mirum si erret Nabuchodonosor, et quidquid super se cernit, deos arbitretur. Verum, ut refert Albertus, aliqui dicunt, quod dii dicuntur angeli, a quibus Prophetæ illuminationes perceperunt, juxta illud Psalmi : Illuminans tu mirabiliter a montibus æternis. Nam ex præcedenti capitulo ejusque expositione, jam patuit, quod angelorum aliqualem notitiam rex habebat. Dicit autem, In semetipso, ad innuendum quod Daniel quasi ad nutum vel exuberanter habuerit spiritum talem.
1.en: [[4:5|who hath in him the spirit of the holy gods|Qui habet spiritum deorum sanctorum in semetipso]], that is, he is enlightened by that spirit with which the holy gods are filled; or, his soul or spirit is of such wisdom that it may be compared to the spirit of the gods, and is such as their spirit is. But he speaks after the manner of the Gentiles, and thinks his false gods holy and knowing things to come beforehand. On which Jerome says, and it is found in the Gloss: "No wonder if Nabuchodonosor errs, and takes for gods whatever he sees above himself." But, as Albert reports, some say that the angels are called gods, the angels from whom the Prophets received their enlightenings, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 75:5|Thou enlightenest wonderfully from the everlasting hills|Illuminans tu mirabiliter a montibus æternis]]. For from the preceding chapter and its exposition it is already clear that the king had some knowledge of angels[[Dan 3:92||]][[Dan 3:95||]]. And he says [[4:5|in him|In semetipso]] [literally "in himself"] to suggest that Daniel had such a spirit as it were at his beck, or in abundance.

1.t: Circa hunc passum Lyra sic ait : Qui habet spiritum deorum sanctorum, ad interpretandum somnia. Propter hoc ars interpretandi somnia, dicebatur divina scientia. Unde Albertus commentator super librum de Somno et vigilia dicit, Socratem Atheniensibus exclamasse laudando scientiam divinationis somniorum, dicentem : Absit a me, ut hanc vestram, quam experti estis per somnia, dicam esse falsam scientiam ; sed hanc divinam me ignorare profiteor. Humana me scire exiliter protestatus sum ; et ut verum fatear, hoc solum me scire arbitratus sum, quod ignoro, eo quod scientiam deorum vel sanctorum non sum adeptus. Verumtamen istis non obstantibus, gentiles multipliciter superstitiosi fuerunt in conjecturis somniorum.
1.en: On this passage Lyra speaks thus: [[4:5|who hath in him the spirit of the holy gods|Qui habet spiritum deorum sanctorum]], for interpreting dreams. For this reason the art of interpreting dreams was called a divine science. Hence Albert, the commentator on the book *On Sleep and Waking* [Aristotle's *De somno et vigilia*], says that Socrates cried out to the Athenians in praise of the science of divining dreams, saying: "Far be it from me to call this science of yours, which you have learnt by experience through dreams, a false science; but I confess that, being divine, it is unknown to me. I have declared that I know human things but slightly; and, to confess the truth, I have thought that I know only this, that I do not know, because I have not attained the knowledge of the gods or of the holy ones." Yet, all this notwithstanding, the Gentiles were superstitious in many ways in their conjectures about dreams.

1.t: Et somnium coram eo locutus sum : quamvis non dubitaverim quin ex revelatione divina ipsum potuisset cognoscere, sicut et somnium primum.
1.en: [[4:5|and I told the dream before him|Et somnium coram eo locutus sum]]: although I did not doubt that he could have known it by divine revelation, as he did the first dream too.

1.t: Quæritur, cur rex sciens Danielem omnibus sapientiorem Chaldæis, eum primo omnium non vocavit. Ad quod quidam respondent, quod Daniel absens fuit, et alibi in negotiis regis occupatus : cunctis enim provinciis regis fuit præpositus. Alii dicunt, quod ministri regis primo induxerunt Chaldæos magistros, ut ipsi amplius honorarentur a rege, si somnium explanarent ; sed divina dispensatione sic contigit, ut Deus Israel in suo famulo exaltaretur, et Daniel sublimior appareret, magisque idoneus apud eum ad loquendum pro filiis Israel, atque ut idololatræ confunderentur, eorumque præsumptio falsa comprobaretur, qua de primo somnio sunt locuti : Rex dicat somnium servis suis, et solutionem indicabimus ei.
1.en: It is asked why the king, knowing Daniel to be wiser than all the Chaldeans, did not call him first of all. To this some answer that Daniel was absent, and busy elsewhere with the king's affairs: for he had been set over all the king's provinces. Others say that the king's ministers brought in the Chaldean masters first, so that they themselves might be the more honoured by the king if these explained the dream; but by God's dispensation it so came about that the God of Israel might be exalted in his servant, and that Daniel might appear the more exalted and the more fit to speak with the king for the children of Israel; and that the idolaters might be confounded, and their false presumption proved, with which they spoke about the first dream: [[Dan 2:7|Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will declare the interpretation of it|Rex dicat somnium servis suis, et solutionem indicabimus ei]].

1.t: Balthasar, princeps ariolorum, id est incantatorum seu divinatorum : quorum principem constituit eum rex, ut dictum est in fine secundi capituli, quia sapientior illis fuit, non quod ariolando aut impie divinando ita vocari meruisset ; quoniam ego scio per experientiam, quod spiritum deorum sanctorum habeas in te : juxta sensum præhabitum ; et omne sacramentum non est impossibile tibi, id est, nullum secretum impossibile est tibi interpretari ac manifestare, propter excellentiam illuminationum tuarum, ita quod istud potes non propria et humana virtute, sed divina et supernaturali : sicut ait Apostolus ad Philippenses, Omnia possum in eo qui me confortat. Hoc nempe dicimur posse, ut ait Philosophus, quod possumus per nos aut per nostros amicos. Hinc viri perfecti et sancti ea posse dicuntur, quæ faciliter valent impetrare a Deo.
1.en: [[4:6|Baltassar, prince of the diviners|Balthasar, princeps ariolorum]], that is, of the enchanters or soothsayers: over whom the king made him chief, as was said at the end of the second chapter[[Dan 2:48||]], because he was wiser than they, not because he had deserved to be so called by practising divination or divining impiously; [[4:6|because I know|quoniam ego scio]] by experience [[4:6|that thou hast in thee the spirit of the holy gods|quod spiritum deorum sanctorum habeas in te]], in the sense given above; [[4:6|and that no secret is impossible to thee|et omne sacramentum non est impossibile tibi]] [literally "and every mystery is not impossible to thee"; *sacramentum* here means a hidden thing], that is, no secret is impossible for thee to interpret and make known, because of the excellence of thy enlightenings; so that thou canst do this not by thine own human power but by power divine and supernatural: as the Apostle says to the Philippians, [[Phil 4:13|I can do all things in him who strengtheneth me.|Omnia possum in eo qui me confortat]]. For, as the Philosopher says, we are said to be able to do what we can do by ourselves or through our friends. Hence perfect and holy men are said to be able to do those things which they can easily obtain from God.

1.t: Visiones somniorum meorum quas vidi, id est visiones somniales in somno factas, et imaginarias interius apprehensas. Superius singulariter dixit rex, Somnium vidi ; nunc autem pluraliter loquitur, Visiones somniorum : quoniam somnium istud figurativum, præsagum futurorum, plurima complectebatur. Ideo propter distinctionem rerum ad ipsum pertinentium, pluraliter explicatur.
1.en: [[4:6|the visions of my dreams that I have seen|Visiones somniorum meorum quas vidi]], that is, dream visions made in sleep, imaginary ones grasped inwardly. Above, the king said in the singular, [[4:2|I saw a dream|Somnium vidi]]; but now he speaks in the plural, [[4:6|the visions of my dreams|Visiones somniorum]]: because this dream, being figurative and foretelling things to come, took in a great many things. Therefore, because of the distinctness of the things that belong to it, it is expressed in the plural.

1.t: Et solutionem earum narra mihi. Paulo ante jam dixit, Somnium coram eo, scilicet Daniele, locutus sum, et in verbis statim sequentibus rex recitat illud : quomodo ergo jam petit illud sibi a Daniele narrari ? Et respondendum, quod petit illud sibi ab eo narrari, id est narratum resumi, ut sigillatim per particulas exponatur. Itaque sicut nonnulli bene dicunt, petit narrationem per modum expositionis, in qua necesse est somnium ab expositore resumi, partesque singulas visionis applicari singulis partibus expositionis. Quamvis vero rex ore tenus visionem suam Danieli protulerit, nunc tamen recitat eam, redigendo eam ad formam epistolæ.
1.en: [[4:6|and the interpretation of them|Et solutionem earum]] [[4:6|tell me|narra mihi]]. A little before he has already said, [[4:5|I told the dream before him|Somnium coram eo, scilicet Daniele, locutus sum]] (that is, before Daniel), and in the words that follow at once the king recites it: how then does he now ask that it be told him by Daniel? The answer is that he asks that it be told him by Daniel in the sense that what has been told be taken up again, so that it may be explained bit by bit. And so, as some rightly say, he asks for a telling by way of exposition, in which the dream must be taken up again by the expounder, and the several parts of the vision applied to the several parts of the exposition. And though the king had set out his vision to Daniel by word of mouth, now he recites it, putting it into the form of a letter.

1.t: Visio capitis mei in cubili meo. Triplex est visio, scilicet cordis aut mentis, et oculorum, ac imaginativæ virtutis, quæ hic visio capitis nominatur, quia vis imaginativa sita est in capite. Idcirco ad innuendum quod erat imaginativa, nec pure intellectualis neque sensibilis, ait : Visio capitis mei in cubili meo. Quod, secundum Albertum, est titulus narrationis sequentis. Quocirca ait Hieronymus : Nabuchodonosor visiones non oculorum et cordis, sed capitis novit : quoniam propter gloriam servorum Dei, futurorum illi mysteria revelantur, videlicet ut per expositionem imaginariæ visionis regis, unus eorum, et per illum exaltarentur et ceteri ad gloriam Dei, consolationemque populi.
1.en: [[4:7|This was the vision of my head in my bed|Visio capitis mei in cubili meo]]. Vision is threefold: of the heart or mind, of the eyes, and of the imaginative power, which is here called the *vision of the head*, because the imaginative power is situated in the head. So, to suggest that it was imaginary, neither purely intellectual nor of the senses, he says: [[4:7|the vision of my head in my bed|Visio capitis mei in cubili meo]]. This, according to Albert, is the title of the narrative that follows. Hence Jerome says: "Nabuchodonosor knew visions not of the eyes and of the heart, but of the head: because for the glory of the servants of God the mysteries of things to come are revealed to him"; that is, so that through the exposition of the king's imaginary vision one of them, and through him the others too, might be exalted, to the glory of God and the comfort of the people.

1.t: Videbam sensu interiori, imaginaria visione ; et ecce arbor in medio terræ, et altitudo ejus nimia, etc. Hoc totum, sicut et cetera quæ sequuntur in visione, sic apparebat : quia species seu similitudines rerum talium formabantur in vi imaginativa regis ministerio angeli sancti, secundum doctrinam S. Dionysii, quæ similitudines talia repræsentabant. Nam et nobis frequenter in somnis apparet, quod aliqua exteriora agamus, videamus aut patiamur ; sed ideo fallimur, quia species rerum pro ipsis rebus accipimus. Nabuchodonosor autem advertit somnium suum aliquid designare, quamvis nescierit quid notaret.
1.en: [[4:7|I saw|Videbam]] with the inner sense, by imaginary vision; [[4:7|and behold a tree in the midst of the earth, and the height thereof was exceeding great|et ecce arbor in medio terræ, et altitudo ejus nimia]], etc. All this, like the rest that follows in the vision, appeared in this way: the species or likenesses of such things [*species*: the images by which things are known] were formed in the king's imaginative power by the ministry of a holy angel, according to the teaching of St. Dionysius, and these likenesses represented such things. For to us too it often seems in dreams that we are doing, seeing or suffering some outward things; but we are deceived in this, because we take the species of things for the things themselves. Nabuchodonosor, however, perceived that his dream signified something, though he did not know what it meant.

1.t: Præterea non decet nos expositionem sancti Danielis præcurrere, idcirco transiliendus est textus qui sequitur, usque ad id : Tu ergo, Balthasar. Ibi enim narratio somnii terminatur, et quæ nunc transiliuntur, in expositione verborum Prophetæ resumentur et exponentur. Interpretationem somnii hujus narra festinus. Arsit enim desiderio sciendi mysterium somnii tanti. Ardenter autem optanti et multum timenti, vix aliquid satis est velox ; petitque celerrime consequi quod affectat. Putavit etiam rex Danielem tam sapientem, quod dilatione, inquisitione, deliberationeve multa non indigeret. Ideo subdit : Tu autem potes auxilio spiritus deorum, non viribus propriis, quia spiritus deorum sanctorum est in te : sicut expositum est.
1.en: Moreover, it is not fitting for us to run ahead of holy Daniel's exposition; and so the text that follows is to be passed over, as far as the words [[4:15|thou, therefore, O Baltassar|Tu ergo, Balthasar]]. For there the telling of the dream ends, and what is now passed over will be taken up again and explained in the exposition of the Prophet's words. [[4:15|tell me quickly the interpretation|Interpretationem somnii hujus narra festinus]] of this dream. For he burned with desire to know the mystery of so great a dream. And to one who longs ardently and fears much, hardly anything is swift enough; he asks to gain at once what he desires. The king also thought Daniel so wise that he would need no delay, inquiry or long deliberation. Therefore he adds: [[4:15|but thou art able|Tu autem potes]], by the help of the spirit of the gods, not by thine own strength, [[4:15|because the spirit of the holy gods is in thee|quia spiritus deorum sanctorum est in te]]: as has been explained.

1.t: Tunc Daniel cœpit intra semetipsum tacitus cogitare quasi una hora. In textu non legitur, quando Danieli ostensa sit desuper interpretatio somnii ejus ; et probabiliter dici potest, quod infra hanc horam, ita quod nunc recollegit spiritum suum in se, et recollectum elevavit ad Deum cum oratione interna atque ferventi affectu pro illuminatione hujus somnii declarativa : alioqui non videtur, cur tanto tempore conticuisset, si jam ante fuisset sibi somnii expositio revelata : sicut in primi somnii expositione ductus ad regem, statim processit ad somnii solutionem. Aliqui tamen affirmant, quod cœpit intra se tacite cogitare, qualiter religio regio culmini servaret honorem, et tamen non absconderet veritatem, id est, qualiter ipsemet Daniel religiosus, regiæ dignitati reverentiam congruam exhiberet, nec tamen veritatem taceret. Et ita præmeditabatur quasi una hora ad ordinandum responsum. Nec obstat quod loquitur Christus, Nolite præmeditari quid respondeatis, etc., quia ut dicit Albertus : Quamvis de fide non sit præmeditandum, quoniam statim scitur quid sit tenendum ; tamen de ordine sermonis, qualiter audientibus proponatur, est præmeditandum. Et hoc verbum Alberti intelligendum est sane.
1.en: [[4:16|Then Daniel|Tunc Daniel]] [[4:16|began silently to think within himself for about one hour|cœpit intra semetipsum tacitus cogitare quasi una hora]]. The text does not say when the interpretation of the king's dream was shown to Daniel from above; and it may probably be said that it was within this hour: so that he now gathered his spirit into himself, and, so gathered, raised it to God with inward prayer and fervent affection, asking for an enlightening that would make this dream plain; otherwise there seems no reason why he should have kept silent for so long, if the exposition of the dream had already been revealed to him: just as at the exposition of the first dream, when brought to the king, he went straight on to the solution of the dream. Some, however, affirm that he began to think silently within himself how religion might keep the honour due to the royal height and yet not hide the truth; that is, how Daniel himself, a man of religion, might show fitting reverence to the royal dignity and yet not keep silent about the truth. And so he premeditated for about an hour, to order his answer. Nor is it against this that Christ says: [[Luke 21:14|not to meditate before how you shall answer|Nolite præmeditari quid respondeatis]], etc.[[Matt 10:19||]] [the margin gives Matt. x, 19 and Luke xxi, 14; Denis's wording is that of Luke 21:14]; because, as Albert says: "Although there is to be no premeditation about the faith, since what is to be held is known at once, yet about the order of the speech, how it is to be put before the hearers, there is to be premeditation." And this saying of Albert is to be understood soundly.

1.t: Et cogitationes ejus conturbabant eum : quia ex revelatione sibi interius facta, vidit regi gravissimam imminere calamitatem, cui condoluit ; et contemplatione divini judicii æquitatisque ejus contremuit. Quod et vultus ejus immutatio patefecit ; atque hoc ipsum rex consideravit. Propter quod subditur : Respondens autem rex, ait : Balthasar, somnium et interpretatio ejus non conturbent te immoderate, id est, non ita dejiciant, ut veritati quid detrahas. Unde Hieronymus asserit : Tacitus intellexit Daniel somnium esse contra regem ; et timorem cordis, vultus pallore signabat ; dolebatque pro eo qui ei honoris plurimum detulit. Quod totum verum est, in quantum perpendit ista adversa, tanquam quædam mala pœnalia ; in quantum vero erant divinæ pietatis remedia, animæ regis salubria, Propheta consolabatur se ipsum. In hoc quoque, quod rex Danielem hortatur et roborat ad denuntiandam veritatem, quantumlibet adversa immineant, typum gerit pœnitentis, qui ad omne flagellum debet esse paratus, ut hic scribit Albertus.
1.en: [[4:16|and his thought troubled him|Et cogitationes ejus conturbabant eum]]: because by the revelation made to him inwardly he saw that a most grievous calamity hung over the king, and he grieved for him; and at the contemplation of God's judgment and its justice he trembled. And the change in his countenance showed this; and the king noticed this very thing. Therefore it is added: [[4:16|But the king answering, said|Respondens autem rex, ait]]: [[4:16|Baltassar, let not the dream and the interpretation thereof trouble thee|Balthasar, somnium et interpretatio ejus non conturbent te]] beyond measure, that is, let them not so cast thee down that thou take anything away from the truth. Hence Jerome asserts: "Daniel understood in silence that the dream was against the king; and he showed the fear of his heart by the paleness of his face; and he grieved for him who had shown him very great honour." All of which is true in so far as he weighed these adversities as certain penal evils [that is, evils that are punishments]; but in so far as they were remedies of God's mercy, healthful to the king's soul, the Prophet took comfort. In this too, that the king exhorts and strengthens Daniel to announce the truth however adverse the things that threaten, he bears the figure of the penitent, who ought to be ready for every scourge, as Albert writes here.

1.t: Respondit Balthasar et dixit : Domine mi rex, somnium his qui te oderunt contingat, et interpretatio ejus hostibus tuis sit. Blande et amicabiliter mutuo se affantur, ad insinuandum quod quidquid dicitur inter eos, ex dilectione procedit, nec se invicem velint offendere. Daniel quoque tam reverenter temperateque loquitur regi cui durissima fuerat relaturus, ne rex ultra modum contristaretur, quia non est afflictio addenda afflicto. Sed mirum videtur, quod Propheta tam sanctus, pœnam regi divino judicio justissime infligendam optat ab eo auferri, ejusque hostibus imprimis : quorum nonnulli rege hoc superbissimo meliores fuerunt. Et respondendum, quod Daniel id optavit, partim ex pietate, partimque zelo justitiæ. Regi enim pie condoluit propter humanitatem ejus ad se ; et hostibus ejus malum imprecabatur, in quantum peccatores fuerunt, et animabus eorum expedivisset in præsenti puniri. Iterum Daniel verbum suum intelligi voluit, præsupposito beneplacito Dei, servatoque ordine æquitatis. Ex simili zelo loquitur Jeremias in libro suo : Da filios eorum in famem, et deduc eos in manum gladii.
1.en: [[4:16|Baltassar answered, and said|Respondit Balthasar et dixit]]: [[4:16|My lord|Domine mi rex]] king, [[4:16|the dream be to them that hate thee|somnium his qui te oderunt]] [Denis's text adds *contingat*, "befall"], [[4:16|and the interpretation thereof to thy enemies|et interpretatio ejus hostibus tuis sit]]. They address each other gently and amicably, to suggest that whatever is said between them proceeds from love, and that they would not wish to offend each other. Daniel, too, speaks so reverently and temperately to the king, to whom he was about to report the hardest things, lest the king be saddened beyond measure, since affliction is not to be added to the afflicted. But it seems strange that so holy a Prophet should wish the punishment which by God's judgment was most justly to be inflicted on the king to be taken away from him, and laid above all on his enemies [*imprimis*; perhaps a misprint for *imprimi*, "to be laid on"], some of whom were better than this most proud king. The answer is that Daniel wished this partly from compassion and partly from zeal for justice. For he grieved with the king in compassion because of the king's kindness towards him; and he called down evil on the king's enemies in so far as they were sinners, and it would have profited their souls to be punished in this present life. Again, Daniel meant his word to be understood with God's good pleasure presupposed and the order of justice kept. From a like zeal Jeremias speaks in his book: [[Jer 18:21|deliver up their children to famine, and bring them into the hands of the sword|Da filios eorum in famem, et deduc eos in manum gladii]].

1.t: Deinceps expositionem orditur. Arborem quam vidisti sublimem atque robustam, id est similitudo arboris hujusmodi tibi præsentata in somno, cujus altitudo pertingit ad cœlum, etc., tu es, rex, per significationem, non per essentiam : quia per speciem et rem illam tu designaris, ita quod quidquid de dispositione illius arboris dicitur, te concernit ; qui magnificatus es potestate, divitiis, fama et gloria, omnique prosperitate mundana, et invaluisti super terram, hostibus prævalendo. Ideo arbor illa apparuit sublimis atque robusta : sublimis, regia dignitate ; robusta, potestate exercitus et armorum. Et magnitudo tua, non corporalis, sed spiritualis, puta majestas et excellentia in regnando, crevit numero subditorum, et pervenit usque ad cœlum, id est ad valde magnam exaltationem et eminentiam : ut per hyperbolen dictum istud intelligatur, sicut et illud in Psalmo, Ascendunt usque ad cœlos, et descendunt usque ad abyssos ; itemque, Posuerunt in cœlum os suum. Hinc proceritas arboris videbatur contingere cœlum. Et potestas tua in terminos universæ terræ orientalis, ubi rex iste monarchiam sortitus est ; vel, in universam terram, per hyperbolen, ad innuendum multitudinem provinciarum sibi subjectarum. Sic enim ad litteram in Isaia, de sola Babylone civitate Dominus loquitur, Visitabo super orbis mala : ut ibidem exponit Hieronymus. Et in Joanne Pharisæi dixerunt de Christo : Ecce totus mundus abiit post eum. Talibusque modis loquendi sacra Scriptura est plena. Idcirco de arbore dictum est : Adspectus illius in omnem terram. Et ubi Hieronymus transtulit, Adspectus ejus, Theodotion transtulit, Dominatio ejus.
1.en: Next he begins the explanation. [[4:17|The tree which thou sawest, which was high and strong|Arborem quam vidisti sublimem atque robustam]], that is, the likeness of such a tree presented to thee in sleep, [[4:17|whose height reached to the skies|cujus altitudo pertingit ad cœlum]], etc., [[4:19|It is thou, O king|tu es, rex]], by signification, not by essence: for by that appearance and that thing thou art designated, so that whatever is said of the state of that tree concerns thee; [[4:19|who art grown great|qui magnificatus es]] in power, riches, fame and glory, and in every worldly prosperity, [[4:19|and become mighty|et invaluisti]] upon the earth, by prevailing over thy enemies. Therefore that tree appeared high and strong: high, by royal dignity; strong, by the power of army and arms. [[4:19|for thy greatness|Et magnitudo tua]], not bodily but spiritual, namely majesty and excellence in reigning, [[4:19|hath grown|crevit]] by the number of thy subjects, [[4:19|and hath reached to heaven|et pervenit usque ad cœlum]], that is, to a very great exaltation and eminence: so that this saying is to be understood as a hyperbole, as is that in the Psalm, [[Ps 106:26|They mount up to the heavens, and they go down to the depths|Ascendunt usque ad cœlos, et descendunt usque ad abyssos]]; and again, [[Ps 72:9|They have set their mouth against heaven|Posuerunt in cœlum os suum]]. Hence the tallness of the tree seemed to touch heaven. [[4:19|and thy power unto the ends of the earth|Et potestas tua in terminos universæ terræ]], that is, of the eastern earth, where this king obtained the monarchy; or, unto the whole earth, by hyperbole, to suggest the multitude of provinces subject to him. For so, in the literal sense, the Lord speaks in Isaias of the single city of Babylon: [[Is 13:11|I will visit the evils of the world|Visitabo super orbis mala]], as Jerome explains in that place. And in John the Pharisees said of Christ: [[John 12:19|Behold, the whole world is gone after him|Ecce totus mundus abiit post eum]]. And holy Scripture is full of such ways of speaking. Therefore it was said of the tree: [[4:17|the sight thereof into all the earth|Adspectus illius in omnem terram]]. And where Jerome translated [[4:17|the sight thereof|Adspectus ejus]], Theodotion translated *The dominion thereof*.

1.t: Rursus, quod dictum est quod magnitudo regis hujus crevit et pervenit usque ad cœlum, intelligi potest de magnitudine suæ elationis ac præsumptionis : quæ usque ad Dei cœli crevit injuriam, cui iste quodammodo voluit similari, per se ipsum volens regnare, plenus ambitione ac fastu, quemadmodum in Isaia dixisse inducitur : In cœlum conscendam, supra astra Dei exaltabo solium meum.
1.en: Again, what was said, that the greatness of this king grew and reached to heaven, can be understood of the greatness of his pride and presumption, which grew even to the affront of the God of heaven, whom he in a manner wished to be like, wishing to reign by himself, full of ambition and arrogance; as in Isaias he is brought in as saying: [[Is 14:13|I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God|In cœlum conscendam, supra astra Dei exaltabo solium meum]].

1.t: Folia ejus, scilicet arboris hujus, pulcherrima : per quæ intelliguntur pretiosissima regis hujus ornamenta, ac multiplex apparatus, vel decus regni, verba atque edicta ; et fructus ejus nimius, id est, divitiarum copiam maximam rex possedit. Et esca universorum in ea : id est, de facultatibus regis ceteri sustentabantur, nec plus quam eis permisit aut contulit, habuerunt. Subter eam habitabant animalia et bestiæ commorantes : id est, rusticani, simplices et vulgares sub ejus potestate ac protectione degebant ; et in ramis ejus, id est altioribus officiis, locis seu dignitatibus ac delationibus potestatis regis istius, volucres cœli, id est nobiles et potentes instar avium alta petentes, leves, petulantes et garruli, conversabantur, tanquam regi quotidie adsistentes. Et ex ea vescebatur omnis caro : id est, omnis homo de regis opibus vescebatur, id solum habendo quod ipse dedit ceteris aut reliquit. Et ipsa distributio accommoda est, atque pro generibus singulorum potius quam pro singulis generum suscipienda.
1.en: [[4:9|Its leaves|Folia ejus]], namely of this tree, [[4:9|were most beautiful|pulcherrima]]: by which are understood the most precious ornaments of this king, and his manifold pomp, or the glory of the kingdom, its words and edicts; [[4:9|and its fruit exceeding much|et fructus ejus nimius]], that is, the king possessed a very great abundance of riches. [[4:9|and in it was food for all|Et esca universorum in ea]]: that is, the rest were sustained from the king's resources, and had no more than he allowed or bestowed on them. [[4:9|under it dwelt cattle and beasts|Subter eam habitabant animalia et bestiæ commorantes]]: that is, country folk, simple and common people lived under his power and protection; [[4:9|and in the branches thereof|et in ramis ejus]], that is, in the higher offices, places or dignities, and the grants of power of this king, [[4:9|the fowls of the air|volucres cœli]], that is, the nobles and the powerful, who like birds seek high places, fickle, wanton and garrulous, [[4:9|had their abode|conversabantur]], as attending on the king daily. [[4:9|and all flesh did eat of it|Et ex ea vescebatur omnis caro]]: that is, every man fed on the king's wealth, having only what he gave or left to the rest. And this distribution is fitting, and is to be taken for the kinds of individuals rather than for the individuals of the kinds [that is, *all flesh* means men of every kind and condition, not every single man].

1.t: Sicque Videbam in visione capitis mei, secundum sensum præhabitum, super stratum meum in somno, exterioribus sensibus quietatis. Et hic brevis est dictorum epilogus. Et quod subditur, est secunda pars somnii regis.
1.en: And thus: [[4:10|I saw in the vision of my head|Videbam in visione capitis mei]], in the sense given before, [[4:10|upon my bed|super stratum meum]] in sleep, the outward senses being at rest. And here is a brief epilogue of what has been said. And what is added next is the second part of the king's dream.

1.t: Ecce vigil et sanctus de cœlo descendit ; et clamavit fortiter, et sic ait. Per vigilem et sanctum, intelligit angelum nunquam dormientem, omnique terrena affectione et labe peccati carentem. Siquidem angeli rite vigiles appellantur, quia ad nostram custodiam, ad divini imperii exsecutionem, ad contemplandum Altissimi vultum, et ad ejus præconia vigilant atque intenti sunt incessanter. De quibus in Isaia habetur : Super muros tuos, Jerusalem, constitui custodes ; tota die et tota nocte in perpetuum non tacebunt. Vigil iste de cœlo descendit, missus a Rege superno, qui loquitur per Jeremiam : Vigilabo ego super verbum meum, ut faciam illud. Clamavitque fortiter : quia et ipse fortis est miles Principis summi, et omnipotentis Domini auctoritatem ac potestatem suo valenti insinuavit clamore. Qui tamen clamor non fuit exterior neque vocalis, sed interior, interiusque auditus per imaginarias repræsentationes, sicut in Apocalypsi Joannes perhibet se audisse voces, quasi tubarum et tonitruorum atque aquarum multarum ; quæ omnia solo interiori suscepit auditu, sicut ibidem exposui. Succidite arborem, et præcidite ramos ejus, et excutite folia ejus, etc.
1.en: [[4:10|behold a watcher, and a holy one came down from heaven|Ecce vigil et sanctus de cœlo descendit]]; [[4:11|He cried aloud, and said thus|et clamavit fortiter, et sic ait]]. By *a watcher and a holy one* he means an angel, who never sleeps and is free from every earthly affection and stain of sin. For the angels are rightly called watchers, because they keep watch and are unceasingly intent on guarding us, on carrying out the divine command, on contemplating the face of the Most High, and on his praises. Of them it is said in Isaias: [[Is 62:6|Upon thy walls, O Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen all the day, and all the night, they shall never hold their peace|Super muros tuos, Jerusalem, constitui custodes ; tota die et tota nocte in perpetuum non tacebunt]]. This watcher came down from heaven, sent by the King on high, who speaks through Jeremias: [[Jer 1:12|I will watch over my word to perform it|Vigilabo ego super verbum meum, ut faciam illud]]. And he cried aloud, because he too is a mighty soldier of the supreme Prince, and by his strong cry he made known the authority and power of the almighty Lord. Yet that cry was not outward or vocal, but inward, and heard inwardly through imaginary representations, as John in the Apocalypse relates that he heard voices as of trumpets and thunders and many waters[[Apoc 1:10||]][[Apoc 4:5||]][[Apoc 6:1||]][[Apoc 1:15||]][[Apoc 14:2||]]; all of which he received by inward hearing alone, as I explained there. [[4:11|Cut down the tree, and chop off the branches thereof: shake off its leaves|Succidite arborem, et præcidite ramos ejus, et excutite folia ejus]], etc.

1.t: Omnia ista ipsemet Daniel infra exposuit, dicendo : Quod autem vidit rex, Nabuchodonosor scilicet, vigilem et sanctum, utpote angelum, descendere de cœlo, et dicere. Omnia ista per imaginarias similitudines ostendebantur interiori visui regis imaginativo, per angelum qui similitudines istas formavit in interiori sensu Nabuchodonosor regis. Succidite arborem, o Chaldæi, et dissipate eam, etc.
1.en: All these things Daniel himself explains below, saying: [[4:20|And whereas the king saw|Quod autem vidit rex]], Nabuchodonosor namely, [[4:20|a watcher, and a holy one|vigilem et sanctum]], that is, an angel, [[4:20|come down from heaven, and say|descendere de cœlo, et dicere]]. All these things were shown by imaginary likenesses to the king's inward imaginative sight, through the angel who formed those likenesses in the inward sense of King Nabuchodonosor. [[4:20|Cut down the tree|Succidite arborem]], O Chaldeans, [[4:20|and destroy it|et dissipate eam]], etc.

1.t: Et vinciatur ferro et ære in herbis foris. Sicque superius dixit : Alligetur vinculo ferreo et æreo in herbis quæ foris sunt. Ex his verbis videri potest alicui, quod Nabuchodonosor tempore suæ amentiæ fuerit vinculatus atque inclusus. Quod et Hieronymus hoc loco sentire videtur. Nam ait : Quærunt a nobis qui historiæ contradicunt, quomodo in vinculo ferreo et æreo fuerit Nabuchodonosor, aut quis eum vinxerit et compedibus alligaverit. Quorum inquisitioni satisfaciens, subdit : Quum perspicuum sit, omnes furiosos, ne se præcipitent et alios invadant, ferreis catenis ligari. In quibus verbis innuitur, quod saltem vinctus exstiterat. Albertus quoque hæc verba, Vinciatur ferro et ære, exponens : Furiosi, inquit, ferreis catenis solent ligari, ut dicit Hieronymus. — Sed huic videtur obviare quod subditur, In herbis quæ foris sunt ; et quod fertur in textu, Et rore cœli conspergatur, et cum feris sit habitatio ejus ; et quod infra habetur, Fœnum ut bos comedes. Ex quibus consequitur, quod in agris seu pratis vel locis silvestribus inter bestias erat ac discurrebat. Quod item ex verbis Hieronymi sequi videtur, dum ait : Quis amentes homines non cernat instar brutorum in agris vivere locisque silvestribus?
1.en: [[4:20|and let it be bound with iron and brass, among the grass without|Et vinciatur ferro et ære in herbis foris]]. And so he said above: [[4:12|let it be tied with a band of iron and of brass, among the grass, that is without|Alligetur vinculo ferreo et æreo in herbis quæ foris sunt]]. From these words it may seem to someone that Nabuchodonosor, in the time of his madness, was chained and shut up. And Jerome seems to hold this in this place. For he says: Those who contradict the history ask us how Nabuchodonosor was in a band of iron and of brass, or who bound him and fastened him with fetters. And answering their inquiry, he adds: Since it is plain that all madmen are bound with iron chains, lest they throw themselves down headlong and attack others. In which words it is suggested that he was at least bound. Albert too, explaining these words, [[4:20|let it be bound with iron and brass|Vinciatur ferro et ære]]: Madmen, he says, are usually bound with iron chains, as Jerome says. But against this seems to stand what is added, [[4:12|among the grass, that is without|In herbis quæ foris sunt]]; and what is set down in the text, [[4:20|and let it be sprinkled with the dew of heaven|Et rore cœli conspergatur]], [[4:20|and let his feeding be with the wild beasts|et cum feris sit habitatio ejus]] [Denis reads *habitatio*, "dwelling"; the edition notes in the margin the reading *pabulum*, "feeding", which is that of the Vulgate]; and what is found below, [[4:22|thou shalt eat grass, as an ox|Fœnum ut bos comedes]]. From which it follows that he was among the beasts and roamed about in the fields or meadows or woodland places. And the same seems to follow from Jerome's words, when he says: Who does not see madmen living like brute beasts in the fields and in woodland places?

1.t: Hinc Lyra affirmat, quod non fuit ligatus neque inclusus tempore furiæ, quia per hoc infirmitas ejus fuisset aggravata : patet enim ad sensum, quod furiosi quum ligantur, magis infirmantur ; et sciebant ejus ministri ex revelatione Danielis, quod Nabuchodonosor in campis non moreretur, sed finaliter in regnum restitueretur. Et istud videtur probabile. Si enim ligatus fuisset et clausus, corpus ejus non fuisset nudum et rore perfusum. Unde quod dictum est, Alligetur vinculo ferreo, Lyra exponit : Id est, infirmitate inducta ex divina sententia, quæ infrangibilis est ; in herbis quæ foris sunt : quia tempore amentiæ habitavit in agris cum bestiis.
1.en: Hence Lyra affirms that he was not bound or shut up in the time of his madness, because by this his sickness would have been made worse: for it is plain to sense that madmen, when they are bound, grow sicker; and his ministers knew from Daniel's revelation that Nabuchodonosor would not die in the fields, but would in the end be restored to his kingdom. And this seems probable. For if he had been bound and shut up, his body would not have been naked and wet with dew. Hence what was said, [[4:12|let it be tied with a band of iron|Alligetur vinculo ferreo]], Lyra explains: That is, by a sickness brought on by the divine sentence, which cannot be broken; [[4:12|among the grass, that is without|in herbis quæ foris sunt]]: because in the time of his madness he dwelt in the fields with the beasts.

1.t: Albertus quoque expositorie ait super illud, Alligetur vinculo ferreo : Id est, tentatione durissima, quæ domet superbiam ejus. Et istæ expositiones litterales possunt consistere, quum juxta similem modum loquendi, Dominus dicat regi Assyriorum : Quum fureres adversum me, superbia tua ascendit in aures meas. Ponam ergo circulum in naribus tuis, et frenum in maxillis tuis. Quod de corporeis freno ac circulo intelligendum non est, sed de repressione suæ superbiæ, et refrenatione suæ blasphemiæ, per occisionem sui exercitus ab angelo sancto.
1.en: Albert too says by way of explanation on the words [[4:12|let it be tied with a band of iron|Alligetur vinculo ferreo]]: That is, by a most severe trial, to tame his pride. And these literal explanations can stand, since in a like manner of speaking the Lord says to the king of the Assyrians: [[Is 37:29|When thou wast mad against me, thy pride came up to my ears|Quum fureres adversum me, superbia tua ascendit in aures meas]]. [[Is 37:29|therefore I will put a ring in thy nose|Ponam ergo circulum in naribus tuis]], [[Is 37:29|and a bit|et frenum]] in thy jaws [Denis reads *in maxillis*, "in thy jaws"; the Vulgate has *in labiis*, "between thy lips"]. Which is not to be understood of a bodily bit and ring, but of the curbing of his pride and the bridling of his blasphemy, by the slaying of his army by the holy angel[[Is 37:36||]].

1.t: Verum non video cur Albertus præmemorata verba de tentatione seu punitione regi illata, magis exponat quam verba sequentia, scilicet, Vinciatur ferro et ære, quum verba ista prorsus ad idem pertineant. Sequens enim verbum, est resumptio præcedentis, ut litteram intuenti patescit. Insuper facile non apparet, quomodo verba Hieronymi sibi invicem consonent, nisi quis dicat quod Nabuchodonosor ad tempus, et forte in principio suæ insaniæ, fuerit vinculatus seu clausus, et postea ad consilium Danielis fuerit ad naturæ relevamen solutus. Aliqui quoque amentes partim ligantur, et incedere permittuntur : sicque ligantur, ne penitus liberum habeant manuum usum.
1.en: But I do not see why Albert should explain the words mentioned before of a trial or punishment inflicted on the king, rather than the words that follow, namely, [[4:20|let it be bound with iron and brass|Vinciatur ferro et ære]], since these words refer altogether to the same thing. For the later saying is a taking up again of the earlier, as is plain to anyone who looks at the letter. Moreover, it is not easy to see how Jerome's words agree with one another, unless one says that Nabuchodonosor was chained or shut up for a time, perhaps at the beginning of his madness, and afterwards, on Daniel's advice, was released for the relief of his nature. Some madmen, too, are partly bound and are allowed to walk about: they are bound in such a way that they do not have the full free use of their hands.

1.t: Hæc est interpretatio sententiæ altissimi Dei, quam per vigilem sanctum pronuntiavit, quæ pervenit ex divina justitia, super dominum meum regem, propter ejus demerita, præsertim ob ejus superbiam. Austeritatem interpretationis circumlinit suavitate verborum, vinum infundens et oleum.
1.en: [[4:21|This is the interpretation of the sentence of the most High|Hæc est interpretatio sententiæ altissimi]] God, which he pronounced through the holy watcher, [[4:21|which is come|quæ pervenit]] from the divine justice [[4:21|upon my lord, the king|super dominum meum regem]], for his demerits, above all for his pride. He coats the harshness of the interpretation with the sweetness of his words, pouring in wine and oil[[Luke 10:34||]].

1.t: Ejicient te ab hominibus, et cum bestiis ferisque erit habitatio tua. Quod qualiter factum sit, infra habetur in littera. Quum enim in amentiam versus esset, idque suis innotuisset ministris, eum tanquam insanum ejecerunt de regno, et ipse instar furentium hinc inde agitabatur. Et fœnum ut bos comedes. Ipse namque se bovem putavit, et illis se junxit, eorum vescens edulio : sicut videmus ad oculum furiosos bestialibus delectari, ex subversione imaginationis quam incurrerunt. Et rore cœli infunderis, id est humectaberis : quia, secundum Albertum, nudus erat.
1.en: [[4:22|They shall cast thee out from among men, and thy dwelling shall be with cattle, and with wild beasts|Ejicient te ab hominibus, et cum bestiis ferisque erit habitatio tua]]. How this was done is told below in the text. For when he had been turned to madness, and this had become known to his ministers, they cast him out of the kingdom as a madman, and he was driven hither and thither like raving men. [[4:22|and thou shalt eat grass, as an ox|Et fœnum ut bos comedes]]. For he thought himself an ox, and joined himself to them, feeding on their food: as we see with our own eyes that madmen take delight in beastly things, from the overturning of the imagination that has befallen them. [[4:22|and shalt be wet with the dew of heaven|Et rore cœli infunderis]], that is, thou shalt be moistened: because, according to Albert, he was naked.

1.t: Septem quoque tempora, id est septem anni, mutabuntur super te, id est, volventur et defluent, durante tua amentia, ita quod septem annis sic eris. Tempora quippe principaliter distinguuntur ad motum solis : ideo septem tempora, sunt septem anni. Hinc in Scripturis utriusque Testamenti, per tempus intelligitur annus ; per tempora, duo anni : sicut quum infra dicitur, In tempus et tempora et dimidium temporis. Et idem ordo verborum in Apocalypsi habetur. Donec scias per experientiam debitæ castigationis : scias, inquam, stabiliter ac perfecte, quod dominetur Excelsus, id est Deus altissimus, cujus respectu cuncta sunt bassa, super regnum hominum, id est, cunctis regnis, tanquam summus, primus, omnipotens dominator præsideat : juxta illud Psalmi, In manu ejus sunt omnes fines terræ ; et cuicumque voluerit, det illud, unum juste deponendo, alterum ad libitum promovendo.
1.en: [[4:22|and seven times|Septem quoque tempora]], that is, seven years, [[4:22|shall pass over thee|mutabuntur super te]], that is, shall roll on and flow by while thy madness lasts, so that thou shalt be thus for seven years. For times are distinguished chiefly by the motion of the sun: therefore seven times are seven years. Hence in the Scriptures of both Testaments a *time* is understood as a year, and *times* as two years: as when it is said below, [[Dan 12:7|unto a time, and times, and half a time|In tempus et tempora et dimidium temporis]]. And the same order of words is found in the Apocalypse[[Apoc 12:14||]]. [[4:22|till thou know|Donec scias]] by experience of due chastisement: know, I say, firmly and perfectly, [[4:22|that the most High ruleth|quod dominetur Excelsus]], that is, God most high, in comparison with whom all things are low, [[4:22|over the kingdom of men|super regnum hominum]], that is, that he presides over all kingdoms as the supreme, first and almighty ruler: according to that of the Psalm, [[Ps 94:4|in his hand are all the ends of the earth|In manu ejus sunt omnes fines terræ]]; [[4:22|and giveth it to whomsoever he will|et cuicumque voluerit, det illud]], justly putting down one and raising up another at his pleasure.

1.t: Quod autem vigil et sanctus præcepit, ut germen radicum ejus, id est arboris, relinqueretur : sic enim superius dixit, Attamen germen radicum ejus in terra dimittite : id (inquam) significat, quod regnum tuum tibi manebit, id est, te exspectabit, et illud recipies, postquam cognoveris, vexatione tibi intellectum præstante, et corde tuo per humilitatem ac supernam illuminationem disposito, potestatem esse cœlestem, id est, esse unam summam ac primam virtutem increatam et independentem, in cœlis regnantem, et terrestria moderantem, providentiam universorum habentem. Itaque per germen radicum arboris, designatur possibilitas redeundi ad regnum.
1.en: [[4:23|But whereas|Quod autem]] the watcher and holy one [[4:23|he commanded|præcepit]], [[4:23|that the stump of the roots thereof, that is, of the tree, should be left|ut germen radicum ejus, id est arboris, relinqueretur]] (for so he said above, [[4:20|but leave the stump of the roots thereof in the earth|Attamen germen radicum ejus in terra dimittite]] [the margin gives v. 12, which says the same; the words are those of v. 20]): that, I say, signifies that [[4:23|thy kingdom shall remain to thee|regnum tuum tibi manebit]], that is, shall await thee, and thou shalt receive it again, [[4:23|after thou shalt have known|postquam cognoveris]], affliction giving thee understanding, and thy heart being made ready by humility and heavenly enlightenment, [[4:23|that power is from heaven|potestatem esse cœlestem]], that is, that there is one supreme and first power, uncreated and independent, reigning in heaven and governing earthly things, having providence over all. So by the stump of the roots of the tree is signified the possibility of returning to the kingdom.

1.t: Nunc exponenda sunt quædam superius transilita. Succidite arborem, et præcidite ramos ejus, id est, regem Nabuchodonosor de regno propellite, et dilatationem sui imperii tollite. Et excutite folia ejus, id est, verba ejus magnifica et ornatum, ostendite vana, et dispergite fructus ejus, id est, opes ipsius auferte ab eo. Aliqui etiam dicunt, quod divitiæ regni Babylonici, durante regis insania, a pluribus rapiebantur. Et fugiant bestiæ quæ subter eam sunt, id est, subditi, inferiores, rusticani et simplices, de regis jugo recedant ; et volucres, id est divites, potentes, et in dignitatibus constituti, de ramis ejus, scilicet Nabuchodonosor, abeant, sub latitudine suæ potestatis non amplius se tuendo. Cor ejus ab humano commutetur, id est, mens seu ratio ejus ab aliorum mente varietur, ita quod in amentiam transferatur. Ratione enim a brutis secernimur : dum ergo usu rationis privamur, brutales efficimur. Et cor feræ detur ei, videlicet judicio rationis nudato.
1.en: Now some things passed over above are to be explained. [[4:11|Cut down the tree, and chop off the branches thereof|Succidite arborem, et præcidite ramos ejus]], that is, drive King Nabuchodonosor out of his kingdom, and take away the breadth of his empire. [[4:11|shake off its leaves|Et excutite folia ejus]], that is, show his grand words and his adornment to be vain, [[4:11|and scatter its fruits|et dispergite fructus ejus]], that is, take his wealth away from him. Some also say that the riches of the Babylonian kingdom, while the king's madness lasted, were plundered by many. [[4:11|let the beasts fly away that are under it|Et fugiant bestiæ quæ subter eam sunt]], that is, let the subjects, the lower sort, the country folk and the simple, withdraw from the king's yoke; [[4:11|and the birds|et volucres]], that is, the rich, the powerful and those set in dignities, [[4:11|from its branches|de ramis ejus]], that is, of Nabuchodonosor, let them go away, no longer sheltering under the breadth of his power. [[4:13|Let his heart be changed from man's|Cor ejus ab humano commutetur]], that is, let his mind or reason be made different from the mind of others, so that it is turned into madness. For by reason we are set apart from the brutes: when therefore we are deprived of the use of reason, we become brutish. [[4:13|and let a beast's heart be given him|Et cor feræ detur ei]], that is, once it is stripped of the judgement of reason.

1.t: In sententia vigilum, id est per sententiam promulgatam per angelos, decretum est, id est, divinitus ordinatum est sic fieri : ita quod institutio seu ordinatio Dei per sententiam angelorum, innotuit mundo de regis hujus punitione præfata. Et licet unus vigil seu angelus verba inducta clamaverit, alii tamen consenserunt, aut executioni sententiæ cooperati sunt. Porro qui die ac nocte, quantum natura permittit, sanctis instant vigiliis, Dei laudibus aut actibus virtuosis vacando, cœlestium vigilum agilitatem sectantur. Hinc ait Hieronymus : Nos quoque crebris pernoctationibus imitamur officia angelorum. Et Christus in Evangelio : Beatus, inquit, servus ille, quem, quum venerit dominus ejus, et pulsaverit januam ejus, invenerit vigilantem ; et rursus, Vigilate itaque, quia nescitis qua hora Dominus vester venturus sit.
1.en: [[4:14|by the sentence of the watchers|In sententia vigilum]], that is, by the sentence promulgated by the angels, [[4:14|This is the decree|decretum est]], that is, it has been divinely ordained that it be so: so that the institution or ordinance of God concerning the punishment of this king, foretold above, was made known to the world through the sentence of the angels. And though one watcher or angel cried out the words given, the others nevertheless agreed, or worked together in carrying out the sentence. Further, those who by day and by night, as far as nature allows, keep holy vigils, giving themselves to the praises of God or to virtuous acts, follow the alertness of the heavenly watchers. Hence Jerome says: We too, by frequent night watches, imitate the offices of the angels. And Christ in the Gospel: Blessed, he says, is that servant whom his lord, when he shall come and knock at his door, shall find watching[[Luke 12:37||]] [Denis's wording joins Luke 12:36–37, in the singular as in Matt 24:46]; and again, [[Matt 24:42|Watch ye therefore, because you know not what hour your Lord will come|Vigilate itaque, quia nescitis qua hora Dominus vester venturus sit]].

1.t: Et sermo sanctorum : id est, eorum qui divinæ æquitati consentiunt in supernis, sermo et verbum est ut taliter fiat ; et petitio eorumdem. Sancti namque expostulant ultionem contra malignos, et Dei omnipotentiam in impiorum justa dejectione declarari precantur, juxta illud Apocalypsis : Usquequo, Domine (sanctus et verus), non judicas, et non vindicas sanguinem nostrum de his qui sunt in terra ?
